  • Mail from every sending service, including third-party senders, is DKIM signed with a key aligned to the From domain.
  • Keys are at least 1024-bit RSA, preferably 2048-bit, and unused selectors are revoked.
  • Keys are rotated on a defined schedule.

Record: domain, selectors, key sizes and signing coverage, taken from real message headers; passing means all legitimate mail is signed with strong keys.

items.title: DMARC policy
items.description:
DMARC tells receivers what to do with mail that fails SPF and DKIM alignment, and gives the client reports on who sends as them.

  • Every domain, including parked and non-sending domains, publishes a DMARC record.
  • The policy is quarantine or reject, not none, and the subdomain policy is as strict.
  • Aggregate reports go to a monitored address.

Record: domain, policy, subdomain policy and reporting address; passing means reject, or quarantine with a dated move to reject, with reports read.

items.title: MTA-STS and TLS-RPT
items.description:
MTA-STS tells sending servers to require TLS with a valid certificate when delivering to the client; TLS-RPT reports delivery failures.

  • An MTA-STS TXT record exists and its policy file is served over HTTPS from the mta-sts host.
  • The policy is in enforce mode, lists every MX host and has a sensible max age.
  • A TLS-RPT record sends reports to a monitored address, and every MX presents a valid certificate.

Record: records, policy mode and MX certificate status; passing means enforce mode with valid certificates and reporting.

items.title: Mail server configuration
items.description:
Internet-facing mail servers can be misused to relay spam or to confirm valid addresses.

  • No server relays mail from external senders to external recipients.
  • Every MX offers STARTTLS with a valid certificate.
  • VRFY and EXPN are disabled, and recipient checks reveal as little as the mail design allows.
  • Banners disclose no internal host names or versions.

Record: server, check and response; passing means no open relay, TLS offered and no address disclosure.

items.title: Web servers, default content and directory listing
items.description:
Default installations leave sample applications, status pages and listings that disclose information or offer an easy way in.

  • No default pages, sample applications or installer remnants remain.
  • Directory listing is off, and server status or diagnostic pages are not public.
  • Backup, old and temporary files are not reachable.

Record: URL, what it exposes and why it matters; passing means only intended content is served.

items.title: HTTP methods, headers and error handling
items.description:
Response details reveal software versions and internals that sharpen other attacks.

  • Server, framework and proxy headers do not disclose exact versions.
  • Unneeded methods (TRACE, PUT, DELETE, WebDAV) are disabled.
  • Error pages are generic, with no stack traces, file paths or internal addresses.

Record: host, header or method and what it disclosed; passing means minimal disclosure and only needed methods.

items.title: Origin servers reachable around a CDN or WAF
items.description:
If the origin behind a CDN or web application firewall accepts direct connections, those protections can be bypassed entirely.

  • Candidate origin addresses are identified from historical DNS, certificate data, mail records and other in-scope hosts.
  • The origin accepts connections only from the CDN's published ranges or through authenticated origin pulls.
  • Direct requests return no application content.

Record: origin address and evidence of direct access; passing means the origin is reachable only through the CDN.

items.title: Publicly exposed storage
items.description:
Storage buckets and containers set for public access are a common cause of data exposure.

  • Storage linked to the client from DNS, web content and code allows no anonymous listing, reading or writing.
  • Provider-level public access blocks are enabled where offered.
  • Exposed objects are reported after minimal access, without downloading bulk data.

Record: resource, provider, permission and a description of the content type; passing means no anonymous access.

items.title: Exposed source code and repositories
items.description:
Public repositories and leftover version control folders can disclose source, credentials and internal design.

  • Web roots expose no version control metadata (.git or .svn folders) or build artefacts.
  • Public repositories belonging to the client, where in scope, hold no secrets in current files or history.
  • Any exposed credential is reported for immediate revocation and not used beyond the rules of engagement.

Record: location, type of secret and age; passing means no secrets or internal code are public.

items.title: Information exposed in public sources
items.description:
Public information shapes phishing, password guessing and targeting, so it is assessed within what the rules of engagement allow.

  • Staff names, roles and the email address format discoverable from public sources are noted.
  • Published documents are checked for metadata revealing user names, software and internal paths.
  • Breach exposure of client domains is checked only through approved sources, without keeping passwords.

Record: category of information and source, with no personal detail beyond need; passing means exposure is known and minimal.

items.title: Internal detail leaked by services
items.description:
Services often leak internal host names, addresses and domain names that help an attacker map the inside.

  • HTTP headers, redirects and error pages include no internal addresses or host names.
  • Services offering NTLM authentication do not reveal internal domain and host names.
  • Certificates and mail headers do not reveal internal naming.

Record: source and information disclosed; passing means no internal detail leaks.

items.title: IPv6 exposure
items.description:
Hosts with IPv6 addresses may expose services that are filtered on IPv4, because firewall rules are often written for one protocol.

  • AAAA records for in-scope names are listed and the IPv6 ranges are agreed in scope.
  • The service inventory is repeated over IPv6 and compared with IPv4.
  • Differences in filtering or TLS configuration between the two are reported.

Record: IPv6 address, services and differences from IPv4; passing means identical exposure on both.

items.title: Services usable for reflection and amplification
items.description:
UDP services that send large replies to small, spoofable requests can be turned against third parties in denial of service attacks.

  • No open recursive DNS, NTP answering monitoring queries, SNMP v1 or v2c, SSDP, memcached over UDP, CLDAP or chargen is reachable.
  • Checks use single, small requests only, with no volume testing.
  • Replies much larger than the request are noted with the ratio seen.

Record: address, service and amplification observed; passing means no reflective UDP service is exposed.

items.title: Validation of findings before reporting
items.description:
Scanner output is a lead, not a finding; NIST SP 800-115 section 4.3 warns of false positives and inconsistent product risk ratings.

  • Each candidate issue is confirmed with direct evidence from this environment.
  • Severity reflects the client's exposure, not the scanner's default rating.
  • False positives and unconfirmed issues are recorded separately.

Record: evidence and validation method per finding; passing means every reported issue is reproducible.

phase_cloud_v2.name: Cloud Configuration Review
phase_cloud_v2.description: Coverage tracker for a cloud configuration review of AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, from scope and provider rules through identity, logging, data, network, compute and organisation guardrails. Check each item for every provider in scope using the named service or setting, and record each deviation from the agreed CIS Benchmark with its evidence.

items.title: Accounts, subscriptions and projects in scope
items.description:
Fixes which estate is reviewed, so findings map to owners and nothing is tested without permission.

  • AWS accounts and OUs, Azure tenant, management groups and subscriptions, Google Cloud organisation, folders and projects are listed by ID.
  • Regions in use are known, including any the client thinks are unused.
  • Read-only review access is granted and limited to that estate.

Record: signed scope with IDs and access method; pass when every in-scope container was enumerated.

items.title: Provider penetration testing rules checked
items.description:
Keeps the work inside each provider's published testing rules.

  • AWS: only services in its penetration testing policy, and none of its prohibited activities (DoS, Route 53 zone walking).
  • Azure: the Microsoft Cloud Unified Penetration Testing Rules of Engagement apply; own tenant only.
  • Google Cloud: no notice needed; the Acceptable Use Policy applies and tests touch only the client's projects.

Record: policies read and any approvals; pass when no planned test falls outside them.

items.title: CIS Benchmark and baseline agreed
items.description:
Sets a named, versioned yardstick for judging each deviation.

  • The CIS Foundations Benchmark for each provider, its version and Level 1 or 2 profile are agreed.
  • Any extra baseline, such as the Microsoft cloud security benchmark or a client standard, is named.
  • Native posture tool output is treated as a lead and confirmed by hand before reporting.

Record: benchmarks, versions and profile; pass when every finding cites a recommendation or client requirement.

items.title: AWS root user protected
items.description:
IAM policies cannot limit the root user, so one stolen root credential means total control of an account.

  • Root has MFA (FIDO security key preferred) and no access keys.
  • Root sign-ins are rare, monitored and alerted on.
  • Member accounts use centralised root access with root credentials removed, where adopted.
  • Root email is a business-managed group address; recovery is restricted.

Record: credential report per account; pass when root has MFA, no keys and no routine use.

items.title: Microsoft Entra Global Administrators and privileged roles
items.description:
Entra roles control the tenant and, through elevation, every Azure subscription.

  • Fewer than five Global Administrators; privileged roles are eligible through PIM, not permanent.
  • Privileged accounts are cloud-only, not synchronised from on-premises AD.
  • Two cloud-only emergency access accounts use phishing-resistant MFA and alert on every sign-in.

Record: role holder counts, PIM settings and emergency account controls; pass when standing privilege is minimal.

items.title: Azure elevated access and root scope assignments
items.description:
A Global Administrator can elevate to User Access Administrator at root scope, reaching every subscription.

  • No unexplained standing assignments exist at root scope (/) or the tenant root management group.
  • Elevated access is removed after use, and each use alerts.
  • Owner, User Access Administrator and Role Based Access Control Administrator at management group scope are few.

Record: assignments at root and management group scope; pass when none is unexplained.

items.title: Google Cloud super administrators and organisation administrators
items.description:
Cloud Identity or Workspace super administrators can take over the Google Cloud organisation.

  • Super administrator accounts are few, dedicated and not used for daily Google Cloud work.
  • They use 2-Step Verification with security keys and recovery options the organisation controls.
  • Organisation Administrator and other organisation-level roles go to a small named group.

Record: role holders and their sign-in controls; pass when access is minimal and strongly protected.

items.title: MFA and sign-in policy for human users
items.description:
Phishing-resistant MFA on every human identity is the main control against reused or phished passwords.

  • AWS: any IAM user with a console password has MFA; people ideally sign in through IAM Identity Center.
  • Azure: Conditional Access requires MFA for all users; mandatory MFA for Azure management is in force.
  • Google Cloud: 2-Step Verification is enforced for everyone with access.

Record: users without MFA and policies that apply; pass when no human can sign in with a password alone.

items.title: Federation and single sign-on for the workforce
items.description:
With federated sign-in, the identity provider and each cloud's trust settings decide who gets in.

  • The identity provider's MFA, conditional access and leaver process cover every route into each cloud.
  • Local cloud users that bypass single sign-on are limited to documented emergency accounts.
  • SAML or OIDC trusts map only intended groups to privileged roles.

Record: trusts, group to role mappings and bypass accounts; pass when all human access is through the governed provider.

items.title: Long-lived keys and service credentials
items.description:
Static keys leak through code, pipeline logs and laptops, and they skip MFA.

  • AWS: IAM user access keys are absent, or rotated with unused keys removed.
  • Google Cloud: service account key creation and upload are disabled by organisation policy, or each key is justified.
  • Azure: app secrets and certificates expire soon; managed identities replace secrets where possible.

Record: each credential with age, last use and owner; pass when none is stale, unowned or over-privileged.

items.title: Broad and unused permissions
items.description:
Over-broad grants turn any compromised identity into wide access across the estate.

  • AWS: AdministratorAccess and all-actions policies sit with few roles; unused access is reviewed.
  • Azure: Owner and Contributor at subscription or management group scope are few; custom roles avoid wildcards.
  • Google Cloud: basic roles (Owner, Editor) are not granted on projects, folders or the organisation.

Record: principals with administrative rights per container and why; pass when each is needed.

items.title: Privilege escalation paths in AWS IAM
items.description:
Some IAM permissions let a non-administrator grant themselves more access.

  • Non-admins cannot create policy versions, attach or put policies, or edit role trust policies.
  • iam:PassRole is scoped to named roles and services, so privileged roles cannot go to new compute.
  • Creating keys or console passwords for other users is restricted; permissions boundaries cover delegation.

Record: each path as principal, permission and resulting access; pass when none leads to higher privilege.

items.title: Privilege escalation paths in Azure RBAC and Entra ID
items.description:
Rights to assign roles or add app credentials can become broad control.

  • Rights to assign roles (Owner, User Access Administrator, Role Based Access Control Administrator) are rare and conditioned.
  • Privileged apps and service principals have no owners outside the admin group, as owners can add secrets.
  • Entra roles managing apps or authentication methods are held by named admins.

Record: escalation paths and holders; pass when no lower-privileged user can gain higher rights.

items.title: Privilege escalation paths in Google Cloud IAM
items.description:
Service account impersonation and policy editing can let a user act above their granted privilege.

  • Service Account User and Service Account Token Creator are granted per service account, not per project.
  • No user can impersonate, or edit the allow policy of, a service account more privileged than themselves.
  • Rights to set IAM policy on projects, folders or the organisation belong to administrators.

Record: impersonation chains and policy editors; pass when no chain raises privilege.

items.title: Cross-account, cross-tenant and external trust
items.description:
Trust given to outside identities is easy to miss and invites third-party compromise.

  • AWS: role trusts name specific accounts, use an external ID for third parties and never trust all principals.
  • Azure: guests, multi-tenant apps and Azure Lighthouse delegations hold only agreed access.
  • Google Cloud: domain restricted sharing limits members to the organisation's domains.

Record: each external trust with partner, rights and purpose; pass when every one is known and least privilege.

items.title: Workload and managed identities
items.description:
Code running on a resource can use its attached identity, so its rights set the blast radius.

  • AWS instance profiles, Lambda execution roles and task roles carry only the actions needed.
  • Azure managed identities are scoped to the resources used, not whole subscriptions.
  • Google Cloud default service accounts are unused and lack Editor; automatic grants are disabled by policy.

Record: attached identities with effective rights; pass when none has administrative or estate-wide access.

items.title: Workload identity federation for pipelines and external workloads
items.description:
Keyless federation is only as safe as its trust conditions, which are often too broad.

  • Pipeline OIDC trusts restrict issuer, audience and subject to the expected repository and branch.
  • Google Cloud pools use attribute conditions; AWS and Entra trusts check the subject claim.
  • Roles reachable through federation are least privilege; production roles need protected branches.

Record: each trust with conditions and reachable roles; pass when only the intended workload gets credentials.

items.title: Control plane audit logging
items.description:
Management-plane logs record who changed what; without them an incident cannot be investigated.

  • AWS: an organisation or multi-Region CloudTrail trail records management events in every account.
  • Azure: Activity Log and Entra sign-in and audit logs are exported to retained storage.
  • Google Cloud: Admin Activity audit logs reach central storage through an organisation-level sink.

Record: logging set-up per account, subscription and project; pass when none lacks control plane logging.

items.title: Data access and service logging
items.description:
Control plane logs miss data reads, so sensitive stores need access logging to show what was taken.

  • AWS: CloudTrail data events or server access logging cover buckets with sensitive data.
  • Azure: diagnostic settings send Key Vault, Storage and database logs to the central workspace.
  • Google Cloud: Data Access audit logs are on for sensitive services such as Cloud Storage and Cloud KMS.

Record: sensitive stores and their access logging; pass when each logs reads and writes.

items.title: Log integrity, retention and separation
items.description:
Logs that the people being audited can alter or delete cannot support an investigation.

  • CloudTrail log file integrity validation is on, with logs in a separate log archive account.
  • Azure and Google Cloud log stores use immutability or locked retention, outside workload subscriptions or projects.
  • Retention meets the agreed period; stopping logging is blocked or alerts.

Record: log stores, retention and who can delete; pass when workload admins cannot remove evidence.

items.title: Alerting on security-relevant changes
items.description:
Logs only help if someone is told when a high-risk change happens.

  • Alerts fire on root or emergency account use, sign-in without MFA, and IAM policy or role assignment changes.
  • Changes to logging, network rules, key policies and guardrails also alert.
  • Alerts reach a monitored queue with an owner and are not routinely suppressed.

Record: alert rules mapped to these events, with a recent firing of each; pass when every class is covered.

items.title: Threat detection services
items.description:
Native detection catches misuse that configuration review cannot see.

  • AWS: GuardDuty runs in every account and Region, with relevant protection plans.
  • Azure: Microsoft Defender for Cloud plans match the workloads, such as servers, storage and Key Vault.
  • Google Cloud: Security Command Center runs at a tier with threat detection for the organisation.

Record: coverage, open high-severity findings and suppressions; pass when coverage is complete and findings triaged.

items.title: Configuration recording, inventory and drift
items.description:
An accurate inventory and change history show what exists and when it drifted.

  • AWS Config records all supported resources in every Region in use, aggregated centrally.
  • Azure Resource Graph with Azure Policy compliance, and Google Cloud Asset Inventory, cover the estate.
  • Infrastructure as code is the source of truth, and drift from it is detected and reviewed.

Record: inventory sources and unmanaged resources; pass when the inventory matches what was enumerated.

items.title: Public object storage
items.description:
Publicly readable buckets and containers remain a leading cause of cloud data exposure.

  • AWS: S3 Block Public Access is on at account level, no bucket policy grants all principals and ACLs are off.
  • Azure: anonymous blob access is disallowed on every storage account.
  • Google Cloud: public access prevention is enforced, with no allUsers or allAuthenticatedUsers grants.

Record: public stores with the data types exposed (sampled, not copied); pass when nothing is public without need.

items.title: Storage keys, shared access signatures and signed URLs
items.description:
Storage bearer tokens work for whoever holds them, so scope and lifetime matter as much as IAM.

  • Azure: Shared Key authorisation is disallowed where possible; SAS tokens are short-lived user delegation SAS.
  • AWS presigned URLs and Google Cloud signed URLs are short-lived and not stored in code or tickets.
  • Google Cloud HMAC keys for Cloud Storage are inventoried, owned and rotated.

Record: long-lived or broad tokens and where found; pass when tokens are short-lived and scoped.

items.title: Storage network restrictions and secure transfer
items.description:
Network rules limit who can reach data even after a credential leaks.

  • Azure storage accounts disable public network access or deny by default, require secure transfer and TLS 1.2.
  • S3 bucket policies on sensitive buckets deny requests not sent over TLS.
  • Google Cloud projects with sensitive data sit in VPC Service Controls perimeters where required.

Record: stores reachable from any network and transport settings; pass when sensitive stores are restricted and TLS-only.

items.title: Encryption at rest and customer-managed keys
items.description:
Default encryption covers most services, so look for gaps and key policy breaches.

  • EBS encryption by default is on in every Region in use; RDS and other stores are encrypted.
  • Azure disks, storage and databases use platform or customer-managed keys as policy requires.
  • Google Cloud resources needing CMEK use Cloud KMS keys, enforced by organisation policy where required.

Record: unencrypted resources and key policy gaps; pass when all data at rest meets the agreed standard.

items.title: Key management services
items.description:
Whoever controls the keys controls the data, so key access, rotation and deletion are reviewed directly.

  • AWS KMS key policies separate admins from users and never allow all principals; rotation is on.
  • Azure Key Vault has soft delete and purge protection, uses Azure RBAC and limits public access.
  • Google Cloud KMS keys have a rotation period and no public IAM bindings.

Record: key policies and settings per store; pass when access is least privilege and no one person can destroy keys.

items.title: TLS on public endpoints and load balancers
items.description:
Public listeners set the protocol and cipher strength clients get, often per load balancer or service.

  • AWS load balancer listeners use HTTPS with a current security policy; HTTP redirects to HTTPS.
  • Azure App Service, Functions and gateways enforce HTTPS only with TLS 1.2 or later.
  • Google Cloud load balancers use an SSL policy with the MODERN or RESTRICTED profile.

Record: endpoints and TLS policies; pass when none accepts deprecated protocols or plain HTTP for sensitive data.

items.title: Security groups, NSGs and firewall rules open to the internet
items.description:
Inbound rules from any address to admin or data ports are a leading route into cloud workloads.

  • No security group, NSG or VPC firewall rule allows 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 to SSH, RDP, database or management ports.
  • No rule allows all ports or all protocols from the internet.
  • AWS default security groups allow no traffic; Google Cloud default network rules are removed.

Record: each open rule with port, source and attached resources; pass when exposure matches documented intent.

items.title: Remote administration paths
items.description:
Brokered, identity-aware access avoids exposing SSH or RDP and logs every session.

  • Admins use Session Manager, Azure Bastion or just-in-time VM access, or IAP TCP forwarding with OS Login.
  • Instances have no public IP address without a documented need.
  • Session access requires MFA and sessions are logged.

Record: how admins reach instances and any direct exposure; pass when administration uses a brokered, logged path.

items.title: Internet-facing services match intent
items.description:
Comparing what configuration exposes with what the client thinks is public finds forgotten endpoints.

  • Public IPs, internet-facing load balancers, API gateways and platform endpoints are listed from configuration.
  • Each has an owner, is expected and is covered by external testing.
  • DNS records pointing at released cloud resources (dangling records) are flagged for removal.

Record: the exposure list with owners and surprises; pass when every public endpoint is known and intended.

items.title: Network flow and DNS logging
items.description:
Flow and DNS logs show which hosts talked to what, needed to scope an incident or spot data leaving.

  • AWS VPC Flow Logs and Route 53 Resolver query logging are on for VPCs in scope.
  • Azure uses virtual network flow logs; NSG flow logs can no longer be created and retire on 30 September 2027.
  • Google Cloud VPC Flow Logs are on for subnets with sensitive or internet traffic.

Record: networks with and without flow logging, and retention; pass when in-scope networks are covered.

items.title: Private endpoints and service perimeters for platform services
items.description:
Private paths keep platform service traffic off the internet.

  • Azure platform resources with sensitive data use private endpoints with public network access off.
  • AWS VPC endpoints carry traffic to sensitive services, with endpoint policies limiting access.
  • Google Cloud Private Service Connect or VPC Service Controls keep managed-service access inside boundaries.

Record: sensitive services reachable publicly; pass when only private paths or explicit allow lists reach them.

items.title: Instance metadata service protections
items.description:
The metadata service issues workload credentials, so request forgery can become cloud access.

  • AWS: IMDSv2 is required (HttpTokens required), including the account default, with a suitable hop limit.
  • Azure: IMDS needs the Metadata: true header and rejects X-Forwarded-For; apps never relay user requests to it.
  • Google Cloud: metadata requests need the Metadata-Flavor: Google header.

Record: instances allowing IMDSv1 and request forgery paths found; pass when tokens are enforced.

items.title: Public images, snapshots and disk exports
items.description:
Shared images and snapshots often carry data, keys and credentials from their source systems.

  • AWS block public access for AMIs and EBS snapshots is on; no RDS snapshot is public.
  • Azure disk and snapshot network access policies block export from any network; gallery images are not public.
  • Google Cloud images and snapshots grant nothing to allUsers or allAuthenticatedUsers.

Record: public or externally shared images or snapshots with owners; pass when none goes beyond agreed accounts.

items.title: Secrets in user data, custom data and start-up scripts
items.description:
Bootstrap data is readable by anyone who can view instance settings or reach metadata, so it must hold no secrets.

  • EC2 user data, Azure custom data and Custom Script Extension public settings, and Compute Engine startup scripts hold no secrets.
  • Google Cloud project-wide metadata, including SSH keys, does not grant broad access.
  • Bootstrap secrets come from a secrets manager at run time.

Record: resources whose bootstrap data holds secrets, with type (redacted); pass when none do.

items.title: Serverless function exposure and permissions
items.description:
Functions are easily published without authentication or with broad roles.

  • Lambda function URLs use AWS_IAM auth unless meant to be public; no policy lets anyone invoke.
  • Azure Functions HTTP triggers are not anonymous for sensitive work; settings use Key Vault references.
  • Cloud Run services and functions grant the invoker role to allUsers only when public by design.

Record: public functions, role rights and secrets in settings; pass when each is authenticated or public by design.

items.title: Container registries and container services
items.description:
Registries hold the images every workload runs; container services hold identities and secrets.

  • ECR, Azure Container Registry and Artifact Registry repositories are private; the ACR admin user is disabled.
  • Image vulnerability scanning is on and findings are acted on.
  • ECS tasks, Azure Container Apps and Cloud Run avoid privileged settings and plain-text secrets in variables.

Record: registry access, scan coverage and service findings; pass when all are private and least privilege.

items.title: Managed databases
items.description:
Managed databases hold the most sensitive data and are often internet-reachable.

  • RDS is not publicly accessible; Azure SQL has public access off or tight rules, and allow Azure services is off.
  • Cloud SQL public IP instances have no 0.0.0.0/0 authorised network and require TLS or the Auth Proxy.
  • Identity-based sign-in is used where supported; deletion protection and backups are on.

Record: database endpoints, network rules and sign-in modes; pass when none is open to the internet.

items.title: Secrets management services
items.description:
Secrets belong in a managed store with per-secret access and rotation, not in code or pipelines.

  • Secrets Manager, Key Vault and Secret Manager hold application secrets, with access granted per secret or vault.
  • Rotation is set for database and service credentials where supported.
  • No secrets sit in tags, plain environment variables, IaC state or shared pipeline variables.

Record: stores, access grants and secrets found elsewhere; pass when secrets are central, scoped and rotated.

items.title: Backups and recovery protection
items.description:
Ransomware operators and insiders target backups first, so backups must survive a compromised admin.

  • AWS Backup vaults use Vault Lock and copy to a separate account or Region.
  • Azure Backup uses immutable vaults, soft delete and multi-user authorisation through Resource Guard.
  • Google Cloud uses backup vaults with enforced retention; restores are tested everywhere.

Record: backup scope, immutability and last restore test; pass when one compromised account cannot delete every copy.

items.title: Organisation-level guardrails
items.description:
Top-level preventive policies stop risky changes, even by account admins.

  • AWS SCPs block disabling CloudTrail, GuardDuty or Config, leaving the organisation, and unapproved Regions.
  • Azure Policy at management group scope denies key risks such as public storage.
  • Google Cloud policies enforce domain restricted sharing, public access prevention and no service account keys.

Record: guardrails, scope and exceptions; pass when key risks are blocked by policy.

phase_mobile_v2.name: Mobile Application Testing (OWASP MASVS)
phase_mobile_v2.description: Coverage tracker for a mobile phase with one item for each OWASP MASVS v2 control in the standard's order, each naming the areas the matching OWASP MASTG tests and MASWE weaknesses cover on Android and iOS. Tick a control once both platforms in scope are checked, and judge the MASVS-RESILIENCE controls against the agreed risk profile.

items.title: MASVS-STORAGE-1 Secure storage of sensitive data
items.description:
MASTG tests cover private and shared storage, preferences, databases and keystores.

  • Android: preferences, databases, DataStore and files hold no clear-text secrets; none on external storage.
  • iOS: files use a fitting Data Protection class; secrets sit in the Keychain with strict accessibility.
  • Encryption keys live in the Android Keystore or iOS Keychain, not in the app package.

Record: stores, data found and protection; pass when sensitive data is platform-encrypted or not stored.

items.title: MASVS-STORAGE-2 Prevention of sensitive data leaks
items.description:
MASTG tests cover leaks through logs, backups, keyboard caches, notifications and third-party SDKs.

  • Release builds write no tokens, credentials or personal data to Logcat or iOS unified logging.
  • Sensitive files are excluded from backups (Android backup rules, iOS backup exclusion).
  • Sensitive fields disable keyboard caching; data reaches no SDK or notification without need.

Record: each leak with channel and data type; pass when nothing sensitive reaches logs, backups or caches.

items.title: MASVS-CRYPTO-1 Strong, current cryptography
items.description:
MASTG tests cover broken ciphers and modes, weak hashes, insecure randomness and IV reuse.

  • No DES, 3DES, RC4, ECB mode, MD5 or SHA-1 in security functions.
  • Keys, IVs and tokens use a secure random source (SecureRandom, SecRandomCopyBytes), never a seeded or predictable one.
  • IVs are not reused, and Android code does not force an outdated security provider.

Record: algorithms, modes and random sources with code locations; pass when only current primitives are used correctly.

items.title: MASVS-CRYPTO-2 Key management
items.description:
MASTG tests cover hard-coded keys, key size, single-purpose keys and keystore use.

  • No keys are hard-coded in code or bundled files.
  • Keys are generated in the Android Keystore or iOS Keychain or Secure Enclave, with adequate size and one purpose each.
  • Key use requires user authentication or an unlocked device where the data warrants it.

Record: keys found, where they are made and kept, and their limits; pass when keys are platform-protected and fit for purpose.

items.title: MASVS-AUTH-1 Secure authentication and authorisation protocols
items.description:
The back end enforces access, but the app must use protocols correctly; MASTG tests cover component access control.

  • Sign-in uses a standard flow such as OAuth 2.0 with PKCE in the system browser, not a WebView.
  • Session tokens expire, are revoked at logout and are checked server-side on every request.
  • Exported components such as Android content providers enforce authorisation.

Record: protocol, token handling and server checks; pass when the back end enforces every decision.

items.title: MASVS-AUTH-2 Secure local authentication
items.description:
MASTG tests cover event-bound biometrics, fallback, enrolment changes and key validity.

  • Android: BiometricPrompt uses a CryptoObject tied to a Keystore key that needs fresh authentication.
  • iOS: Keychain items use biometric access control, not only a LocalAuthentication result.
  • Keys are invalidated on new enrolment; passcode fallback is blocked for sensitive actions.

Record: implementation and bypass results per platform; pass when unlock needs a key released by authentication.

items.title: MASVS-AUTH-3 Additional authentication for sensitive operations
items.description:
Payments, credential changes and similar actions need step-up authentication. MASWE covers step-up, data after logout and non-repudiation.

  • Sensitive actions need re-authentication or a second factor, checked by the back end.
  • After logout or expiry, sensitive data and screens are no longer reachable.
  • Critical actions are signed or logged so they cannot plausibly be denied.

Record: sensitive operations and the extra check each needs; pass when none completes on the base session alone.

items.title: MASVS-NETWORK-1 Secure network traffic
items.description:
MASTG tests cover cleartext settings, HTTP URLs, TLS versions, hostname checks, user CAs and raw sockets.

  • Android: Network Security Configuration blocks cleartext and user CAs; no TrustManager accepts all.
  • iOS: ATS has no broad (NSAllowsArbitraryLoads) or weak TLS exceptions; no delegate accepts bad certificates.
  • All traffic seen, SDKs and WebViews included, is TLS 1.2 or later.

Record: endpoints, protocols and exceptions; pass when nothing is cleartext or accepts bad certificates.

items.title: MASVS-NETWORK-2 Identity pinning
items.description:
MASTG tests cover missing pins in Android Network Security Configuration and iOS ATS, and expired pins.

  • Android: Network Security Configuration pin sets exist, include a backup pin and expire in the future.
  • iOS: pinning uses NSPinnedDomains in Info.plist or code, for the developer's own domains.
  • A pin mismatch blocks the connection rather than falling back.

Record: pinned domains, method and result with an untrusted certificate; pass when other keys are refused.

items.title: MASVS-PLATFORM-1 Secure use of IPC mechanisms
items.description:
MASTG tests cover exported components, intents, PendingIntents, App Links, URL schemes and universal links.

  • Android: exported components enforce permissions; intents carry no sensitive extras; PendingIntents are immutable.
  • iOS: URL scheme and universal link handlers check input and source; extensions leak nothing.
  • App Links are verified; deep links need confirmation for sensitive actions.

Record: components and links tested; pass when other apps cannot read data or trigger actions.

items.title: MASVS-PLATFORM-2 Secure use of WebViews
items.description:
MASTG tests cover native bridges, file and origin access, URL loading handlers, Safe Browsing and debugging.

  • Android: file and content access are off; JavaScript interfaces serve trusted origins; Safe Browsing is on.
  • iOS: WKWebView, not UIWebView; script bridges use content world isolation and pass no secrets.
  • WebViews load only trusted HTTPS content, not URLs from other apps.

Record: settings, interfaces and sources; pass when untrusted content cannot reach native code or files.

items.title: MASVS-PLATFORM-3 Secure use of the user interface
items.description:
MASTG tests cover leaks via screenshots, app switcher, notifications, clipboard, accessibility and overlays.

  • Android: sensitive screens set FLAG_SECURE or the Compose equivalent and resist overlays.
  • iOS: content is hidden when backgrounded; the general pasteboard is avoided or set to expire and stay local.
  • Passwords are masked and notifications hide sensitive content on the lock screen.

Record: screens and channels where data leaked; pass when sensitive data is hidden in each.

items.title: MASVS-CODE-1 Up-to-date platform version
items.description:
Supporting old OS versions keeps users on platforms without security fixes. MASTG tests check platform version APIs and declared versions.

  • Android: minSdkVersion is recent and targetSdkVersion meets current Google Play requirements.
  • iOS: the minimum deployment target is a supported iOS version.
  • The app warns or limits features when run on an unsupported OS.

Record: declared versions and behaviour on an old OS; pass when outdated platforms are refused or handled.

items.title: MASVS-CODE-2 Enforced app updates
items.description:
Old versions must stop working once a critical fix ships. MASTG tests check enforced updating APIs in code and at runtime.

  • The back end sets a minimum version; older builds are refused or forced to update.
  • Android uses Google Play in-app updates (immediate flow); iOS checks the store or back end and blocks use.
  • The check is enforced on the server, not only by a client-side comparison.

Record: update mechanism and old-build behaviour; pass when old builds lose protected functions.

items.title: MASVS-CODE-3 No components with known vulnerabilities
items.description:
MASTG tests cover dependency and SBOM scanning and compiler protections (PIC, stack canaries, ARC on iOS).

  • Dependencies (Gradle, CocoaPods, Swift Package Manager) are listed and checked against vulnerability databases.
  • Native libraries are position independent and built with stack canaries.
  • Deprecated or unmaintained libraries and APIs are replaced.

Record: components with versions and known issues; pass when no exploitable known flaw is left unaddressed.

items.title: MASVS-CODE-4 Validation of untrusted input
items.description:
MASTG tests cover SQL injection in providers, unsafe deserialisation, dynamic code loading and WebView content.

  • Queries use parameters; content providers never build SQL from caller input.
  • Untrusted data is not deserialised into arbitrary objects (Android Serializable, iOS NSCoding without NSSecureCoding).
  • Code is not loaded dynamically from writable or remote locations.

Record: entry points tested and results; pass when untrusted input cannot change queries, objects or code.

items.title: MASVS-RESILIENCE-1 Platform integrity checks
items.description:
MASTG tests cover root, jailbreak and emulator detection, for apps whose risk profile needs it.

  • Detection exists in code and runs at sensitive points, not only at start-up.
  • Device attestation, such as Play Integrity device verdicts, is validated on the server.
  • The response (block, limit or report) matches the agreed risk profile.

Record: checks found, their response and how readily they were defeated; pass when they meet the agreed requirement.

items.title: MASVS-RESILIENCE-2 Anti-tampering
items.description:
MASTG tests cover signing schemes and key sizes, file integrity checks and hook detection.

  • Android uses APK Signature Scheme v2 or later with an adequate key; iOS uses a current code signature format.
  • The app checks its own files and resources and detects hooking at runtime.
  • App attestation (Play Integrity app verdict or App Attest) is checked on the server.

Record: signing details and how tampering is detected and handled; pass when controls meet the agreed requirement.

items.title: MASVS-RESILIENCE-3 Anti-static analysis
items.description:
MASTG tests cover obfuscation of security-relevant code, native debug symbols, StrictMode and log detail.

  • Code and resources are obfuscated where the risk profile requires.
  • Native binaries are stripped of debug symbols; StrictMode and debug code are absent from release builds.
  • Logs reveal no implementation detail or verbose errors.

Record: obfuscation level and debug artefacts found; pass when release builds carry no debug material and meet the agreed level.

items.title: MASVS-RESILIENCE-4 Anti-dynamic analysis
items.description:
MASTG tests cover debuggable builds, WebView debugging, and debugger and virtual device detection.

  • Android release builds are not debuggable; iOS release builds lack the get-task-allow entitlement.
  • The app detects attached debuggers and instrumentation and responds as designed.
  • WebView debugging is off in release builds.

Record: debug settings and detection behaviour; pass when releases are not debuggable and detection meets the agreed requirement.

items.title: MASVS-PRIVACY-1 Minimised access to sensitive data and resources
items.description:
MASTG tests cover permissions, purpose strings, iOS entitlements, SDK data use and personal data in traffic.

  • Permissions (Android manifest, iOS purpose strings) match features and are asked for at time of use.
  • Third-party SDKs collect nothing before consent is given.
  • Network traffic carries no personal data that is undeclared or unneeded.

Record: permissions, SDKs and personal data flows; pass when each is necessary and consented.

items.title: MASVS-PRIVACY-2 Prevention of user identification
items.description:
Identifiers and fingerprinting signals can track users across apps. MASWE covers anonymisation, identifiers and privacy-preserving APIs; judge against the design.

  • Resettable, scoped identifiers are used, not hardware IDs or persistent fingerprints.
  • Data sent to analytics is pseudonymised or aggregated.
  • Fraud-prevention signals are not reused for advertising or analytics.

Record: identifiers collected and where they go; pass when users cannot be tracked beyond the stated purpose.

items.title: MASVS-PRIVACY-3 Transparency about data collection
items.description:
Users must be told what is collected and why. MASTG tests compare declarations with what SDKs and traffic show, including iOS tracking domains.

  • The Google Play Data safety section and Apple privacy details match observed collection.
  • Tracking domains contacted on iOS are declared in the privacy manifest.
  • The privacy policy is reachable from the app and covers background collection.

Record: declared against observed data and domains; pass when declarations are complete and accurate.

items.title: MASVS-PRIVACY-4 User control over their data
items.description:
Users should be able to view, change and delete their data and withdraw consent. MASWE covers these controls; check them directly.

  • Account and data deletion is offered in the app and completed on the back end.
  • Consent is as easy to withdraw as to give, and SDKs stop collecting when it is.
  • Consent is asked again before new data types are collected.

Record: controls offered and the back-end effect of each; pass when users can manage and delete their data.

phase_wireless_v2.name: Wireless Review
phase_wireless_v2.description: Coverage tracker for a wireless phase: authorised network inventory, security modes and keys, enterprise EAP and server certificate validation, management frame protection, guest isolation and captive portals, rogue and look-alike networks, WPS, controller management and signal reach. Test only networks and devices confirmed as the client's, keep the evidence each item names, and tick it once covered or recorded as not applicable.

items.title: Inventory of authorised wireless networks
items.description:
Agrees which networks belong to the client before testing, giving rogue detection and every later check a baseline (NIST SP 800-115 section 4.4).

  • Authorised SSIDs are listed with purpose (corporate, guest, IoT, voice), bands and security mode.
  • Access point BSSIDs or vendor ranges and controller details are recorded.
  • A passive survey across every channel and band in use (2.4, 5 and 6 GHz) is compared with the list.

Record: the agreed inventory and survey results; passing means every observed network is accounted for.

items.title: Scope boundaries and neighbouring networks
items.description:
Radio signals ignore property lines, so the test must not touch networks or devices that are not the client's.

  • Active testing targets only BSSIDs confirmed as the client's.
  • Neighbouring and visitor networks seen in the survey are recorded but never probed.
  • Client devices are tested only when managed by the organisation and named in scope.

Record: confirmed targets and excluded networks; passing means no activity against third-party networks or devices.

items.title: Encryption and authentication mode per network
items.description:
The security mode of each SSID sets the baseline risk for everything else on it.

  • Corporate networks use WPA3-Enterprise or WPA2-Enterprise with AES (CCMP or GCMP).
  • Pre-shared key networks use WPA3-Personal (SAE), or WPA2-Personal with a strong key where devices require it.
  • TKIP is not offered on any network.

Record: SSID, advertised modes, ciphers and key management; passing means current modes with AES only.

items.title: WPA3 transition modes
items.description:
Transition modes let WPA2 and WPA3 clients share one SSID, which keeps WPA2's weaknesses within reach of anyone who connects that way.

  • SSIDs advertising both WPA2-Personal and WPA3-SAE are identified, along with whether clients can be pushed back to WPA2.
  • Management frame protection is optional rather than required in transition mode; where that applies is noted.
  • A dated plan exists to move to WPA3 only once clients allow.

Record: SSID and transition settings; passing means WPA3 only, or transition mode with a dated plan.

items.title: Open and legacy networks
items.description:
Open and WEP networks give no meaningful protection to their traffic or to the networks behind them.

  • No network uses WEP, and open authentication is used only for a deliberately isolated guest network.
  • Open guest networks use Enhanced Open (OWE) where clients support it.
  • Legacy devices that force weak modes sit on isolated SSIDs and VLANs.

Record: networks with open, WEP or other legacy modes and what they reach; passing means none, or an isolated guest network only.

items.title: Pre-shared key strength
items.description:
A WPA2 pre-shared key can be tested offline once handshake material is captured, so its length and randomness are what protect the network.

  • Where authorised, the key's resistance to offline guessing is assessed within an agreed time box.
  • Keys are long random strings, not words, company names, addresses or phone numbers.
  • The same key is not reused across SSIDs or sites.

Record: whether the key was recovered within the time box and any pattern weakness, never the key itself; passing means not recovered and not reused.

items.title: Pre-shared key rotation and distribution
items.description:
A shared key leaks with every leaver, contractor and printed notice.

  • Keys are rotated on a schedule and after staff or contractor changes.
  • Keys are not displayed in public areas, printed on access points or sent in plain messages.
  • Per-user or per-device keys are used instead of one shared key where the platform supports them.

Record: key age, distribution method and any exposure found; passing means recent rotation and limited distribution.

items.title: Enterprise EAP methods
items.description:
The EAP method decides whether users' credentials can be exposed to a look-alike network.

  • EAP-TLS with device or user certificates (or TEAP) is used; PEAP-MSCHAPv2 and EAP-TTLS with password inner methods are justified.
  • Legacy methods such as LEAP and EAP-MD5 are refused by the RADIUS server.
  • Machine and user authentication behave as the client intends.

Record: methods offered by the server and used by clients; passing means certificate-based EAP, or password methods with strict server validation.

items.title: Client validation of the server certificate
items.description:
If managed clients do not validate the RADIUS server certificate, they will hand credentials to any network using the same name.

  • Supplicant profiles trust only the organisation's issuing CA and name the expected servers.
  • Users cannot accept unknown servers or certificates when prompted.
  • Where authorised, a managed test device confirms the profile refuses a server with an untrusted certificate.

Record: profile settings and observed behaviour; passing means connections to untrusted servers are refused.

items.title: RADIUS and authentication server configuration
items.description:
The authentication server holds the policy that decides who joins which network and where they land.

  • The server certificate comes from a private CA, uses a strong key and is in date.
  • Policies map users and devices to the right VLANs and reject disabled accounts and revoked certificates.
  • RADIUS shared secrets between access points or controllers and servers are long and unique.

Record: certificate details and policy mapping evidence; passing means a private CA, revocation checking and correct VLAN mapping.

items.title: Management frame protection
items.description:
Without protected management frames (IEEE 802.11w), anyone in range can forge disconnection frames that push clients off the network and towards others.

  • Management frame protection is required on WPA3 and enterprise SSIDs and at least optional elsewhere.
  • Clients that do not support it are recorded.
  • Wireless intrusion detection alerts on floods of disconnection frames.

Record: SSID and setting (disabled, optional, required); passing means required wherever clients allow.

items.title: Guest isolation and wireless segmentation
items.description:
Guest and BYOD networks must reach the internet only, and corporate wireless must reach only what its design allows.

  • From a guest connection, internal ranges, management interfaces and the wireless controller are unreachable.
  • Guest DNS does not resolve internal names.
  • Corporate wireless VLANs are separated from server and management networks as designed.

Record: reachability results per network; passing means guest reaches the internet only and corporate wireless follows the design.

items.title: Client-to-client isolation
items.description:
On shared networks, one client should not be able to reach another.

  • On guest and public networks, traffic between associated clients is blocked.
  • Isolation holds across access points on the same SSID, not just within one.
  • Multicast and broadcast discovery traffic between clients is limited.

Record: results between two test devices on each network; passing means clients cannot reach each other.

items.title: Captive portals
items.description:
A captive portal is only a control if traffic is actually blocked until the user is authorised.

  • Before authorisation nothing passes except traffic to the portal, including DNS to external servers and IPv6.
  • Authorisation is not tied only to a MAC or IP address another device could copy.
  • The portal uses HTTPS and handles any credentials or personal data securely.

Record: what passed before authorisation and how sessions are tracked; passing means nothing passes and sessions cannot be taken over.

items.title: Rogue and unauthorised access points
items.description:
An unauthorised access point connected to the wired network bypasses every perimeter control (NIST SP 800-115 sections 4.4.1 and 4.4.3).

  • The survey flags SSIDs, BSSIDs and vendors not on the authorised list, and ad hoc or Wi-Fi Direct networks.
  • Unknown devices on the premises are located and checked for a connection to internal networks.
  • The client's wireless intrusion detection flags the same devices.

Record: each unauthorised device, location and connection; passing means none connect to internal networks and detection works.

items.title: Client behaviour towards look-alike networks
items.description:
Checks whether managed devices join a network that imitates a corporate or remembered SSID, the usual way credentials and traffic are captured. Run only with authorisation, against managed devices.

  • Managed devices do not join an open network carrying a corporate or remembered public SSID.
  • Devices do not broadcast saved network names in probe requests, especially for hidden SSIDs.
  • Users are never asked to accept a new server certificate.

Record: device type, profile and behaviour; passing means no automatic connection.

items.title: Wi-Fi Protected Setup
items.description:
The WPS PIN method can be worked out in a feasible number of attempts on many devices, exposing the network key.

  • WPS is disabled on all access points, routers and extenders, including those outside central management.
  • Printers and other devices offering WPS or Wi-Fi Direct are identified.
  • Devices that cannot disable WPS have the PIN method off or lock out repeated attempts.

Record: devices advertising WPS and the methods offered; passing means none.

items.title: IoT, voice and device-specific networks
items.description:
Networks set up for scanners, cameras, handsets or building systems often use shared keys and reach more than they should.

  • Each device network reaches only the servers its devices need.
  • Its key is unique, strong and rotated, or devices use certificates.
  • Devices on it cannot reach corporate user or server networks.

Record: SSID, devices, key handling and reachability; passing means device networks are isolated and separately keyed.

items.title: Controller and access point management
items.description:
Whoever controls the wireless controller or access points controls every network they broadcast.

  • Management interfaces are unreachable from client and guest networks.
  • Management uses HTTPS and SSH with named accounts; Telnet, HTTP and SNMP v1 or v2c are off and defaults are changed.
  • Firmware is supported and current, and access point console ports and recovery modes are protected.

Record: management endpoints, reachability, protocols and firmware; passing means management is reachable from admin networks only.

items.title: Wireless monitoring and intrusion detection
items.description:
Monitoring decides whether rogue devices, impersonation and disruption are noticed at all.

  • Wireless intrusion detection or prevention covers every site and band in use.
  • Alerts for rogue access points, impersonated SSIDs and disconnection floods reach someone who acts on them.
  • Automatic containment, if used, is limited to confirmed rogues in the client's own premises.

Record: alerts raised during the test against its timeline; passing means test activity was detected and handled.

items.title: Signal reach beyond the premises
items.description:
Measures how far networks are usable outside the building, which sets who can attempt everything above.

  • Signal strength and the ability to associate are recorded from car parks, public areas, site boundaries and other floors.
  • Transmit power and antenna placement cover the premises, not beyond.
  • Guest and corporate networks usable from outside are noted.

Record: locations, signal levels and whether association succeeded; passing means corporate networks are unusable from public areas.

std_osstmm3_v2.name: Security Testing Methodology (OSSTMM 3)
std_osstmm3_v2.description: Coverage tracker for a test run to ISECOM's OSSTMM 3: rules of engagement, test definition and operational security terms, then the 17 test modules applied to every channel in scope, ending with the attack surface measurement and the STAR. Tick an item only when it is done for each channel in scope and its evidence is filed.

items.title: Rules of engagement: permission and contract
items.description:
Rules that apply before any interaction: owner permission and a contract stating limits.

  • Written permission from the owner or a proper authority covers every target.
  • The statement of work gives each test's limits and dangers, and remote analysts' origin.
  • Survivability, denial of service, process and social engineering tests need explicit consent.
  • Emergency contacts, confidentiality, changes and conflicts of interest are written down.

Record: signed permission and contract; pass is nothing tested beyond them.

items.title: Rules of engagement: scope definition and test plan
items.description:
The scope is fixed in the contract before any service is verified, and the plan stays within the analysts' competence.

  • The contracted scope exists before testing starts, and changes follow the agreed process.
  • The limits of each test relative to the scope are explained to the client.
  • The plan holds no technique beyond the assigned analysts' proven competence.
  • Every planned test maps to a contracted target, channel and vector.

Record: scope and plan versions used; pass is every test traceable to the contract.

items.title: Rules of engagement: test process
items.description:
Process rules protect the public, the client and the scope while tests run; check them during the work.

  • Public safety and privacy, in and out of scope, and both locations' laws are respected.
  • Only key people chosen by the client are told, so defences are not raised.
  • Unprivileged testing comes first; privileged tests use two typical accounts the client issues.
  • Serious findings are reported at once; the scope is never left less secure.

Record: immediate notifications and changes reverted; pass is no rule breached.

items.title: Rules of engagement: reporting
items.description:
Reporting rules govern what results contain and how they travel, including duties to staff.

  • Individuals' privacy is protected; untrained staff appear only anonymously or as statistics.
  • Unknowns and anomalies are marked, and working and failed controls are both reported.
  • Metrics are factual and quantitative; advice is valid and practical.
  • Only those who did the work sign; delivery is end-to-end confidential, with receipt confirmed.

Record: delivery and receipt confirmation; pass is a report checkable against each rule.

items.title: Assets, engagement zone, scope and vectors defined
items.description:
Section 2.1 builds the test outward from the assets, so porosity counts compare between tests.

  • Assets to protect are listed, with the engagement zone where interaction with them happens.
  • The scope adds everything outside that zone the assets need to keep operating.
  • Vectors record how the scope interacts internally and with the outside.
  • The defined test is checked against the rules of engagement before work starts.

Record: asset list, zone, scope and vector table; pass is each vector tied to the assets it reaches.

items.title: Channels in scope (Human, Physical, Wireless, Telecommunications, Data Networks)
items.description:
OSSTMM groups five channels into three classes, and each channel is tested separately for each vector.

  • Each channel is in or out with a reason: Human and Physical (PHYSSEC), Wireless (SPECSEC), Telecommunications and Data Networks (COMSEC).
  • Targets, vectors, analysts and equipment are named for every channel in scope.
  • Chapters 7 to 11 apply the same 17 modules; tick a module below only when done for each channel.

Record: channel and vector matrix; pass is no in-scope channel without targets and an owner.

items.title: Test type agreed for each channel
items.description:
Section 2.3 defines six common test types by what the analyst and the target each know in advance.

  • One type is agreed per channel: Blind, Double Blind, Gray Box, Double Gray Box, Tandem or Reversal.
  • What the target was told (scope, timing, channels, vectors) matches the type chosen.
  • Information supplied to analysts is logged, so results are not credited to discovery.

Record: type per channel and the briefing given; pass is a type signed off before testing.

items.title: Four Point Process and Trifecta applied
items.description:
OSSTMM prefers the Four Point Process to simple echo testing, since a silent target can look secure when it is not.

  • Each target is worked through Induction, Inquest, Interaction and Intervention.
  • Results answer the Trifecta: how operations work, how that differs from management's view, and how they need to work.
  • Conclusions resting on a single echo response are flagged as limited.

Record: analysis notes per target; pass is each conclusion backed by more than one response.

items.title: Test errors identified and reconciled
items.description:
Section 2.8 treats errors as part of the result; logging them keeps false confidence out of the metrics.

  • Each reported state is checked as a possible false positive or false negative.
  • Results affected by unstable targets, sampling or limits on the analyst are marked with the cause.
  • Errors are reconciled before any figure feeds the attack surface measurement.

Record: error log against findings; pass is no unreconciled error in the figures.

items.title: Porosity counted: visibility, access and trust
items.description:
OSSTMM measures operational security (OpSec) as the openings in the separation between assets and threats.

  • Visibility: every target whose existence within the scope can be shown.
  • Access: every separate point where someone can interact with a target.
  • Trust: every case of one in-scope target accepting interaction from another without checks.
  • Counts are kept per channel and vector so that tests can be compared.

Record: porosity tally with evidence; pass is a count another analyst can reproduce.

items.title: Class A interactive controls identified
items.description:
The five Class A controls act on interactions directly, so map them against every access and trust point.

  • Authentication: credentials are needed before interaction is allowed.
  • Indemnification: warnings, terms or insurance place liability on the other party.
  • Resilience and Continuity: a failure leaves assets protected and interaction still available.
  • Subjugation: interaction can only follow the process the owner defines.

Record: control map per access and trust point; pass is each point checked for all five.

items.title: Class B process controls identified
items.description:
The five Class B controls protect the process around an interaction rather than the interaction itself.

  • Non-repudiation: no party can deny its part in an interaction.
  • Confidentiality and Privacy: the content, and how the interaction happens, stay known only to the parties.
  • Integrity: the parties can tell when assets or processes have changed.
  • Alarm: someone is told when OpSec or a control fails or is circumvented.

Record: control map per access and trust point; pass is each control tested, not assumed.

items.title: Limitations classified
items.description:
Each flaw is classed as one of five limitation types, weighed against controls in the measurement.

  • Vulnerability: denies authorised access, gives privileged access to the unauthorised, or lets someone hide.
  • Weakness or Concern: undermines a Class A or a Class B control respectively.
  • Exposure: anything unjustified revealing targets or assets, directly or not.
  • Anomaly: something unidentified, uncontrolled and unexplained by normal operations.

Record: each finding's type and affected control; pass is none unclassified.

items.title: Posture Review (module 1)
items.description:
The first regulatory module sets out what each target must comply with and how it normally operates.

  • Policies, laws and regulations that apply to each channel and target location are identified.
  • Culture, operating hours and normal working patterns are recorded.
  • Fragile or sensitive assets that limit testing are flagged before work starts.
  • The posture is confirmed with the client, not inferred.

Record: posture summary per channel; pass is each later finding traceable to a rule it breaks.

items.title: Logistics (module 2)
items.description:
Logistics measures the conditions of the test itself, which set the margin of accuracy of every result.

  • Distance, latency and paths between analysts and targets are known per channel.
  • Timing is set: time zones, business hours, holidays and a pace the targets can bear.
  • Interference that could distort results, such as congestion or radio noise, is noted.

Record: conditions and error margins per channel; pass is results reported with their limits.

items.title: Active Detection Verification (module 3)
items.description:
Before the main interactions, establish what can detect, filter or alter the test, so results are read correctly.

  • Monitoring is identified per channel: guards, filtering, intrusion detection, call screening, help desk checks.
  • Whether interactions are blocked, moderated or altered in transit is established.
  • How predictable detection and response are is recorded, with times where measurable.

Record: detection found per channel; pass is each later result marked as made with or without it.

items.title: Visibility Audit (module 4)
items.description:
This module finds which in-scope targets can be shown to exist; presence counts, not only what can be seen.

  • Targets are found by enumeration and by checking those supplied or researched.
  • Human: reachable staff and roles. Physical: sites and assets. Wireless and Telecommunications: emitters and numbers. Data Networks: live systems.
  • Targets found outside the scope are reported, not tested.

Record: visibility count and target list per channel; pass is a list matched to the client's inventory.

items.title: Access Verification (module 5)
items.description:
Access Verification measures where and how each visible target can be interacted with.

  • Every access point per target is listed: doors, phone lines, radio interfaces, network services, help desks.
  • The type and depth of interaction each allows, and the authentication it needs, are recorded.
  • Access is tested without credentials first, then with the accounts the client supplied.

Record: access count with authentication per point; pass is no access point left unexamined.

items.title: Trust Verification (module 6)
items.description:
Trust Verification finds where targets accept interaction from others without the usual checks.

  • Trusts between in-scope targets, and from outside the scope, are mapped per channel.
  • Human: whether staff trust someone who misrepresents themselves, using approved pretexts only.
  • Data Networks: shared credentials, trusted hosts, single sign-on and partner links are mapped.
  • How far each trust stretches is shown without causing harm.

Record: trust count with evidence; pass is every trust justified by the posture.

items.title: Controls Verification (module 7)
items.description:
This module tests whether the Class B process controls actually work on the access and trust points found.

  • Non-repudiation: actions on each channel can be tied to whoever made them.
  • Confidentiality and privacy: content and the means of interaction are protected from outsiders.
  • Integrity: changes to assets or processes are noticed by the parties.
  • Each control is tested on every channel in scope.

Record: pass or fail per control per channel; pass is evidence behind every result.

items.title: Process Verification (module 8)
items.description:
The first information module checks that security processes are maintained and followed as the posture requires.

  • Maintenance of security levels (reviews, updates, checks) happens as policy says.
  • Staff keep to process when asked to deviate or when given misinformation.
  • Due diligence and indemnification steps, such as notices and agreements, exist where required.

Record: gaps between written process and practice; pass is practice matching the posture.

items.title: Configuration Verification (module 9)
items.description:
This module examines the normal working state of targets for problems that sit beneath the security measures.

  • Configuration controls on systems and equipment match the posture.
  • Common configuration errors and defaults are checked per channel and given a limitation type.
  • Human channel: the training and awareness staff receive are compared with policy.
  • Physical channel: barrier, access control and alarm set-up is reviewed, not defeated.

Record: deviations per channel; pass is targets working as designed and as required.

items.title: Property Validation (module 10)
items.description:
Property Validation looks for unlicensed or illegal intellectual property used, shared or sold within the scope.

  • Software and media on in-scope systems are checked against the licences held.
  • Services, channels or people distributing protected material are identified.
  • Material is recorded by reference only, never copied or passed on.

Record: instances and locations; pass is none found, or each reported to the client contact.

items.title: Segregation Review (module 11)
items.description:
Segregation Review checks how personal and private information is separated, contained and disclosed.

  • Where personal data is held, and its type and volume, are mapped per channel.
  • Disclosure to people not entitled to it is tested within the agreed privacy limits.
  • Public information that could be joined to internal data is noted, not harvested.

Record: containment map with disclosures; pass is personal data held only where the posture allows.

items.title: Exposure Verification (module 12)
items.description:
This module searches public sources for information that indirectly reveals targets, assets or channel infrastructure.

  • Websites, job adverts, filings, forums and document metadata are searched for each channel.
  • Each exposure is linked to the visibility, access, trust or control it reveals.
  • Searching stays passive and keeps no more personal data than proof needs.

Record: exposures with source and date; pass is nothing public that reveals an access point or control.

items.title: Competitive Intelligence Scouting (module 13)
items.description:
This module looks for freely available information that a competitor or other outsider could use to harm the owner.

  • Business details are gathered from public sources: products, partners, suppliers, plans.
  • Organisational details, such as structure, key staff and processes, are judged for what they give away.
  • Findings are weighed by potential harm, not by volume.

Record: what was found and how it could be used; pass is little of value discoverable.

items.title: Quarantine Verification (module 14)
items.description:
The first interactive controls module tests how hostile or unwanted interactions are contained, in both directions.

  • Containment is identified per channel: mail and file filtering, visitor holding, call screening, network isolation.
  • Containment levels and duration are measured, with how and by whom items are released.
  • Only harmless test material named in the plan is used to trigger containment.

Record: what was held, for how long, and how release works; pass is containment both ways.

items.title: Privileges Audit (module 15)
items.description:
Privileges Audit maps how privileges are granted and the impact if they are misused or escalated.

  • How people and systems are identified before privileges are granted is checked per channel.
  • Whether privileges can be obtained by fraud, or reused from elsewhere, is tested within limits.
  • Whether a supplied low-privilege account can reach higher privileges is tested and logged.

Record: each privilege path with evidence; pass is no unauthorised gain of privilege.

items.title: Survivability Validation (module 16)
items.description:
This module measures how targets resist excessive or adverse change before continuity or resilience fails.

  • Survivability or denial of service tests have written permission, limits and stop conditions.
  • Continuity: services stay available when a part fails or is overloaded.
  • Resilience: a failure leaves targets closed and safe, not open.
  • Human and Physical: cover for absent key staff and safety arrangements are reviewed, not stressed.

Record: tests run, limits and outcomes; pass is no disruption beyond what was agreed.

items.title: Alert and Log Review (module 17)
items.description:
The final module is a gap analysis between what the analysts did and what the target recorded or noticed.

  • Every timestamped test action is matched to alerts and log entries per channel.
  • Alarm: who was told, how quickly, and whether the right person acted.
  • Storage and retrieval: records were kept for the required time and retrieved intact.
  • Human: what staff noticed and reported is gathered after testing, with client agreement.

Record: gap analysis per channel; pass is all test activity visible in the record.

items.title: Results analysed critically before reporting
items.description:
Chapter 3 asks analysts to test their own conclusions before reporting, keeping facts and assumptions apart.

  • Each result is read against the OpSec model (porosity, controls, limitations), not a list of known issues.
  • Results that match a familiar pattern are rechecked as possible errors.
  • Conclusions resting on intuition are confirmed by testing or marked as such.
  • Method, limits and untested areas are reported transparently.

Record: reasoning for each significant result; pass is no claim beyond the evidence.

items.title: Trust relationships analysed
items.description:
Chapter 5 gives ten trust properties and a set of trust rules for judging whether a trust is justified.

  • Each trust found in Trust Verification is assessed against the trust properties.
  • Trusts resting on fallacies, such as familiarity standing in for evidence, are flagged.
  • The assessment goes to the client to decide which trusts to keep.

Record: each trust with its assessment; pass is every trust justified by evidence.

items.title: Attack surface measurement (rav) calculated
items.description:
Chapter 4 turns the counts into a rav, ISECOM's scale measurement of the attack surface, which a STAR requires.

  • Porosity, controls and limitations are counted per channel and vector from evidence.
  • The OpSec, controls, limitations and actual security formulas are applied as chapter 4 sets out.
  • Inputs are kept with the result, and comparison with earlier tests uses the same scope.

Record: rav worksheet and inputs; pass is a figure another analyst can reproduce.

items.title: STAR (Security Test Audit Report) completed
items.description:
Chapter 13 sets out the STAR, the standard OSSTMM deliverable that states what was tested and the resulting measurement.

  • Scope, channels, vectors, test type, dates and analysts are stated.
  • The rav and its porosity, controls and limitations figures are given per channel.
  • Tests not performed, with reasons, and unknowns are listed.
  • If a certified STAR is wanted, an ISECOM Licensed Auditor produces it.

Record: completed STAR with the report; pass is a test another team could repeat.

std_ptes_v2.name: Penetration Testing Execution Standard (PTES)
std_ptes_v2.description: Coverage tracker for a test run to the Penetration Testing Execution Standard, following its seven sections from Pre-engagement Interactions to Reporting and their sub-sections. Tick an item once it is done and its record is filed; the exploitation and post exploitation items cover authorisation, care, recording and clean-up, never technique.

items.title: Pre-engagement Interactions: scope and time estimation
items.description:
Scoping comes first because the estimate, the contract and every later boundary depend on it.

  • What is and is not to be tested is written down in plain terms.
  • The time estimate draws on comparable past engagements, with a margin for the unexpected.
  • The estimate includes reporting, QA and retest time, not only testing.

Record: scope statement and estimate basis; pass is an estimate traceable to the scope.

items.title: Pre-engagement Interactions: scoping meeting
items.description:
The scoping meeting settles only what will be tested; rules of engagement and cost are handled separately.

  • Ranges, domains, applications and sites in scope are confirmed with the client.
  • The client confirms it owns every target, including DNS, mail, hosting and security appliances.
