  • Countries and regions hosting targets are noted, as local law can change what is allowed.

Record: minutes listing each target and its owner; pass is no target without a confirmed owner.

items.title: Pre-engagement Interactions: questionnaires
items.description:
PTES question sets for each test type draw out goals and constraints before the scope is final.

  • General questions and the sets for each test type in scope (network, web application, wireless, physical, social engineering) are answered.
  • Business unit managers and systems administrators answer their own sets where relevant.
  • Answers that change scope or risk are carried into the scope document.

Record: completed questionnaires on file; pass is no open question affecting scope.

items.title: Pre-engagement Interactions: scope creep and payment terms
items.description:
Work beyond the agreed scope is a commercial and legal risk, so it is priced and signed before it starts.

  • Extra requests go into a statement of work at the contracted hourly rate and wait for countersignature.
  • Retest windows and their time limit are fixed in the contract.
  • Payment terms (net 30, half upfront or recurring) are agreed before testing starts.

Record: each change request and its approval; pass is no unapproved work.

items.title: Pre-engagement Interactions: start and end dates
items.description:
Explicit dates prevent open-ended work and tell the client's teams when activity is expected.

  • Start and end dates, and testing hours for each target, are agreed in writing.
  • Blackout periods, change freezes and business peaks are recorded.
  • The retest period, and how far it may be extended, is stated.

Record: agreed dates and windows; pass is all activity logged inside them.

items.title: Pre-engagement Interactions: IP ranges and domains validated
items.description:
Testing a system owned by someone else has serious legal consequences, so every range and domain is validated first.

  • Each range and domain is checked against registry and ownership records and tied to the client.
  • Whether firewalls, IDS or IPS and other intermediate devices are in scope is decided.
  • Upstream providers and other third parties on the path are identified.

Record: validated target list with ownership evidence; pass is no unvalidated target.

items.title: Pre-engagement Interactions: dealing with third parties
items.description:
A client cannot authorise testing of systems a provider owns, so each provider agrees on its own terms.

  • Cloud services: notice or approval under the provider's testing policy, with a security contact.
  • ISP and web hosting: terms reviewed, scope and timing shared, testing kept to what is allowed.
  • MSSPs: told about tests of systems they run, unless measuring them is agreed.
  • Countries where servers are hosted are confirmed and their law checked.

Record: each provider's approval or exemption; pass is none outstanding.

items.title: Pre-engagement Interactions: acceptable social engineering pretexts
items.description:
Pretexts should reflect current attacks yet stay acceptable at work, and PTES wants them approved in writing first.

  • Every planned pretext is listed and approved in writing by the client.
  • Distressing themes, and impersonation of real third parties without consent, are excluded.
  • Any change during testing goes back for approval.

Record: approved pretext list; pass is no pretext used that is not on it.

items.title: Pre-engagement Interactions: DoS testing
items.description:
Stress and denial of service testing can damage production, so it is decided before the engagement starts.

  • Whether DoS or stress testing is in scope is stated, either way.
  • Where availability matters, such testing moves to a non-production copy of production.
  • Tests that might degrade service as a side effect are treated the same way.

Record: the written decision; pass is no availability impact the client did not accept.

items.title: Pre-engagement Interactions: goals
items.description:
Goals tie the test to business risk, with compliance secondary, so findings are weighed by what matters.

  • Primary goals are stated in business terms, not as a compliance tick.
  • Secondary goals, such as a compliance need, support the primary ones.
  • Business analysis checks maturity; a less mature client may need a vulnerability assessment first.

Record: agreed goals in the scope document; pass is each goal testable and owned.

items.title: Pre-engagement Interactions: communication and emergency contacts
items.description:
Contacts and an incident route keep testing safe, and PTES treats them as part of the engagement.

  • The contact list covers testers, their manager and client technical and business leads, each with two 24/7 means.
  • Incident definition, severity levels and the reporting process are agreed.
  • Status report frequency is set; sensitive material moves only by agreed encrypted means.

Record: shared contact list; pass is every contact tested before day one.

items.title: Pre-engagement Interactions: rules of engagement
items.description:
Scope says what is tested and rules of engagement say how; PTES lists what to settle in writing.

  • Timeline, locations and time of day to test are agreed.
  • Disclosure of sensitive information and evidence handling are defined.
  • Status meetings, and how shunning (the client blocking testers) is handled, are set.
  • Signed permission to test, accepting the risk of instability, and legal points are on file.

Record: signed rules of engagement; pass is every tester briefed on them.

items.title: Pre-engagement Interactions: capabilities and technology in place
items.description:
A good test also measures detection and response at each stage, so existing capability is noted first.

  • Monitoring and response capability relevant to the scope is described by the client.
  • The plan names the stages watched: gathering, footprinting, scanning, infiltration, aggregation, exfiltration.
  • When detection occurs, the time and the testing intensity in use are logged.

Record: detection timeline against test activity; pass is evidence for each detection claim.

items.title: Intelligence Gathering: level and target selection
items.description:
PTES defines three levels of intelligence gathering by depth; the level and targets are set before gathering starts.

  • Level 1, 2 or 3 is agreed to match the goals and time available.
  • Targets are named, including related domains and subsidiaries, and checked against scope.
  • Rules of engagement limits, test length and end goal are considered first.

Record: level chosen and target list; pass is no gathering against unapproved targets.

items.title: Intelligence Gathering: OSINT
items.description:
Open sources show what an attacker could learn about the organisation and its people.

  • Corporate: locations, relationships, org chart, metadata, marketing, infrastructure and financial reporting.
  • Individual: employees' public presence, only as far as the agreed level and privacy rules allow.
  • Each item notes source, date and reliability, as OSINT can be wrong or out of date.

Record: sourced findings; pass is no personal data kept beyond what the test needs.

items.title: Intelligence Gathering: covert gathering
items.description:
Covert gathering covers on-location and offsite observation and human intelligence, so it needs explicit authority.

  • On-location and offsite gathering are authorised for named sites and dates.
  • Human intelligence work follows the approved pretexts.
  • Observation stays on public or authorised ground and does not record the public.

Record: what was observed, where and when; pass is all activity inside the authorisation.

items.title: Intelligence Gathering: footprinting
items.description:
Footprinting confirms hosts and services externally and internally, ending in a target list for the next phase.

  • Customer external and internal ranges are confirmed before any active work.
  • Passive reconnaissance comes before active footprinting, which stays inside validated ranges.
  • The target list notes versions, patch levels and lockout thresholds found.

Record: established target list; pass is every entry in scope.

items.title: Intelligence Gathering: identify protection mechanisms
items.description:
Knowing the defences shapes the pace of testing and how detection results are read.

  • Network, host, application, storage and user protections are identified for each target group.
  • Where detection is being measured, protections are noted and never disabled.
  • Protections that could block or distort results are raised with the client.

Record: protections per layer; pass is each later result read in their light.

items.title: Threat Modeling: business asset analysis
items.description:
PTES centres the threat model on assets and attackers; this step finds what an attacker would want.

  • Organisational data is listed: policies, product and research, marketing, financial, technical, employee and customer data.
  • Human assets, such as executives, assistants, administrators and HR staff, are identified.
  • Assets are agreed with the client where possible.

Record: asset list in the threat model; pass is each finding later scored against it.

items.title: Threat Modeling: business process analysis
items.description:
Processes show how assets create value, and several minor processes can combine into a critical weakness.

  • Critical business processes are listed and ranked with the client.
  • Each maps to its technical infrastructure, information assets, people and third parties.
  • Dependencies shared between processes are noted.

Record: process maps; pass is each in-scope system linked to a process.

items.title: Threat Modeling: threat agents and capability
items.description:
This step names who would attack and what they could realistically do, so testing reflects credible threats.

  • Internal and external agents are listed: staff, contractors, suppliers, competitors, organised crime, nation states, hacktivists.
  • Capability is assessed: tools, access to exploits, communication means and reach into the organisation.
  • Each community is matched to the assets it could reach.

Record: agent and capability table; pass is a test plan reflecting the most credible agents.

items.title: Threat Modeling: motivation and comparable incidents
items.description:
Motivation, and incidents at similar organisations, check that the model is realistic.

  • Likely motivations (profit, hacktivism, grudge, reputation, access to partners) are noted per agent.
  • Recent compromises of comparable organisations in the sector are reviewed.
  • The model goes into the report so that findings are scored against it.

Record: final threat model; pass is a model agreed with the client and used in scoring.

items.title: Vulnerability Analysis: active and passive testing
items.description:
Depth and breadth of testing are set against the goals, then covered with active and passive methods.

  • Depth (how thorough) and breadth (how many targets) are set and checked against the goals.
  • Active testing pairs automated coverage with manual connection to each relevant service.
  • Passive analysis, such as metadata and traffic on authorised segments, is used where in scope.

Record: coverage per target; pass is no in-scope target untested.

items.title: Vulnerability Analysis: validation
items.description:
Tool output is a lead, not a finding; validation removes false positives and duplicates that skew risk.

  • Results from several tools are correlated so that one issue is reported once.
  • Each candidate is confirmed by manual or protocol-specific checks, or discarded.
  • Attack trees show how confirmed issues relate; risky checks run in an isolated lab first.

Record: each issue confirmed or discarded with a reason; pass is no unvalidated finding.

items.title: Vulnerability Analysis: research
items.description:
Research decides whether an issue is real and exploitable here, using public sources and, if agreed, a replica.

  • Public research checks vulnerability databases, vendor advisories, default credentials and hardening guides.
  • Private research runs in a replica environment, not on production, unless agreed.
  • Potential avenues stay hypotheses until tested.

Record: sources consulted per finding; pass is each rating backed by a source or a test.

items.title: Exploitation: purpose and authorisation
items.description:
Exploitation establishes access past security restrictions; on a commercial test it stays inside what was authorised.

  • Each target is in the validated scope, and the rules of engagement permit exploiting it.
  • Attempts that risk instability or data loss are cleared with the client contact first.
  • The entry point and high-value assets sought are tied to the agreed goals.

Record: the approval behind each attempt; pass is no attempt without one.

items.title: Exploitation: countermeasures and evasion
items.description:
Countermeasures affect both success and safety, and whether to avoid detection is the client's decision.

  • Countermeasures on each target (anti-malware, memory protections, WAF, alert staff) are identified first.
  • The rules of engagement state whether evasion is allowed or detection is being measured.
  • Any detection triggered is logged with time and context.

Record: countermeasures met and detections; pass is conduct matching the agreed stance.

items.title: Exploitation: precision strike
items.description:
PTES favours targeted, researched attempts over broad noisy ones, which also limits risk to the client.

  • Each attempt targets a validated issue and a stated goal.
  • Broad or high-volume attempts are used only when measuring response is agreed.
  • Custom or tailored code is reviewed and tried off production first.

Record: each attempt and outcome in the activity log; pass is no untargeted activity.

items.title: Exploitation: overall objective
items.description:
The objective is the path of least resistance to the agreed goals with the greatest business impact.

  • Each successful path is tied to a goal and the impact it shows.
  • Work on unknown flaws (the zero-day angle) happens only if agreed, in a replica, with disclosure arranged.
  • Paths not pursued, and why, are noted for the client.

Record: attack path narratives with timestamps; pass is each path reproducible from evidence.

items.title: Post Exploitation: rules of engagement to protect the client
items.description:
PTES sets rules for what testers may do once inside, to protect the client's services, data and staff.

  • No critical service changes without agreement; each change is logged and reverted if possible.
  • Passwords are masked in reports; personal data is used only where policy and consent allow.
  • Regulated data stays on client systems; signs of earlier compromise are kept and handed over.
  • Logs stay untouched unless the contract allows otherwise.

Record: timestamped action log; pass is each change shown as restored or reported.

items.title: Post Exploitation: protecting yourself
items.description:
The testing firm's own safeguards are in place before access is used, since testers will handle sensitive data.

  • The contract says the work is done on the client's behalf.
  • The client's acceptable use policy covers equipment, data ownership and monitoring.
  • Tester media is fully encrypted; recording and interception law is checked before any capture.
  • A procedure exists for finding that a third party is compromised.

Record: confirmations on file; pass is all in place before post exploitation starts.

items.title: Post Exploitation: infrastructure analysis and high value targets
items.description:
A compromised system's value lies in what it reveals and connects to; this informs the scope but never widens it.

  • Network configuration and services visible from the system are recorded.
  • High value or high profile targets (people, data, systems) and their business impact are identified.
  • Anything out of scope is reported, not pursued.

Record: value assessment per compromised system; pass is every onward target in scope.

items.title: Post Exploitation: pillaging and sensitive data
items.description:
Pillaging gathers what serves the goals from compromised hosts; the test is proving impact without over-collecting.

  • Collection is limited to proof; screenshots of structure or permissions are preferred to copies.
  • Credentials and personal data found are encrypted, reported and not reused beyond scope.
  • Earlier audit reports or configuration data found are noted as findings.

Record: inventory of data accessed and its handling; pass is nothing kept past the agreed date.

items.title: Post Exploitation: data exfiltration and persistence
items.description:
Exfiltration tests whether controls see data leaving; persistence keeps access for the test. Both need approval.

  • Exfiltration paths are mapped and tested with agreed marker data, not real data, unless authorised.
  • Control strength and the response team's reaction are recorded.
  • Any persistence is approved, authenticated, documented and listed for removal.

Record: paths, outcomes and a persistence register; pass is every item accounted for.

items.title: Post Exploitation: further penetration into infrastructure
items.description:
Moving on from or through a compromised system is done only towards agreed goals and within scope.

  • Each onward step targets an in-scope system and is logged with time and source.
  • Goals are reassessed with the client contact at agreed points.
  • Steps that risk service impact are approved first.

Record: onward path with timestamps; pass is no out-of-scope system touched.

items.title: Post Exploitation: cleanup
items.description:
Cleanup returns systems to their earlier state, and the client gets a list of what was and was not restored.

  • Tools, scripts and temporary files placed during testing are removed.
  • Changed settings are restored and test accounts deleted.
  • Persistence is removed and confirmed gone.
  • Anything that could not be removed is reported with its location.

Record: cleanup log matched to the action log; pass is nothing unaccounted for.

items.title: Reporting: report structure
items.description:
PTES splits the report into an executive summary and a technical report so that each audience can follow it.

  • Both parts are present, and each finding is consistent across them.
  • House branding does not displace required content.
  • Delivery and storage use the agreed secure means, with copies controlled.

Record: QA sign-off; pass is a report that survives peer review against this list.

items.title: Reporting: the executive summary
items.description:
The executive summary tells leadership the aims, results and next steps in business terms.

  • Background gives the purpose and any change to objectives.
  • Overall posture says whether goals were met, separating systemic from symptomatic issues.
  • Risk ranking explains its method; general findings and a recommendation summary follow.
  • A strategic roadmap orders remediation by business objectives and the threat model.

Record: reviewed summary; pass is a non-technical reader able to act on it.

items.title: Reporting: technical report
items.description:
The technical report gives the detail needed to reproduce and fix each issue.

  • The introduction covers people, contacts, scope, objectives, approach and grading structure.
  • Information gathering, vulnerability assessment, exploitation and post exploitation each carry evidence.
  • Risk and exposure quantify business risk and root causes, followed by a conclusion.
  • Out-of-scope and untested areas are stated.

Record: technical report after QA; pass is every finding with evidence, rating and fix.

std_nist_sp800_115_v2.name: Technical Security Testing (NIST SP 800-115)
std_nist_sp800_115_v2.description: Coverage tracker following NIST SP 800-115, Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment (2008), in the publication's own order: review techniques, target identification and analysis, target vulnerability validation, security assessment planning, execution and post-testing activities. The number in each title points to the section; tick each item once covered or recorded as not applicable.

items.title: Documentation review (3.1)
items.description:
Reviews the technical side of policies and procedures to find gaps and to tune later techniques, for example using the password policy to plan password testing.

  • Security policies, architecture, requirements, standard operating procedures and system security plans are current.
  • Interconnection agreements and incident response plans exist and match how systems are run.
  • Outdated procedures and missing guidance for newer systems are noted.

Record: documents reviewed with versions, and gaps found; this shows guidance exists, not that controls work.

items.title: Log review (3.2)
items.description:
Checks that controls log what they should and that logging follows policy; logs can also reveal misconfiguration and past intrusion attempts.

  • Authentication, system, firewall, router, IDS or IPS, application and antimalware logs record the expected events.
  • Logons, privilege use, account changes and policy changes are captured.
  • Activity another control should have stopped, such as IDS alerts for traffic the firewall should drop, is flagged.

Record: sources, period covered and gaps against policy; passing means required events are logged and kept.

items.title: Ruleset review (3.3)
items.description:
Examines router access lists and firewall and IDS or IPS rulesets for gaps, unintended paths and inefficiency.

  • Every rule is still needed and temporary rules have been removed.
  • Only traffic the policy allows is permitted, denying by default and naming specific addresses and ports.
  • Specific rules come before general ones, and no rule lets traffic bypass other defences.
  • Unneeded IDS or IPS signatures are disabled and needed ones tuned.

Record: rules of concern and why; passing means least privilege with no redundant or bypassing rules.

items.title: System configuration review (3.4)
items.description:
Compares system settings with a hardening baseline or configuration checklist, by hand or with automated tools such as SCAP-based checkers.

  • Services, applications, account and password settings, and logging and backup settings are compared with the baseline.
  • Automated checks are used where feasible for speed and consistency, with the rest checked by hand.
  • The administrative access needed to read settings is authorised.

Record: baseline used, systems checked and deviations; passing means systems match the baseline or carry recorded exceptions.

items.title: Network sniffing (3.5)
items.description:
Passively captures traffic, where authorised, to see what is on the network and how it communicates.

  • Capture points are deliberate: the perimeter, behind firewalls and IDS or IPS, in front of critical systems, and where encryption must be confirmed.
  • Unencrypted protocols, unauthorised services and devices, and sensitive data in clear are identified.
  • Switched networks use port mirroring or taps, and coverage limits are noted.

Record: capture points, periods and observations, with any credentials protected; passing means nothing sensitive in clear.

items.title: File integrity checking (3.6)
items.description:
Establishes whether file integrity checking exists and would detect changes to important files.

  • The reference database was built from a known-good system and is stored where an intruder cannot alter it, such as offline.
  • Strong cryptographic hashes are used.
  • The baseline is updated after patches, so legitimate changes do not bury real ones.

Record: coverage, baseline age and storage, and whether an authorised test change was detected; passing means critical files are watched against a protected, current baseline.

items.title: Network discovery (4.1)
items.description:
Identifies live hosts and network topology, passively by observing traffic or actively by probing.

  • Passive and active methods are combined: passive misses silent hosts, while active is hindered by filtering and address translation.
  • Old or fragile systems are probed gently, as some scans can make them fail.
  • Unknown devices are traced to a switch port and an owner.

Record: ranges, methods, live hosts and a topology view; passing means discovery matches the asset inventory.

items.title: Network port and service identification (4.2)
items.description:
Identifies open ports, services and versions on discovered hosts to find potentially vulnerable services and targets.

  • Operating system and service identification use protocol behaviour and banners, treated as indications rather than proof.
  • Hosts hidden by filtering are reached from another segment where scope allows.
  • Insecure protocols and unauthorised applications are flagged for manual follow-up.

Record: host, port, service and version, with scan position and time; passing means every service is known and authorised.

items.title: Vulnerability scanning (4.3)
items.description:
Identifies hosts, their attributes and known vulnerabilities, including outdated software, missing patches and misconfigurations.

  • Vulnerability data is updated before each scan, and authenticated scanning is used where authorised.
  • A skilled tester validates results, as false positives are common and product risk ratings are inconsistent.
  • Severity is set for the environment, not copied from the scanner.

Record: scanner, profile, coverage and validated results; passing means every reported item is confirmed.

items.title: Passive wireless scanning (4.4.1)
items.description:
Listens across all channels without transmitting, to find wireless devices and networks and flag unauthorised ones.

  • SSID, device type, channel, MAC address, signal strength and packet counts are recorded per device.
  • Devices off the authorised list, unknown vendors, unauthorised SSIDs, misconfigured authorised SSIDs and ad hoc networks are flagged.
  • Dwell time per channel and walking pace are set so devices are not missed.

Record: survey route, duration and devices found; passing means every device is authorised and correctly configured.

items.title: Active wireless scanning (4.4.2)
items.description:
Builds on passive results by connecting to discovered devices to verify their configuration and, where authorised, test them.

  • Authorised devices are checked against requirements for authentication, encryption and administrative access.
  • Devices belonging to neighbouring organisations are excluded.
  • Effort focuses on identifying and locating potential rogue devices.

Record: devices tested, checks run and results; passing means devices meet the wireless security requirements.

items.title: Wireless device location tracking (4.4.3)
items.description:
Locates suspicious devices so the organisation can deal with them under its own policy.

  • Signal strength and suitable antennas narrow down the physical location.
  • Wireless intrusion detection sensors help where a device cannot be found by hand.
  • Activity is assessed before removal, and the policy action (shut down, reconfigure, remove) is agreed with the organisation.

Record: device, location, evidence and agreed action; passing means every suspect device is located and resolved.

items.title: Bluetooth scanning (4.4.4)
items.description:
Checks Bluetooth devices against security requirements, allowing for their short range and mobility.

  • Passive scanning samples publicly accessible areas and is repeated over time.
  • The organisation's own Bluetooth infrastructure is included, and rogue devices are handled by policy.
  • Active checks of security mode, PIN strength and power setting run only on devices confirmed as the organisation's.

Record: locations, times, devices and compliance results; passing means organisational devices meet requirements.

items.title: Password cracking (5.1)
items.description:
Assesses password strength from hashes obtained in scope, to find weak accounts and check compliance with the password policy.

  • Written authorisation covers how hashes are obtained, where they are processed and how they are destroyed.
  • Dictionary, hybrid and brute force approaches suit the policy being tested; salting defeats precomputed tables.
  • Results are summarised against policy, not by individual.

Record: approach, time spent, share recovered and policy gaps, with no passwords in the report; passing means passwords resist the agreed effort.

items.title: Penetration testing phases: planning and discovery (5.2.1)
items.description:
Planning sets rules, management approval and goals with no testing done; discovery then gathers information and analyses vulnerabilities.

  • Documented management approval and agreed rules exist before discovery begins.
  • Information gathering covers services, host and address details, staff contacts and banners, within scope.
  • Vulnerability analysis compares findings with sources such as the National Vulnerability Database.

Record: approval reference, sources used and candidate vulnerabilities; passing means a justified target list before any attack.

items.title: Penetration testing phases: attack and reporting (5.2.1)
items.description:
The attack phase verifies candidate vulnerabilities by authorised attempts, feeding what is learnt back into discovery; reporting runs alongside every phase.

  • Each attempt is within the rules of engagement and logged with time, target and outcome.
  • Where access is gained, what could be read, changed or removed is assessed without causing damage.
  • Failed attempts are recorded, and periodic updates go to the organisation.

Record: each attempt, its outcome and evidence; passing means each candidate is confirmed or ruled out.

items.title: Penetration testing logistics (5.2.2)
items.description:
Sets scenarios and constraints so the test reproduces likely, damaging attacks without causing the damage.

  • Outsider and insider scenarios are chosen, with outsider testing usually first.
  • Policy limits on tools and timing are applied, and testing stops where going further would cause damage.
  • Regular network and vulnerability scanning fills the gaps between penetration tests.

Record: scenarios, starting knowledge and access, and constraints; passing means scenarios match the agreed threat model.

items.title: Social engineering (5.3)
items.description:
Tests the human element, user awareness and whether staff follow procedure, in person, by phone or by email and messaging.

  • Each pretext and target group is authorised in writing before use.
  • Targets fit the objective, from high-value individuals to a broad population.
  • Successful and unsuccessful attempts are both recorded, and results feed training rather than singling out individuals.

Record: approach, dates, population and outcome rates; passing means staff followed procedure.

items.title: Developing a security assessment policy (6.1)
items.description:
Confirms an approved policy defines why, how often and by whom assessments are carried out.

  • The policy covers requirements, roles and accountability, methodology, frequency and documentation.
  • Senior officials have approved it, and it is shared with relevant executives and any third-party assessors.
  • It is reviewed at least annually and when requirements change.

Record: policy reference, version and approval date; passing means this assessment runs under it.

items.title: Prioritising and scheduling assessments (6.2)
items.description:
Places this assessment in the organisation's schedule by system impact and assessment history.

  • Priority reflects the system's impact rating and when it was last assessed.
  • Frequency reflects regulation, known weaknesses, planned upgrades and monitoring needs.
  • Scope reflects size, complexity, the feasibility of sampling and available resources.

Record: why this system, why now, and the scope decision; passing means scope is justified by priority.

items.title: Selecting and customising techniques (6.3)
items.description:
Chooses techniques to fit the objectives, the viewpoint and the risk the organisation will accept.

  • Objectives, such as compliance, finding exploitable weaknesses or testing detection and response, are set first.
  • The viewpoint is chosen: external or internal, overt or covert (section 2.4).
  • Cost, time, skills and production risk are weighed, using test systems or test data where feasible and off-hours for risky tests.

Record: objectives, viewpoint and techniques with reasons; passing means each technique traces to an objective.

items.title: Assessor selection and skills (6.4.1)
items.description:
Confirms the people doing the work have the skills each technique needs and that the choice between internal and third-party assessors is deliberate.

  • Each assessor's skills match the techniques they will run.
  • The choice of internal or third-party assessors weighs independence, cost and knowledge of the environment.
  • Third-party assessors are bound by agreements covering confidentiality and handling of the organisation's data.

Record: assessor names, roles and relevant qualifications; passing means every technique is covered by a competent assessor.

items.title: Location selection (6.4.2)
items.description:
Decides where testing is done from, which shapes what it can see and what it costs.

  • External testing runs from outside the perimeter and internal testing from inside it, as the chosen viewpoint requires.
  • Whether work is on site or remote is agreed, with the access and connectivity each needs.
  • Practical needs of on-site work (desk space, network ports, escorts) are arranged in advance.

Record: each test location and why; passing means locations match the chosen viewpoints.

items.title: Technical tools and resources selection (6.4.3)
items.description:
Ensures tools and assessor systems are suitable and trustworthy, since they will hold the organisation's most sensitive results.

  • Tools come from trusted sources and are tried in a non-production setting before use.
  • Assessor systems are dedicated to testing, hardened and protect stored results, for example with disk encryption.
  • Vulnerability data and tool updates are applied before the assessment.

Record: tool set with versions and the assessor systems used; passing means trusted, current tools on secured systems.

items.title: Assessment plan development (6.5)
items.description:
Turns the planning decisions into an approved plan with rules of engagement; Appendix B gives a rules of engagement template.

  • The plan states objectives, scope, systems, techniques, schedule, roles and deliverables.
  • Rules of engagement cover logistics, communication and incident handling, target systems, test execution, data handling and reporting.
  • Appropriate officials approve and sign the plan.

Record: plan and rules of engagement references with approval dates; passing means signed approval before any testing.

items.title: Legal considerations (6.6)
items.description:
Confirms legal review of the assessment, especially for intrusive or covert testing and anything touching personal data.

  • The organisation's legal adviser has reviewed the plan and rules of engagement.
  • Privacy issues from capturing traffic or reading data are addressed.
  • Written authorisation for the assessors, and liability, are settled.

Record: legal review reference and authorisation letter; passing means written authorisation and legal sign-off both exist.

items.title: Coordination (7.1)
items.description:
Keeps the organisation informed during testing, so test activity is not mistaken for an attack and real incidents are not missed.

  • Points of contact, notification steps and communication channels are agreed.
  • The incident response team knows how to verify suspected test activity.
  • Assessors follow the organisation's reporting procedure if they detect a real security incident.

Record: contacts, notifications made and their times; passing means every notification followed the agreed process.

items.title: Assessing (7.2)
items.description:
Carries out the techniques in the plan, within the rules of engagement, and handles anything unexpected.

  • Testing follows the approved plan, with any deviation agreed first.
  • Unexpected conditions, such as signs of an earlier compromise, service instability or sensitive data, trigger the agreed stop and notify steps.
  • Activity is logged as it happens.

Record: the activity log and any deviations or stoppages; passing means testing matched the plan.

items.title: Analysis (7.3)
items.description:
Turns raw results into validated findings and looks for the root causes behind them, during and after testing.

  • False positives are removed and each finding is confirmed.
  • Findings are grouped by root cause, such as patch management, missing security baselines, architecture weaknesses, training or policy gaps.
  • Risk is judged in the organisation's own context.

Record: validated findings with root cause and risk; passing means each finding is confirmed and attributed to a cause.

items.title: Data collection (7.4.1)
items.description:
Collects what the assessment needs and records how it was obtained.

  • Only data needed for the objectives is collected.
  • Assessor activity logs record time, target, technique and result.
  • Information on architecture and configuration is collected where it supports findings.

Record: what was collected and the activity log; passing means collection matched the plan.

items.title: Data storage and data transmission (7.4.2, 7.4.3)
items.description:
Protects assessment data, effectively a map of the organisation's weaknesses, while it is held and while it moves.

  • Results, evidence and any credentials are stored encrypted, with access limited to the assessment team.
  • Data travels only over encrypted channels or as encrypted files.
  • Storage locations and copies are tracked.

Record: storage locations, protection and transfers made; passing means no unprotected copy exists.

items.title: Data destruction (7.4.4)
items.description:
Ensures assessment data is destroyed once no longer needed, in line with policy and the contract.

  • The retention period and destruction method are agreed.
  • Assessor systems, removable media and cloud storage are all covered.
  • Destruction is confirmed to the organisation in writing.

Record: destruction date, method and confirmation; passing means no data remains past the agreed period.

items.title: Mitigation recommendations (8.1)
items.description:
Recommends how to address each finding and the root cause behind it.

  • Recommendations cover technical fixes and, where the cause is not technical, process or policy changes.
  • Each recommendation is tied to a finding and specific enough to act on.
  • Recommendations are prioritised by risk.

Record: recommendations per finding and root cause; passing means every finding has an actionable recommendation.

items.title: Reporting (8.2)
items.description:
Produces reports suited to each audience and handles them as sensitive documents.

  • Management receives a summary; system and security staff receive the technical detail.
  • Findings carry risk ratings, evidence and mitigation recommendations.
  • Reports are marked, stored and distributed as sensitive.

Record: report versions, recipients and delivery date; passing means each audience received what it needs, securely.

items.title: Remediation/mitigation (8.3)
items.description:
Makes sure recommended actions are actually carried out and verified, which is the point of the assessment.

  • Remediation is planned and tracked, for example in a plan of action and milestones.
  • Fixes are tested before deployment where they could affect operations.
  • Implemented fixes are verified, for example by retesting the original findings.

Record: remediation status per finding and verification evidence; passing means every finding is fixed and verified, or formally accepted.

web_owasp_asvs5_v2.name: Application Security Verification (OWASP ASVS 5.0)
web_owasp_asvs5_v2.description: Coverage tracker for verifying an application against OWASP ASVS 5.0.0, one item per section of chapters V1 to V17, noting the level (L1, L2 or L3) at which each requirement starts. Agree the target level first, tick a section once its requirements at that level are verified or recorded as not applicable, and note where documentation, configuration or code access was needed rather than black-box testing.

items.title: V1.1 Encoding and sanitization architecture
items.description:
Fixes where decoding and output encoding happen.

  • Input is decoded to canonical form once, where expected, before validation or sanitisation (L2).
  • Encoding and escaping happen last, just before or inside the target interpreter (L2).
  • Data is stored unencoded, so it is never encoded twice.

Record: where decoding and encoding happen; pass is single decoding and late, context-specific encoding.

items.title: V1.2 Injection prevention
items.description:
Requires context-correct encoding and safe query interfaces.

  • Output is encoded for its HTML, attribute, CSS, header, URL or JavaScript and JSON context, allowing only safe URL schemes (L1).
  • Database queries of every kind, stored procedures included, are parameterised or use an ORM (L1).
  • OS calls are parameterised or use command-line encoding (L1).
  • LDAP, XPath, LaTeX and regular expression construction is protected (L2).
  • CSV and spreadsheet exports escape leading formula characters (L3).

Record: each interpreter and outcome; pass is no input altering structure.

items.title: V1.3 Sanitization
items.description:
Covers sanitising where encoding is not possible.

  • Rich-text HTML uses a well-known sanitiser; eval and expression languages such as SpEL are avoided (L1).
  • SVG, Markdown, CSS, XSL and similar scriptable content is sanitised or disabled (L2).
  • Outbound requests are checked against protocol, domain, path and port allowlists (SSRF, L2).
  • Template, JNDI, memcache, format string and SMTP or IMAP inputs are protected (L2).
  • Regular expressions avoid exponential backtracking (L3).

Record: each sink and outcome; pass is untrusted content sanitised or refused.

items.title: V1.4 Memory, string, and unmanaged code
items.description:
Applies where the application or its components include memory-unsafe code.

  • String handling, memory copies and pointer arithmetic use safe functions that stop stack, buffer and heap overflows (L2).
  • Sign, range and input checks prevent integer overflows (L2).
  • Freed memory is released and dangling pointers cleared to prevent use-after-free (L2).

Record: whether unmanaged code is in scope and how it was assessed, usually by code review; record not applicable for fully managed stacks.

items.title: V1.5 Safe deserialization
items.description:
Covers XML parser settings, deserialisation of untrusted data and parser consistency.

  • XML parsers use a restrictive configuration with external entity resolution disabled (XXE, L1).
  • Deserialisation of untrusted data uses type allowlists, and mechanisms documented as unsafe are never used with it (L2).
  • Parsers handling the same data type (JSON, XML, URL) parse consistently and use the same character encoding (L3).

Record: parsers and deserialisation points found; pass is safe configuration and no untrusted object creation.

items.title: V2.1 Validation and business logic documentation
items.description:
Requires written validation rules and business limits that testing can be measured against.

  • Documentation defines validation rules for each data item's expected structure (L1).
  • It defines how combined items are checked for logical and contextual consistency (L2).
  • Business logic limits are documented per user and across the application (L2).

Record: documents provided and gaps; the rules found become the test cases for V2.2 to V2.4.

items.title: V2.2 Input validation
items.description:
Requires positive validation of input against business expectations at a trusted layer.

  • Input is checked against allowlisted values, patterns, ranges or expected structure; L1 may focus on input used for business or security decisions, L2 and above cover all input (L1).
  • Validation is enforced at a trusted service layer, never relying on client-side checks (L1).
  • Combinations of related items are checked against predefined rules (L2).

Record: inputs tested with out-of-range and inconsistent values; pass is server-side rejection.

items.title: V2.3 Business logic security
items.description:
Requires business flows to run in order, within limits and atomically.

  • Each user's flows run in the expected sequence without skipped steps (L1).
  • Documented business limits are enforced (L2).
  • Operations are transactional, succeeding fully or rolling back (L2).
  • Limited resources such as seats or delivery slots are locked against double booking (L2).
  • High-value flows need approval by more than one user (L3).

Record: flows tested out of order and concurrently; pass is limits and sequence held throughout.

items.title: V2.4 Anti-automation
items.description:
Requires protection against automated overuse of application functions.

  • Anti-automation controls stop excessive calls that could exfiltrate data, create junk data, exhaust quotas or deny service (L2).
  • Business flows require realistic human timing and reject overly rapid submissions (L3).
  • Controls are exercised only at rates agreed with the client.

Record: rates attempted and controls triggered; pass is throttling before harm occurs.

items.title: V3.1 Web frontend security documentation
items.description:
Requires documentation of the browser security features the application depends on.

  • Documentation lists the browser features required, such as HTTPS, HSTS and CSP (L3).
  • It says how the application behaves when a feature is missing, such as warning or blocking (L3).
  • The documented fallback is exercised in practice under V3.7.

Record: whether the documentation exists and what it requires; pass is complete feature and fallback definitions.

items.title: V3.2 Unintended content interpretation
items.description:
Stops browsers rendering responses in the wrong context.

  • APIs, uploads and other resources requested directly are not rendered as documents, using Sec-Fetch checks, CSP sandbox or attachment disposition (L1).
  • Text meant as text is inserted with safe functions such as textContent or createTextNode (L1).
  • Client code avoids DOM clobbering through explicit declarations, strict typing and namespacing (L3).

Record: resources requested directly and how they render; pass is no unintended rendering or execution.

items.title: V3.3 Cookie setup
items.description:
Sets cookie attributes and name prefixes.

  • Cookies set Secure, using __Secure- where __Host- is not used (L1).
  • SameSite suits each cookie's purpose (L2).
  • __Host- is used unless sharing with other hosts is intended (L2).
  • Script-inaccessible cookies such as session tokens set HttpOnly and arrive only via Set-Cookie (L2).
  • Name and value together stay within 4096 bytes (L3).

Record: each cookie and its attributes; pass is all cookies meeting the level.

items.title: V3.4 Browser security mechanism headers
items.description:
Requires headers that make browsers enforce policy.

  • HSTS on every response, max-age of a year or more, subdomains included from L2 (L1).
  • CORS allow-origin is fixed or allowlisted; a wildcard only for non-sensitive data (L1).
  • CSP sets object-src and base-uri to 'none' with allowlists, nonces or hashes (L2); per-response nonces or hashes at L3.
  • Responses send nosniff, a Referrer-Policy and CSP frame-ancestors (L2).
  • CSP reporting, and Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy on documents (L3).

Record: headers per response type; pass is each present and correctly valued.

items.title: V3.5 Browser origin separation
items.description:
Protects sensitive functions from cross-origin requests.

  • Sensitive requests need an anti-forgery token or non-safelisted header, or a preflight that cannot be avoided (L1).
  • Sensitive functions avoid safe methods such as GET, or use strict Sec-Fetch checks (L1).
  • Separate applications use separate hostnames; postMessage input from untrusted origins is dropped (L2).
  • No JSONP or authorised data in scripts, and authenticated resources resist cross-origin embedding (L3).

Record: functions tested cross-origin; pass is no forged change or cross-origin read.

items.title: V3.6 External resource integrity
items.description:
Covers client assets hosted by third parties such as CDNs.

  • External scripts, stylesheets and web fonts are static and versioned (L3).
  • Each external asset is protected with Subresource Integrity (L3).
  • Where SRI is not possible, a documented security decision justifies each asset (L3).

Record: external assets and their integrity attributes; pass is SRI on every external asset or a recorded justification.

items.title: V3.7 Other browser security considerations
items.description:
Covers obsolete client technology, redirects and HSTS preload.

  • No Flash, ActiveX, Silverlight, Java applets or similar (L2).
  • Automatic redirects to other domains use an allowlist (L2).
  • Users are warned and can cancel before leaving for an external URL (L3).
  • The top-level domain is HSTS preloaded (L3).
  • Behaviour matches the documentation when browser features are missing (L3).

Record: technologies and redirects found; pass is none unsupported or unrestricted.

items.title: V4.1 Generic web service security
items.description:
Sets baseline expectations for HTTP services and APIs.

  • Response bodies have a matching Content-Type with a safe charset (L1).
  • Only user-facing endpoints redirect HTTP to HTTPS (L2).
  • Users cannot override intermediary headers such as X-Forwarded-* or X-User-ID (L2).
  • Unused HTTP methods are blocked (L3).
  • Highly sensitive messages carry per-message signatures (L3).

Record: responses and headers per endpoint; pass is correct types and no spoofable trusted headers.

items.title: V4.2 HTTP message structure validation
items.description:
Prevents request smuggling and header injection across the HTTP chain.

  • Every component frames messages correctly for its HTTP version (L2).
  • Generated messages have no conflicting Content-Length (L3).
  • HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 messages with connection-specific headers or CR or LF in fields are refused (L3).
  • Outgoing URIs and headers stay within receivers' length limits (L3).

Record: chain components and ambiguous-framing handling, tested with care; pass is consistent rejection.

items.title: V4.3 GraphQL
items.description:
Covers GraphQL-specific denial of service and schema exposure.

  • A query allowlist, depth or amount limits, or cost analysis stop expensive nested queries (L2).
  • Introspection is disabled in production unless the API is meant for other parties (L2).
  • Limits are confirmed to apply to batched and aliased operations too.

Record: limits observed and schema exposure; pass is bounded query cost and no unintended introspection.

items.title: V4.4 WebSocket
items.description:
Covers WebSocket transport, origin checks and session handling.

  • All WebSocket connections use WSS (L1).
  • The handshake checks Origin against an allowlist (L2).
  • Dedicated tokens, used where normal sessions cannot be, meet the session management requirements (L2).
  • Those tokens are obtained or validated through the already authenticated HTTPS session (L2).

Record: handshakes and token handling; pass is encrypted, origin-checked, authenticated channels.

items.title: V5.1 File handling documentation
items.description:
Requires documented rules for every upload feature.

  • Permitted types, extensions and maximum size, including unpacked size, are defined per feature (L2).
  • Documentation says how files are made safe for users to download and process (L2).
  • It defines what happens when a malicious file is detected (L2).

Record: the rules or their absence; pass is a complete rule set that V5.2 to V5.4 tests can follow.

items.title: V5.2 File upload and content
items.description:
Requires uploads to be checked for size, type and archive hazards.

  • Files are limited to sizes the application can process safely (L1).
  • Extension and content are validated, for example by magic bytes; security-relevant files at L1, all files from L2 (L1).
  • Archives are checked for unpacked size and file count before extraction (L2).
  • Per-user quotas, symlink refusal in archives and image pixel limits apply (L3).

Record: files tried and outcomes; pass is oversized, mismatched and hazardous files refused.

items.title: V5.3 File storage
items.description:
Covers where and how uploaded and generated files are kept.

  • Files from untrusted input stored in public folders are never executed as server-side code (L1).
  • File paths come from internal or trusted data, and any user-supplied names are strictly validated against traversal, LFI, RFI and SSRF (L1).
  • Decompression and similar processing ignore user-supplied paths (zip slip, L3).

Record: storage locations and naming observed; pass is no execution and no user control of paths.

items.title: V5.4 File download
items.description:
Covers how served files are named and screened.

  • User-submitted file names are validated or ignored, and Content-Disposition names the file (L2).
  • Served file names are encoded or sanitised, for example following RFC 6266 (L2).
  • Files from untrusted sources are antivirus scanned before being served (L2).

Record: download responses and headers; pass is safe naming and scanned content.

items.title: V6.1 Authentication documentation
items.description:
Requires documented authentication defences and pathways.

  • Rate limiting, anti-automation and adaptive responses against credential stuffing and brute force are documented, including how malicious lockout is avoided (L1).
  • A list of context-specific words banned from passwords is documented (L2).
  • Every authentication pathway is documented with the controls and strength it must enforce (L2).

Record: documents reviewed; they set the expected results for V6.2 and V6.3.

items.title: V6.2 Password security
items.description:
Sets password rules in line with current guidance.

  • Minimum 8 characters (15 recommended), any characters, no composition rules (L1).
  • Users can change passwords, giving the current one (L1).
  • The top 3000 common passwords are rejected (L1).
  • Masking, paste and password managers work, and passwords are checked exactly as entered (L1).
  • 64 or more characters allowed, no forced rotation, context words and breached passwords rejected (L2).

Record: the policy at registration, change and reset; pass is the level fully met.

items.title: V6.3 General authentication security
items.description:
Covers defences common to all authentication.

  • Stuffing and brute force defences work as documented, and default accounts such as admin are absent (L1).
  • MFA or an equivalent combination is required (L2), with phishing-resistant hardware at L3.
  • No undocumented pathways, and consistent strength across all (L2).
  • Users are told of suspicious attempts and credential changes (L3).
  • Email is never an authentication factor, and failures reveal no valid users (L3).

Record: each pathway and its controls; pass is consistent, documented strength.

items.title: V6.4 Authentication factor lifecycle and recovery
items.description:
Covers initial secrets, recovery and factor replacement.

  • Initial passwords and activation codes are random, policy-compliant and short-lived or single-use (L1).
  • No password hints or secret questions (L1).
  • Reset does not bypass MFA, and lost factors need identity proofing equal to enrolment (L2).
  • Renewal reminders come in time, and admins can start but not set a user's reset (L3).

Record: recovery flows tested; pass is no route in weaker than normal login.

items.title: V6.5 General multi-factor authentication requirements
items.description:
Sets properties for lookup secrets, out-of-band codes and TOTPs.

  • Codes and lookup secrets are single-use, from a CSPRNG, with at least 20 bits of entropy (L2).
  • Low-entropy lookup secrets are stored with an approved salted password hash (L2).
  • Out-of-band requests expire within 10 minutes, TOTPs within 30 seconds (L2).
  • Factors are revocable, biometrics secondary only, and TOTP time is trusted (L3).

Record: code properties and lifetimes; pass is single-use, short-lived, unpredictable codes.

items.title: V6.6 Out-of-band authentication mechanisms
items.description:
Covers SMS, phone and push-based authentication.

  • SMS or phone codes go only to validated numbers, with a stronger option offered and the risks explained (L2); L3 must not offer them.
  • Out-of-band requests and codes are bound to the original authentication request (L2).
  • Code-based methods are rate limited against brute force (L2).
  • Push notifications are rate limited against push bombing, with number matching as a further aid (L3).

Record: channels offered and limits observed; pass is bound, rate-limited out-of-band checks.

items.title: V6.7 Cryptographic authentication mechanism
items.description:
Covers smart cards, FIDO keys and other key-based authenticators.

  • The cryptographic authenticators in use, if any, are identified first.
  • Certificates used to verify cryptographic assertions are stored so they cannot be modified (L3).
  • Challenge nonces are at least 64 bits long and unique (L3).

Record: authenticator types and challenge properties; record not applicable where none is used.

items.title: V6.8 Authentication with an identity provider
items.description:
Covers federation with external identity providers.

  • With several IdPs, users are keyed on IdP plus user ID to stop cross-IdP spoofing (L2).
  • Assertion signatures (JWT, SAML) are always validated; unsigned ones are rejected (L2).
  • SAML assertions are used once only within their validity (L2).
  • Required strength or recency is read from acr, amr and auth_time, with a documented fallback (L2).

Record: logins tested with altered and replayed assertions; pass is rejection each time.

items.title: V7.1 Session management documentation
items.description:
Requires documented session lifetimes, limits and federation behaviour.

  • Inactivity timeout and absolute lifetime are documented, with any deviation from NIST SP 800-63B justified (L2).
  • The number of concurrent sessions allowed and the action at the limit are defined (L2).
  • Systems sharing sessions in a federation, and how lifetimes and termination are coordinated, are documented (L2).

Record: documented values; they set the expected results for V7.3 to V7.6.

items.title: V7.2 Fundamental session management security
items.description:
Sets core properties of session tokens.

  • Session tokens are verified by a trusted back-end service (L1).
  • Sessions use dynamically generated tokens, not static API secrets or keys (L1).
  • Reference tokens are unique, from a CSPRNG and carry at least 128 bits of entropy (L1).
  • A new token is issued at every authentication, re-authentication included, and the old one ended (L1).

Record: token samples before and after login; pass is fresh, unpredictable, server-verified tokens.

items.title: V7.3 Session timeout
items.description:
Requires enforced inactivity and absolute session limits.

  • An inactivity timeout enforces re-authentication as the documented decision sets out (L2).
  • An absolute maximum lifetime enforces re-authentication as documented (L2).
  • Observed timings are compared with the V7.1 documentation.

Record: timings measured; pass is enforcement matching the documented values.

items.title: V7.4 Session termination
items.description:
Covers ending sessions on logout, expiry and account changes.

  • Ended sessions cannot be reused; self-contained tokens need revocation lists, per-user cut-offs or key rotation (L1).
  • Disabling or deleting an account ends its sessions (L1).
  • Users can end other sessions after a factor change, and logout is on every page (L2).
  • Admins can end sessions for one user or all users (L2).

Record: tokens replayed after each termination event; pass is immediate rejection.

items.title: V7.5 Defenses against session abuse
items.description:
Requires re-authentication and session visibility for sensitive changes.

  • Changing email, phone, MFA or recovery details needs full re-authentication (L2).
  • Users can view active sessions and end any or all of them after re-authenticating with a factor (L2).
  • Highly sensitive operations need further authentication or secondary verification (L3).

Record: sensitive changes attempted from an existing session; pass is a re-authentication prompt each time.

items.title: V7.6 Federated re-authentication
items.description:
Covers session alignment between relying parties and identity providers.

  • Relying party and IdP session lifetimes and termination behave as documented, re-authenticating when required (L2).
  • Creating an application session needs user consent or an explicit action (L2).
  • Silent creation of new sessions through the IdP is checked for.

Record: single sign-on behaviour observed; pass matches the documented design.

items.title: V8.1 Authorization documentation
items.description:
Requires documented access rules that testing can be checked against.

  • Function-level and data-specific access rules are documented (L1).
  • Field-level read and write rules are documented, including state-dependent ones (L2).
  • Environmental and contextual attributes, and how they lead to allow, challenge, deny or step-up decisions, are documented (L3).

Record: documents reviewed; build the role and data matrix for V8.2 to V8.4 from them.

items.title: V8.2 General authorization design
items.description:
Requires explicit permission checks at function, data and field level.

  • Functions are restricted to consumers with explicit permission (L1).
  • Data access is restricted per item, preventing IDOR and BOLA (L1).
  • Field access, for reading and writing, is restricted, preventing BOPLA (L2).
  • Adaptive controls on context such as location or device apply at session start and throughout (L3).

Record: the access matrix tested per role and object; pass is no access beyond explicit permission.

items.title: V8.3 Operation level authorization
items.description:
Covers where and when authorisation decisions are made.

  • Rules are enforced at a trusted service layer, never in client-side code (L1).
  • Permission changes take effect immediately, or misuse is alerted on and reverted (L3).
  • Downstream services decide on the originating user's permissions, not an intermediary's (L3).

Record: tests after permission changes and across service hops; pass is current, server-side, user-based decisions.

items.title: V8.4 Other authorization considerations
items.description:
Covers multi-tenancy and administrative access.

  • Cross-tenant controls stop any operation affecting a tenant the consumer has no rights in (L2).
  • Admin interfaces use layered controls such as continuous identity checks, device posture and risk analysis, not network location alone (L3).
  • Tenant identifiers in requests are tested with accounts in two tenants.

Record: cross-tenant tests and admin access controls; pass is complete isolation.

items.title: V9.1 Token source and integrity
items.description:
Ensures self-contained tokens such as JWTs are trusted only once verified.

  • Signatures or MACs are validated before any content is used (L1).
  • Only allowlisted algorithms are accepted, never 'none', and key confusion is prevented (L1).
  • Verification keys come from trusted pre-configured sources, with jku, x5u and jwk headers allowlisted (L1).

Record: token handling with altered signatures, algorithms and key references; pass is rejection each time.

items.title: V9.2 Token content
items.description:
Ensures token claims are checked for validity period, type and audience.

  • Tokens are accepted only within their validity period, such as nbf and exp (L1).
  • Token type and purpose are checked, so only access tokens drive authorisation and only ID tokens prove authentication (L2).
  • The aud claim is validated against an allowlist (L2).
  • Issuers using one key for several audiences include a unique audience restriction (L2).

Record: claims tested; pass is rejection of expired, wrong-type and wrong-audience tokens.

items.title: V10.1 Generic OAuth and OIDC security
items.description:
Covers token exposure and binding of flows to their originating session.

  • Tokens go only to components that need them; with a backend-for-frontend, the browser never holds access or refresh tokens (L2).
  • PKCE code_verifier, state and nonce are unguessable, per transaction and bound to the client and user agent session (L2).
  • Codes and ID tokens are accepted only for flows started by the same session (L2).

Record: flows traced end to end; pass is tokens confined and responses bound to their flow.

items.title: V10.2 OAuth client
items.description:
Covers protections the client application must apply.

  • The code flow is protected against CSRF with PKCE or a checked state value (L2).
  • Clients using more than one authorisation server defend against mix-up, for example by validating iss (L2).
  • Only the required scopes and parameters are requested (L3).

Record: authorisation requests and responses captured; pass is protected, minimal-scope flows.

items.title: V10.3 OAuth resource server
items.description:
Covers how APIs accept and act on access tokens.

  • Only tokens for this audience are accepted (L2).
  • Decisions use delegated claims such as sub, scope and authorization_details (L2).
  • Users are identified by non-reassignable claims, typically iss with sub (L2).
  • Required strength or recency is checked via acr, amr and auth_time (L2).
  • Sender-constrained tokens (mTLS or DPoP) stop replay (L3).

Record: tokens with altered audience, scope and subject; pass is correct rejection.

items.title: V10.4 OAuth authorization server
items.description:
Covers the authorisation server's own controls.

  • Exact redirect URI matching, and single-use codes valid for at most 10 minutes, or 1 minute at L3 (L1).
  • Only needed grants, never implicit or password, and refresh token replay mitigated (L1).
  • PKCE required without plain, controlled dynamic registration, and absolute, revocable refresh tokens (L2).
  • Confidential clients authenticate on back-channel requests and get only needed scopes (L2).
  • PAR, per-client response modes, sender-constrained tokens and strong client authentication (L3).

Record: configuration and flow tests; pass is the level fully met.

items.title: V10.5 OIDC client
items.description:
Covers relying party checks on ID tokens, providers and logout.

  • ID token replay is prevented, for example by checking nonce (L2).
  • Users are identified by the non-reassignable sub claim (L2).
  • Provider metadata must name exactly the expected issuer (L2).
  • aud must equal the client_id (L2).
  • Back-channel logout tokens are type-checked to prevent forced logout (L2).

Record: ID and logout tokens tested; pass is rejection of replayed or misaddressed tokens.

items.title: V10.6 OpenID Provider
items.description:
Covers settings on the OpenID Provider itself.

  • Only code, ciba, id_token or id_token code responses are allowed, with code preferred and implicit token flows refused (L2).
  • Forced logout is mitigated by user confirmation or by validating id_token_hint (L2).
  • Provider configuration is compared with the responses observed in testing.

Record: allowed response values and logout behaviour; pass is restricted responses and confirmed logout.

items.title: V10.7 Consent management
items.description:
Covers user consent at the authorisation server.

  • Users consent to each authorisation request, always explicitly when the client cannot be assured (L2).
  • Consent screens show what is granted, the requesting application and how long it lasts (L2).
  • Users can review, change and revoke consents (L2).

Record: consent screens and revocation tested; pass is informed, revocable consent.

items.title: V11.1 Cryptographic inventory and documentation
items.description:
Requires knowing what cryptography is used and how keys are managed.

  • A key management policy and lifecycle follow a standard such as NIST SP 800-57, without oversharing keys (L2).
  • An inventory of keys, algorithms and certificates records where each may be used (L2).
  • Discovery mechanisms find every use of cryptography (L3).
  • A migration plan covers new standards such as post-quantum cryptography (L3).

Record: documents reviewed, as this is largely documentation-based; pass is a current inventory and policy.

items.title: V11.2 Secure cryptography implementation
items.description:
Covers how cryptography is implemented.

  • Industry-validated libraries or hardware are used (L2).
  • Crypto agility lets algorithms, keys and parameters be swapped and data re-encrypted (L2).
  • Every primitive gives at least 128 bits of security, for example 3072-bit RSA or 256-bit ECC (L2).
  • Operations are constant-time and fail securely, with no padding oracle (L3).

Record: libraries and parameters identified; pass is validated implementations of adequate strength.

items.title: V11.3 Encryption algorithms
items.description:
Covers the choice of ciphers, modes and integrity protection.

  • No insecure modes such as ECB or weak padding such as PKCS#1 v1.5 (L1).
  • Only approved ciphers and modes, such as AES with GCM (L1).
  • Encrypted data is protected against modification by authenticated encryption or an approved MAC (L2).
  • Nonces and IVs are never reused for the same key and data pair (L3).
  • Combined encryption and MAC operate as encrypt-then-MAC (L3).

Record: algorithms and modes observed; pass is approved, authenticated encryption only.

items.title: V11.4 Hashing and hash-based functions
items.description:
Covers hash functions, password storage and key derivation.

  • Only approved hash functions for cryptographic use, never MD5 (L1).
  • Passwords use an approved, deliberately slow password hashing function with current parameters (L2).
  • Signature and integrity hashes are collision resistant with adequate length (L2).
  • Password-derived keys use approved key derivation with stretching (L2).

Record: functions and parameters identified; pass is approved, tuned functions.

items.title: V11.5 Random values
items.description:
Covers randomness for values that must not be guessed.

  • Non-guessable values come from a CSPRNG with at least 128 bits of entropy; UUIDs do not meet this (L2).
  • The generator stays secure under heavy demand (L3).
  • Samples of tokens and identifiers collected in testing show no pattern.

Record: where random values are used and their source; pass is CSPRNG output of adequate entropy.

items.title: V11.6 Public key cryptography
items.description:
Covers key generation, signatures and key exchange.

  • Approved algorithms and modes are used for key generation, seeding and signatures (L2).
  • Key generation cannot produce weak keys, such as RSA keys open to Fermat factorisation (L2).
  • Key exchange such as Diffie-Hellman uses approved algorithms with secure parameters (L3).

Record: algorithms and key sizes seen in certificates and protocols; pass is approved choices throughout.

items.title: V11.7 In-use data cryptography
items.description:
Covers protecting sensitive data while it is being processed.

  • Full memory encryption protects sensitive data in use (L3).
  • Data minimisation limits exposure during processing, with data encrypted again as soon as feasible (L3).
  • Evidence comes from hosting and architecture documentation rather than black-box testing.

Record: platform capabilities confirmed with the client; pass is documented in-use protection.

items.title: V12.1 General TLS security guidance
items.description:
Sets the baseline TLS configuration.

  • Only current TLS versions such as 1.2 and 1.3, latest preferred (L1).
  • Only recommended suites, strongest first (L2); at L3, only suites with forward secrecy.
  • mTLS client certificates are validated as trusted before use (L2).
  • OCSP stapling or similar revocation checking, and Encrypted Client Hello, are enabled (L3).

Record: protocols, suites and certificate checks per endpoint; pass is the level's configuration.

items.title: V12.2 HTTPS communication with external facing services
items.description:
Covers TLS on public HTTP endpoints.

  • TLS protects all client connections to external HTTP services, with no fallback to cleartext (L1).
  • External services use publicly trusted certificates (L1).
  • Every public hostname and port in scope has been checked.

Record: endpoints and certificate details; pass is TLS everywhere with trusted certificates.

items.title: V12.3 General service to service communication security
items.description:
Covers encryption and authentication between internal components.

  • All inbound and outbound connections, databases, monitoring and partners included, are encrypted without fallback (L2).
  • TLS clients validate server certificates, and internal HTTP services use TLS (L2).
  • Internal certificates are trusted only via specific internal CAs or specific self-signed certificates (L2).
  • Services authenticate each other strongly, for example with TLS client certificates (L3).

Record: internal links reviewed with architecture access; pass is encrypted, authenticated links.

items.title: V13.1 Configuration documentation
items.description:
Requires documented communication needs, resource limits and secret rotation.

  • All communication needs are documented, including external services and user-supplied destinations (L2).
  • Connection limits per service and behaviour when they are reached are defined (L3).
  • Resource management, timeouts and retry strategies are defined for each external system (L3).
  • Critical secrets and their rotation schedule are documented (L3).

Record: documents reviewed; they are the baseline for testing V13.2 and V13.3.

items.title: V13.2 Backend communication configuration
items.description:
Covers how back-end components authenticate and what they may reach.

  • Back-end calls outside the user session use service accounts, short-lived tokens or certificates, not static secrets (L2).
  • Back-end accounts are least privilege with no default credentials (L2).
  • An allowlist limits external resources the application and web server may reach (L2).
  • Each connection follows its documented limits, timeouts and retries (L3).

Record: service credentials and egress rules reviewed; pass is least privilege and restricted egress.

items.title: V13.3 Secret management
items.description:
Covers creation, storage and use of back-end secrets.

  • Secrets live in a secrets manager such as a vault, never in source code or build artefacts, hardware-backed at L3 (L2).
  • Access to secrets follows least privilege (L2).
  • Cryptographic operations happen inside an isolated security module (L3).
  • Secrets expire and rotate as documented (L3).

Record: any secret found in client code, repositories or responses; pass is none exposed or hard-coded.

items.title: V13.4 Unintended information leakage
items.description:
Covers deployment leftovers and debug features that leak information.

  • No source control metadata such as .git or .svn is deployed or reachable (L1).
  • Debug modes are off and directory listings are disabled in production (L2).
  • TRACE is unsupported, and internal documentation and monitoring endpoints are not exposed (L2).
  • Detailed back-end version information is hidden (L3).
  • The web tier serves only specified file extensions (L3).

Record: items found with URLs; pass is nothing unintended reachable.

items.title: V14.1 Data protection documentation
items.description:
Requires sensitive data to be classified with protection rules.

  • All sensitive data is identified and classified, including merely encoded data such as Base64 strings or JWT contents (L2).
  • Classification reflects the privacy and data protection rules that apply (L2).
  • Each protection level has documented requirements for encryption, integrity, retention, logging and access (L2).

Record: classification reviewed; it defines what V14.2 and V14.3 tests look for.

items.title: V14.2 General data protection
items.description:
Covers how sensitive data is sent, cached, shared and kept.

  • Sensitive data is never sent in URLs or query strings (L1).
  • Server-side caches keep no sensitive data, or purge it after use (L2).
  • Sensitive data is not sent to untrusted parties such as trackers (L2).
  • Controls match each data class's documented protection level (L2).
  • Cache deception is prevented, minimum data is returned, retention is enforced and file metadata is stripped (L3).

Record: requests and responses showing data handling; pass is minimal, protected data.

items.title: V14.3 Client-side data protection
items.description:
Covers data left behind in the browser.

  • Authenticated data is cleared from client storage when the session ends, with Clear-Site-Data as an aid (L1).
  • Sensitive responses send anti-caching headers such as Cache-Control: no-store (L2).
  • Browser storage holds no sensitive data apart from session tokens (L2).

Record: storage contents and cache headers after logout; pass is nothing sensitive left behind.

items.title: V15.1 Secure coding and architecture documentation
items.description:
Requires documented component management and resource-heavy functions.

  • Risk-based remediation time frames for vulnerable components and library updates are defined (L1).
  • An inventory such as an SBOM covers all third-party libraries from trusted, maintained repositories (L2).
  • Time-consuming or resource-demanding functions and their protections are documented (L2).
  • Risky components and dangerous functionality are highlighted (L3).

Record: documents reviewed; they define the expectations for V15.2.

items.title: V15.2 Security architecture and dependencies
items.description:
Covers component currency, availability protection and isolation.

  • No component exceeds its documented update time frame (L1).
  • Resource-heavy functions are protected against availability loss (L2).
  • Production has no test code, samples or development features (L2).
  • Dependencies come only from expected repositories, preventing dependency confusion (L3).
  • Dangerous functionality and risky components are isolated, for example by sandboxing (L3).

Record: component versions and extras found; pass is current components and a lean build.

items.title: V15.3 Defensive coding
items.description:
Covers coding weaknesses often visible from outside.

  • Responses return only needed fields, never whole objects (L1).
