  • Back-end URL calls do not follow redirects unless intended (L2).
  • Mass assignment is blocked by per-action field limits (L2).
  • Client IPs come from trusted proxy fields for logging and rate limits (L2).
  • Strict types and comparisons, with prototype and parameter pollution prevented (L2).

Record: fields returned, accepted and parsed; pass is no over-exposure or type confusion.

items.title: V15.4 Safe concurrency
items.description:
Covers race conditions and thread safety.

  • Shared objects use thread-safe types and synchronisation (L3).
  • Checks and the actions that depend on them are atomic, avoiding TOCTOU races (L3).
  • Locks are used consistently, avoid deadlock and stay within the owning code (L3).
  • Resource allocation prevents thread starvation (L3).

Record: parallel requests on state-changing functions plus code review notes; pass is consistent results under concurrency.

items.title: V16.1 Security logging documentation
items.description:
Requires an inventory of the logging performed.

  • An inventory covers logging at each layer: events, formats, storage, use, access and retention (L2).
  • Events generated during testing are compared with the inventory.
  • Gaps between the inventory and the V16.3 security events are noted.

Record: inventory reviewed; pass is a complete, current inventory.

items.title: V16.2 General logging
items.description:
Covers log content, timing and handling.

  • Entries record when, where, who and what (L2).
  • Time sources are synchronised, with UTC or explicit offsets (L2).
  • Logs go only to documented destinations in a format the processor can correlate (L2).
  • Sensitive data is logged per its protection level, credentials excluded and tokens masked (L2).

Record: sample entries for test activity; pass is complete, consistent and redacted entries.

items.title: V16.3 Security events
items.description:
Requires the events investigators need to be logged.

  • All authentication attempts, successful and failed, are logged with factor details (L2).
  • Failed authorisation is logged (L2); at L3 all decisions and sensitive data access are logged too.
  • Documented security events and attempts to bypass controls are logged (L2).
  • Unexpected errors and control failures such as back-end TLS errors are logged (L2).

Record: test actions matched to log entries with the client; pass is every expected event recorded.

items.title: V16.4 Log protection
items.description:
Covers the integrity and confidentiality of logs.

  • Logged data is encoded to prevent log injection (L2).
  • Logs are protected from unauthorised access and modification (L2).
  • Logs are sent securely to a logically separate system for analysis and alerting (L2).

Record: log handling evidence; pass is encoded, protected, centrally held logs.

items.title: V16.5 Error handling
items.description:
Covers safe failure behaviour.

  • Unexpected errors return a generic message with no stack traces, queries, keys or tokens (L2).
  • The application stays secure when external resources fail, for example via circuit breakers (L2).
  • Exceptions fail closed, so no transaction proceeds after a validation error (L2).
  • A last-resort handler catches all unhandled exceptions (L3).

Record: error responses and failure behaviour; pass is generic errors and fail-closed handling.

items.title: V17.1 TURN server
items.description:
Applies where the application uses WebRTC with a TURN relay.

  • TURN services in use, including third-party ones, are identified first.
  • TURN relays only to addresses not reserved for special use, blocking internal, loopback and broadcast ranges in IPv4 and IPv6 (L2).
  • TURN resists exhaustion when legitimate users open many ports (L3).

Record: relay targets attempted within scope and limits seen; pass is no relay to reserved ranges.

items.title: V17.2 Media
items.description:
Covers DTLS-SRTP protection and media server resilience.

  • The DTLS key is managed under the key policy, with approved suites and a secure DTLS-SRTP profile (L2).
  • SRTP authentication blocks RTP injection, and malformed SRTP does not halt processing (L2).
  • SRTP floods from legitimate users, recording included, do not halt processing (L3).
  • No DTLS ClientHello race, and certificates match the SDP fingerprint (L3).

Record: media server configuration and behaviour; pass is authenticated, resilient media.

items.title: V17.3 Signaling
items.description:
Covers signalling server resilience.

  • Signalling keeps processing legitimate messages during a flood, using rate limiting (L2).
  • Malformed signalling messages do not cause denial of service (L2).
  • Load and malformed-message tests stay within limits agreed with the client.

Record: behaviour under load and malformed input; pass is continued service.

web_owasp_api_top10_2023_v2.name: API Security Testing (OWASP API Security Top 10 2023)
web_owasp_api_top10_2023_v2.description: Coverage tracker for an API phase based on the OWASP API Security Top 10 2023, one item per risk with the concrete checks behind it. Tick a risk once every in-scope endpoint it applies to has been tested against it and the evidence is recorded.

items.title: API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization
items.description:
Establishes whether callers can act on objects they do not own by changing identifiers.

  • Every endpoint taking an object ID in the path, query, body or a header is listed.
  • Each is called by two users of the same role with swapped IDs, for read, update and delete.
  • Nested and indirect references, such as file keys and GraphQL node IDs, are included.
  • Ownership is checked per object server-side, not only by matching the token's user ID to a parameter.
  • List, search and export endpoints return only the caller's objects.
  • Random or unpredictable IDs are not treated as the control.

Record: endpoint, operation, accounts and response; pass is refusal of every foreign object.

items.title: API2:2023 Broken Authentication
items.description:
Establishes whether authentication and recovery resist guessing, credential stuffing and token abuse.

  • All authentication flows are known, including refresh, recovery, magic links and mobile routes.
  • Login and recovery endpoints have anti-brute-force controls stricter than general rate limits.
  • Tokens are checked for signature, algorithm and expiry; unsigned or weakly signed JWTs are refused.
  • Credentials and tokens never travel in URLs.
  • Changing email, password or MFA settings requires the current password or re-authentication.
  • API keys do not authenticate users, and internal services require authentication too.

Record: flows and token checks; pass is strong, consistent authentication on every flow.

items.title: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
items.description:
Establishes whether callers can read or change individual properties they should not.

  • Responses are compared with what each role should see, with no hidden sensitive properties.
  • Extra properties in requests, such as role, owner, price or status, are rejected or ignored.
  • Update endpoints change only the properties the caller may edit.
  • GraphQL fields and nested objects are covered as well.
  • Filtering happens on the server, never left to the client.

Record: object types and the properties exposed or writable; pass is minimal output and an allowlist of writable properties.

items.title: API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption
items.description:
Establishes whether limits stop a client exhausting resources or running up costs.

  • Rate limits apply per client and per operation, stricter on costly ones.
  • Body, string, array and upload sizes are capped.
  • Page size and record count parameters have server-side maximums.
  • GraphQL batching and query cost are limited.
  • Paid actions such as SMS, email, calls and biometric checks have per-user limits and spending caps.
  • OTP checks and recovery requests are throttled per account.

Record: limits observed within agreed test rates; pass is limits enforced with a clear rejection.

items.title: API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization
items.description:
Establishes whether lower-privileged callers can use admin or other roles' functions.

  • Privileged endpoints are found from documentation, client code and naming patterns.
  • Each is called as every lower role and anonymously.
  • Changing the HTTP method, such as GET to PUT or DELETE, unlocks nothing.
  • Older API versions and alternative paths enforce the same role checks.
  • Admin functions inside regular controllers are checked, not just admin paths.
  • Access is denied by default unless explicitly granted.

Record: function, role and response; pass is refusal of every out-of-role call.

items.title: API6:2023 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
items.description:
Establishes whether flows that harm the business when automated are protected.

  • Sensitive flows are agreed with the client, such as purchase, booking, referral, posting and sign-up.
  • Automating each flow at scale is detected or slowed by device checks, human verification or behaviour signals.
  • The API applies the same protection as the web or mobile front end.
  • Machine-facing APIs such as B2B and partner endpoints have equivalent limits.
  • Non-human patterns, such as checkout seconds after add-to-basket, are flagged.

Record: flows reviewed and controls seen within agreed limits; pass is protection matched to business risk.

items.title: API7:2023 Server Side Request Forgery
items.description:
Establishes whether URL-fetching features can reach destinations they should not.

  • Features accepting URLs or remote references are listed: webhooks, imports, previews, custom SSO and file fetches.
  • Internal, loopback, link-local and cloud metadata destinations are refused.
  • Redirects are not followed, or each hop is revalidated.
  • Allowlists cover schemes, ports, hosts and expected media types.
  • Raw fetched responses are never returned to the caller.
  • Blind cases are checked with an agreed external callback endpoint.

Record: feature, destinations reached and evidence; pass is only intended destinations reachable.

items.title: API8:2023 Security Misconfiguration
items.description:
Establishes whether the API stack is hardened end to end.

  • TLS protects all API traffic, internal hops included where visible.
  • Only required HTTP methods are enabled.
  • CORS trusts only named origins, and browser-facing APIs send security headers.
  • Errors carry no stack traces or internal detail.
  • Cache-control headers prevent caching of sensitive responses.
  • Unneeded features are off, components are patched and cloud permissions are tight.
  • All servers in the chain parse requests the same way, so none can be desynchronised.

Record: each deviation with its request and response; pass is a consistently hardened stack.

items.title: API9:2023 Improper Inventory Management
items.description:
Establishes whether every API host, version and data flow is known and governed.

  • Hosts, versions and environments found are reconciled with the client's inventory.
  • Old versions are retired, or protected to the same standard as current ones.
  • Non-production APIs hold no production data, or are protected as production.
  • Documentation is current and available only to authorised users.
  • Third-party data flows are known, justified and approved.

Record: undocumented hosts, versions and flows found; pass is a complete, governed inventory.

items.title: API10:2023 Unsafe Consumption of APIs
items.description:
Establishes whether data from third-party APIs is treated as untrusted.

  • Integrations are listed with the data each supplies.
  • Third-party data is validated and sanitised before use or storage.
  • Calls to integrations use TLS.
  • Redirects from integrated services follow an allowlist, never blindly.
  • Timeouts and resource limits apply to third-party responses.
  • Providers' API security posture has been assessed.

Record: integrations reviewed, often with design or code access; pass is validated, bounded, encrypted consumption.

web_owasp_top10_2025_v2.name: Web Application Risks (OWASP Top 10 2025)
web_owasp_top10_2025_v2.description: Coverage tracker based on the OWASP Top 10 2025, one item per category, for confirming each category has been considered and for grouping findings for the reader. The Top 10 is an awareness list rather than a test method, so drive the testing from the WSTG checklist and use these checks to confirm nothing was missed.

items.title: A01:2025 Broken Access Control
items.description:
Establishes whether access is enforced on the server across roles, objects and functions.

  • Everything except public resources is denied by default.
  • Other users' records cannot be read or changed by altering identifiers (IDOR).
  • Lower roles and anonymous users cannot reach or force-browse to privileged functions.
  • Tampered JWTs, cookies or hidden fields grant nothing, and invalidated tokens stay invalid.
  • CORS allows only trusted origins, and APIs enforce access control on POST, PUT and DELETE.
  • SSRF and CSRF, which this edition maps to this category, are covered.

Record: access matrix results and each failure; pass is server-side enforcement everywhere.

items.title: A02:2025 Security Misconfiguration
items.description:
Establishes whether every layer of the stack is hardened.

  • No default accounts, sample apps, unnecessary services, ports or features.
  • Errors show no stack traces or overly detailed messages.
  • Security headers are present and correctly valued.
  • Server, framework and database security settings are secure, including new features after upgrades.
  • Cloud storage and service permissions are least privilege.
  • XML parsers are hardened against XXE.
  • No static secrets are embedded in code, configuration or pipelines.

Record: each misconfiguration with evidence; pass is a consistently hardened configuration.

items.title: A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures
items.description:
Establishes whether components and the build chain are known, current and controlled.

  • Client and server components, transitive ones included, are inventoried, ideally in an SBOM.
  • Components are supported, with no unpatched known vulnerabilities.
  • Components come from trusted sources, with signed packages preferred.
  • Unused dependencies and features have been removed.
  • Repositories, CI/CD and artefact stores use MFA, least privilege and separation of duties.
  • Patching is risk-based and timely rather than waiting for a fixed cycle.

Record: components with versions and advisories; pass is current, inventoried, trusted components.

items.title: A04:2025 Cryptographic Failures
items.description:
Establishes whether sensitive data is protected with sound cryptography.

  • Data classification shows what must be encrypted at rest and in transit.
  • TLS 1.2 or later with forward secrecy and HSTS; no cleartext protocol carries sensitive data.
  • No MD5, SHA-1, ECB, CBC or PKCS#1 v1.5 is in use, and encryption is authenticated.
  • Keys are not default, weak, reused or committed to source, and IVs are never reused.
  • Passwords use salted, adaptive hashing such as Argon2, scrypt or PBKDF2.
  • Randomness comes from a properly seeded CSPRNG, and sensitive responses are not cached.

Record: algorithms, protocols and key handling observed; pass is current algorithms and protected keys.

items.title: A05:2025 Injection
items.description:
Establishes whether untrusted input can change the meaning of interpreter commands.

  • All inputs are covered: parameters, headers, cookies, URLs, JSON, SOAP and XML.
  • SQL, NoSQL, ORM, OS command, LDAP and EL or OGNL injection are assessed.
  • Cross-site scripting, which this category includes, is covered.
  • Queries are parameterised, including inside stored procedures.
  • Table, column and sort identifiers are allowlisted, as they cannot be escaped.
  • Prompt injection in LLM features is tracked separately under the LLM Top 10.

Record: each input, interpreter and outcome; pass is no input altering a command or query.

items.title: A06:2025 Insecure Design
items.description:
Establishes whether the controls the business risk calls for were designed in.

  • Threat models exist for authentication, access control, business logic and key flows.
  • Business limits on quantity, value and frequency are defined and enforced.
  • Tenants are segregated by design across all tiers.
  • Plausibility checks exist at each tier, front end to back end.
  • Misuse cases such as bots, scalping or workflow abuse are tested.
  • Trust boundaries are clear and credentials are never stored unprotected.

Record: design weaknesses with business impact; pass is controls present by design.

items.title: A07:2025 Authentication Failures
items.description:
Establishes whether authentication resists automated and credential-based attacks.

  • Credential stuffing, password spraying and brute force are blocked or slowed.
  • No default credentials exist, and weak or breached passwords are rejected.
  • Password rules follow NIST SP 800-63B, with no forced rotation.
  • MFA is enforced with no weak fallback.
  • Recovery avoids knowledge-based answers, and no route enumerates accounts.
  • A new session ID follows login, sessions end on logout and timeout, and JWT aud and iss are validated.

Record: each authentication path tested; pass is consistent, strong authentication.

items.title: A08:2025 Software or Data Integrity Failures
items.description:
Establishes whether code, updates and data are verified before being trusted.

  • Updates and plugins are signed and verified before use.
  • Dependencies come only from trusted repositories.
  • CDN-hosted and third-party scripts are integrity-protected.
  • CI/CD is segregated and access-controlled, and changes are reviewed.
  • Serialised data from clients is never trusted without a signature or integrity check.
  • Unintended object attributes cannot be set through mass assignment.

Record: integrity checks observed; pass is verified sources and tamper-evident data.

items.title: A09:2025 Security Logging and Alerting Failures
items.description:
Establishes whether attacks are logged, alerted on and acted upon.

  • Logins, failures, access control failures and high-value transactions are logged with user context.
  • Log data is encoded against injection and excludes sensitive data.
  • Logs are protected from tampering and backed up off the host.
  • Alert thresholds and escalation exist, and the client confirms whether testing raised alerts.
  • High-value transactions have an append-only audit trail.
  • Logging and alerting events are not visible to users.

Record: test activity matched to alerts with the client; pass is timely detection of the testing.

items.title: A10:2025 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions
items.description:
Establishes whether errors and unexpected conditions fail safely.

  • Missing, malformed or extreme parameters cause no crash or detail leakage.
  • Failures fail closed: partial transactions roll back and no access is granted on error.
  • Insufficient privilege and resource exhaustion are handled gracefully.
  • A global exception handler exists, and errors are logged and alerted.
  • Rate limits and quotas prevent conditions caused by excessive use.
  • Error messages are generic and consistent.

Record: conditions triggered and outcomes; pass is safe failure to a known state.

ai_owasp_llm_top10_2026_v2.name: LLM Application Testing (OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026)
ai_owasp_llm_top10_2026_v2.description: Coverage tracker for an application built on a large language model, based on the OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026, one item per risk with the concrete checks behind it. Tick a risk once every model input, output and integration it applies to has been reviewed; where the model acts as an agent with tools and memory, also use the project's OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications.

items.title: LLM01:2026 Prompt Injection
items.description:
Establishes whether any input route can make the model act outside its intended behaviour.

  • Input routes are mapped: user text, retrieved content, tool and MCP output, images, audio and memory.
  • Direct attempts to override the system instructions do not change role, scope or tool use.
  • Instructions planted in retrieved or trusted-channel content are not followed.
  • Encoded, multilingual and invisible-character instructions are filtered at ingest and at render.
  • Privileged actions pass deterministic policy checks and human confirmation, whatever the model says.
  • Memory writes are controlled, logged and reviewed.

Record: each route and outcome; pass is no route pushing behaviour past intended limits.

items.title: LLM02:2026 Sensitive Information Disclosure
items.description:
Establishes whether confidential data can leak through any output channel.

  • Answers, tool-call arguments, reasoning traces, retrieved chunks and logs are all treated as outputs.
  • Retrieval enforces document and chunk authorisation in the index query, before the model sees data.
  • Users cannot obtain other users' or tenants' data through the model.
  • System prompts hold no secrets or regulated data.
  • Log-probabilities, confidence values and timing are not exposed without need.
  • Observability and telemetry stores restrict and redact prompts and responses.

Record: channels reviewed and data obtained; pass is no unauthorised data reachable.

items.title: LLM03:2026 Excessive Agency
items.description:
Establishes whether the model's tools are limited to what the use case needs.

  • Each tool is listed, and unused or open-ended tools such as shell access are removed.
  • Tool permissions on downstream systems are least privilege, read-only where possible.
  • Tools act in the user's own context, not under a generic high-privilege identity.
  • High-impact actions need human approval that shows the exact action.
  • Authorisation is enforced in code or a policy point, never left to the model.
  • Tool use is logged, monitored and rate-limited with circuit breakers.

Record: the tool inventory with permissions and approvals; pass is least functionality, permission and autonomy.

items.title: LLM04:2026 Supply Chain
items.description:
Establishes whether models, adapters, datasets and serving components are trusted and verified.

  • An SBOM or AI BOM covers models, adapters, datasets and libraries, with licences.
  • Models and adapters come from verified sources with signatures or pinned hashes.
  • Unsafe serialisation formats are avoided or loaded only in safe modes.
  • Conversion, merge and quantisation steps are controlled as high-risk promotion points.
  • Serving frameworks and packages are current, and AI-suggested dependencies are confirmed to exist.
  • Supplier terms and privacy policies do not allow unexpected use of application data.

Record: components with provenance and versions; pass is verified, inventoried, current components.

items.title: LLM05:2026 Data and Model Poisoning
items.description:
Establishes whether data and model artefacts are protected wherever they are ingested or reused.

  • Lineage of training, fine-tuning and embedding data is tracked with version control and signing.
  • Ingested data is validated and comes from vetted suppliers.
  • Write access to corpora, RAG sources and feedback loops is restricted.
  • Automated retraining and feedback loops need validation and human oversight.
  • Chat templates, tokeniser configs and adapters are verified before deployment.
  • Red teaming probes for backdoor triggers after each training or alignment cycle.

Record: pipelines reviewed and controls found; pass is controlled, validated, traceable data flows.

items.title: LLM06:2026 Unbounded Consumption
items.description:
Establishes whether usage limits prevent denial of service, runaway cost and model extraction.

  • Rate limits and quotas apply per user and key, counting requests and tokens per period.
  • Input size and output length, reasoning budgets included, are capped.
  • Hard spending caps stop inference when reached.
  • Agent runs have step, recursion, time and cost limits.
  • Log-probabilities are not exposed, and extraction-style query patterns are detected.
  • Inference endpoints require authentication, and serving frameworks are patched.

Record: limits observed within agreed bounds; pass is limits enforced before harm.

items.title: LLM07:2026 Misinformation
items.description:
Establishes whether incorrect or unsupported output can be acted on unchecked.

  • Outputs that drive decisions, tool calls or code are identified.
  • Claims are grounded in authoritative, current sources and cited.
  • Generated code and package names are verified before use.
  • High-impact actions separate generation from execution, with verification or approval.
  • Structured outputs with mandatory fields reduce critical omissions.
  • Users can tell verified facts from model-generated content.

Record: workflows tested with misleading scenarios; pass is verification before reliance.

items.title: LLM08:2026 Hidden Context Exposure
items.description:
Establishes whether extracted hidden context would help an attacker, and whether any control depends on it staying hidden.

  • System prompts, tool schemas and retrieved policy text are reviewed, and extraction is attempted.
  • No credentials, tokens or connection strings appear in hidden context.
  • Authorisation and privilege separation are enforced outside the model.
  • Refusal and filtering do not rely only on prompt instructions.
  • Knowing the output format does not let attackers craft output that downstream systems trust.

Record: context recovered and its sensitivity; pass is nothing sensitive in context and no reliance on secrecy.

items.title: LLM09:2026 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
items.description:
Establishes whether retrieval stores, vector memory and semantic caches enforce access and resist manipulation.

  • Tenant and user scope is enforced inside the index query, on the server.
  • Similarity scores and raw vectors are not returned to clients.
  • Content of different trust levels is kept in separate indexes.
  • Ingested content is normalised and provenance-tracked, and write access to corpora is restricted.
  • Semantic caches cannot serve one user's content to another.
  • Embeddings are deleted with their sources and protected like the source data.

Record: retrieval tests across users and tenants; pass is no cross-scope retrieval or inference.

items.title: LLM10:2026 Improper Output Handling
items.description:
Establishes whether model output is validated and encoded before it reaches other systems.

  • Every downstream sink is listed: browser, database, shell, file system, email and terminal.
  • Output is encoded for its context, and Markdown or HTML rendering cannot run script.
  • Generated SQL is parameterised and generated file paths are validated.
  • Output never reaches eval or a shell.
  • Auto-loaded images and link previews cannot send data to outside hosts.
  • Control characters are stripped before terminal or log output.

Record: each sink and outcome; pass is model output treated as untrusted input everywhere.

adv_mitre_attack_enterprise_v2.name: Adversary Simulation Coverage (MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise)
adv_mitre_attack_enterprise_v2.description: Coverage tracker for an adversary simulation mapped to the fifteen MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise tactics in v20, after v19 split Defense Evasion into Stealth and Defense Impairment. Tick a tactic once its agreed technique families have been emulated or recorded as out of scope, noting for each technique ID whether it was prevented, detected and responded to.

items.title: Reconnaissance (TA0043)
items.description:
Measures what an adversary could learn before acting, and whether the client notices.

  • Families: Active Scanning (T1595), Gather Victim Identity Information (T1589), Search Open Websites/Domains (T1593).
  • Phishing for Information (T1598) only if approved as social engineering.
  • Prevention: exposure the client could reduce, such as published staff details.
  • Detection and response: whether scanning or probing was seen and acted on.

Record: technique IDs, sources and dates; pass is each marked prevented, detected or missed.

items.title: Resource Development (TA0042)
items.description:
Covers infrastructure, accounts and capabilities built for the simulation, and whether monitoring spots them.

  • Families: Acquire Infrastructure (T1583), Establish Accounts (T1585), Develop Capabilities (T1587), Stage Capabilities (T1608).
  • Compromise Accounts (T1586) and Compromise Infrastructure (T1584) are never done to real third parties.
  • Detection and response: lookalike domain or brand monitoring, and any takedown.

Record: inventory of all created resources; pass is each listed with an owner and removal date.

items.title: Initial Access (TA0001)
items.description:
Tests the entry routes taken from the threat scenarios, and how far controls stop or flag them.

  • Families: Phishing (T1566), Valid Accounts (T1078), External Remote Services (T1133), Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190).
  • Supply Chain Compromise (T1195) and Trusted Relationship (T1199) are simulated, never done to a real supplier.
  • Prevention: mail filtering, MFA and patching. Detection and response: alerts, user reports, time to contain.

Record: each route tried with outcome and times; pass is every planned route covered.

items.title: Execution (TA0002)
items.description:
Tests whether adversary-controlled code or commands can run on in-scope systems, and what is seen when they do.

  • Families: Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059), User Execution (T1204), Scheduled Task/Job (T1053).
  • Where in scope: Cloud Administration Command (T1651), Direct Prompt Injection (T1699), Indirect Prompt Injection (T1698).
  • Prevention: application control. Detection: process telemetry and alerts. Response: isolation.

Record: technique IDs per host with outcome; pass is each marked prevented, detected or missed.

items.title: Persistence (TA0003)
items.description:
Tests whether a foothold survives reboots and credential changes, using only persistence that is approved and registered.

  • Families: Create Account (T1136), Account Manipulation (T1098), Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547), Server Software Component (T1505).
  • Each mechanism placed is logged with host, time and removal step.
  • Detection and response: alerts on new accounts or autostart changes, and whether the client removed them.

Record: persistence register; pass is every item removed and confirmed at close.

items.title: Privilege Escalation (TA0004)
items.description:
Tests whether limited access can become administrative access on the systems that lead to the objectives.

  • Families: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism (T1548), Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068), Valid Accounts (T1078).
  • Domain or Tenant Policy Modification (T1484) is agreed first and reversed afterwards.
  • Prevention: least privilege and patching. Detection: alerts on privileged group or policy changes.

Record: each path to higher privilege with evidence; pass is each marked prevented, detected or missed.

items.title: Stealth (TA0005)
items.description:
Tests whether activity that blends in with normal behaviour, without weakening any defence, is still detected.

  • Families: Masquerading (T1036), Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027), System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218), Valid Accounts (T1078).
  • Indicator Removal (T1070) is simulated, never applied to the client's real logs.
  • Detection: analytics that still flag blended activity. Response: time to investigate.

Record: technique IDs with detection outcome; pass is each recorded for the blue team.

items.title: Defense Impairment (TA0112)
items.description:
Covers breaking or blinding security tooling, the riskiest tactic to emulate, so every change needs explicit approval.

  • Families: Disable or Modify Tools (T1685), Disable or Modify System Firewall (T1686), Prevent Command History Logging (T1690).
  • Prefer test hosts, or tamper attempts that are logged and reversed at once.
  • Detection: tamper protection, alerts when tools stop or logs go quiet. Response: time to restore.

Record: each change and its reversal; pass is every one approved, accounted for and undone.

items.title: Credential Access (TA0006)
items.description:
Tests whether credentials, tokens or tickets can be obtained, and how captured secrets are protected during the test.

  • Families: OS Credential Dumping (T1003), Unsecured Credentials (T1552), Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558), Brute Force (T1110).
  • Guessing respects lockout limits; captured secrets are stored encrypted and masked in reports.
  • Detection and response: credential theft alerts and forced resets.

Record: credential types obtained and how; pass is each marked prevented, detected or missed.

items.title: Discovery (TA0007)
items.description:
Tests how much of the environment an adversary can map from inside, and whether the enumeration stands out.

  • Families: Account Discovery (T1087), Domain Trust Discovery (T1482), Permission Groups Discovery (T1069), Cloud Infrastructure Discovery (T1580).
  • Enumeration is paced to avoid load on production.
  • Detection: alerts on unusual enumeration or decoy accounts. Response: investigation opened.

Record: technique IDs and what each revealed; pass is each marked detected or missed.

items.title: Lateral Movement (TA0008)
items.description:
Tests whether the adversary can move between systems towards the objectives, and where segmentation stops it.

  • Families: Remote Services (T1021), Use Alternate Authentication Material (T1550), Internal Spearphishing (T1534).
  • Each hop is to an in-scope host and logged with source and time.
  • Prevention: segmentation and admin tiering. Detection: unusual logons. Response: containment.

Record: path map with timestamps; pass is each hop marked prevented, detected or missed.

items.title: Collection (TA0009)
items.description:
Tests whether data of interest can be found and gathered, limited to what proves the objective.

  • Families: Data from Information Repositories (T1213), Data from Network Shared Drive (T1039), Email Collection (T1114), Data Staged (T1074).
  • Real data is viewed, not taken, unless agreed; marker files stand in where possible.
  • Detection: data loss and unusual access alerts. Response: action on the account used.

Record: what was reachable and how it was handled; pass is no real data kept.

items.title: Command and Control (TA0011)
items.description:
Tests whether egress controls and monitoring spot the channels used to direct compromised hosts.

  • Families: Application Layer Protocol (T1071), Encrypted Channel (T1573), Web Service (T1102), Protocol Tunneling (T1572).
  • Channels are registered with the control team, protected, and can be shut at once.
  • Prevention: egress filtering. Detection: beaconing or anomaly alerts. Response: time to block.

Record: each channel, its lifetime and detection; pass is every channel accounted for and closed.

items.title: Exfiltration (TA0010)
items.description:
Tests whether data could leave the environment and whether its departure is seen, using agreed marker data.

  • Families: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (T1041), Exfiltration Over Web Service (T1567), Transfer Data to Cloud Account (T1537).
  • Real data leaves only if explicitly authorised; volumes and destinations are logged.
  • Prevention: egress and data loss controls. Detection and response: time to alert and block.

Record: paths, volumes and outcomes; pass is each marked prevented, detected or missed.

items.title: Impact (TA0040)
items.description:
Impact is shown by proving capability, such as the rights to encrypt data or stop services, not by causing harm.

  • Families mapped as scenarios: Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486), Inhibit System Recovery (T1490), Service Stop (T1489), Data Manipulation (T1565).
  • Any live demonstration uses test assets and explicit approval.
  • Detection: whether precursors such as backup tampering alert. Response: recovery readiness.

Record: the agreed demonstration and evidence; pass is impact proven without disruption.

adv_red_team_engagement_v2.name: Threat-Led Red Team Engagement
adv_red_team_engagement_v2.description: Coverage tracker for a threat-led red team run on the phases that TIBER-EU (2025) and the Bank of England's CBEST describe: preparation, threat intelligence, the red team test plan, active testing and closure. Tick an item when its decision or deliverable is on file; the items cover process, objectives and control, never technique.

items.title: Framework, authority and oversight confirmed
items.description:
A threat-led test runs under a framework whose authority oversees it, so establish which applies before anything else.

  • TIBER-EU: the authority's notice is received and a TIBER Cyber Team Test Manager is assigned.
  • CBEST: the regulator leads, and the firm names an executive sponsor.
  • A test outside any framework names a senior sponsor to hold the same oversight role.

Record: notification and named oversight roles; pass is no step taken before this is on file.

items.title: Control team formed and kept secret
items.description:
A small control team, often called the white team, runs the test; only its members know of it.

  • TIBER-EU Control Team and its Lead, or CBEST Control Group and Co-ordinator, are named with backups.
  • Members can reach the top of incident escalation and see blue team detections.
  • Code names are used in all documents, and NDAs are signed where needed.
  • A leak is reported at once: to the regulator under CBEST; under TIBER-EU it can void recognition.

Record: membership and secrecy arrangements; pass is no one outside the team told.

items.title: Initiation documents and project plan
items.description:
Initiation sets out the plan, contacts and secure channels that the whole test relies on.

  • TIBER-EU initiation documents: project charter and plan, control team lead contacts, testers used, secure channels, code name.
  • Under TIBER-EU they reach the Test Manager within three months of notification.
  • CBEST: launch and engagement stages done, with the Project Initiation Document final by procurement.

Record: approved initiation pack; pass is secure channels tested before use.

items.title: Scope: critical functions, systems and flags
items.description:
Scoping fixes which business functions the test targets and what counts as compromising them.

  • TIBER-EU Scope Specification Document: critical or important functions, supporting systems and flags, approved by the management body.
  • CBEST Scope Specification: important business services, key systems and compromise actions, signed off by the executive sponsor.
  • Functions left out are justified, and testing on live production is the norm.

Record: signed scope; pass is every flag tied to a function and a system.

items.title: Risk assessment and authority to halt
items.description:
The entity owns the risk, so the control team assesses it before and during testing and can stop it.

  • Risks cover data exposure to providers, disruption, unintended escalation and incomplete restoration.
  • Backup and restoration of in-scope systems are confirmed before live testing.
  • The control team can halt the test, temporarily or completely, at any time.
  • CBEST: the Control Group approves the tester's Penetration Test Risk Management Plan.

Record: risk assessment versions and halt log; pass is no risk without an owner.

items.title: Escalation route for detections and real incidents
items.description:
A realistic test can look like a real attack, so escalation must neither leak the test nor ignore a real incident.

  • Trusted contacts at the top of incident escalation can deconflict quickly.
  • External steps (CSIRT, law enforcement, information sharing) are not triggered by the test, or are contained.
  • A real incident during testing pauses the test and goes to normal response.

Record: the agreed route and each use of it; pass is no external escalation caused by the test.

items.title: Providers procured and contracted
items.description:
Independent, qualified providers and sound contracts protect the entity and the value of the result.

  • TIBER-EU: an external threat intelligence provider is mandatory; internal red teamers only exceptionally, with Test Manager approval.
  • CBEST: CREST-accredited providers, with the regulator's legal and privacy clauses in the contracts.
  • Contracts cover confidentiality, indemnification, data destruction and prohibited actions.

Record: signed contracts; pass is procurement complete before testing.

items.title: Permission to test every system and provider
items.description:
Testing without the owner's permission risks breaching computer misuse law, so permission must cover every target.

  • Permission covers each in-scope system, including those run by ICT third parties.
  • Third parties that underpin a service either agree to the test or are excluded.
  • CBEST: the test moves past procurement only once the regulator is told contracts are in place.

Record: permission per system and provider; pass is no target without one.

items.title: Targeted threat intelligence produced
items.description:
Intelligence on the entity and its likely attackers drives the scenarios, so it comes before any planning.

  • TIBER-EU TTI report: actionable intelligence on the entity, threat context and threat actor profiles.
  • CBEST: direction, intelligence, validation and assessment stages lead to the Threat Intelligence Report.
  • Exposure found, such as leaked credentials or lookalike domains, is passed to the control team.

Record: accepted intelligence report; pass is every scenario traceable to it.

items.title: Threat scenarios selected
items.description:
Scenarios turn the intelligence into end-to-end tests of the scoped functions.

  • TIBER-EU: at least three threat-led scenarios, together covering confidentiality, integrity and availability.
  • An optional scenario X, not threat-led, is recorded as such.
  • Selection weighs the provider's advice, Test Manager input and red team feasibility.

Record: selected scenarios with rationale; pass is every flag covered by a scenario.

items.title: Red team test plan approved
items.description:
The plan turns each scenario into steps with clear objectives, and is approved before active testing.

  • TIBER-EU: approved by the control team and Test Manager, with time split across the in, through and out phases.
  • CBEST: each step lists prerequisites, target flags, success criteria, possible de-chaining and timings.
  • Alternative approaches are prepared for each phase.

Record: approved plan version; pass is no testing before approval.

items.title: Flags, milestones and success criteria set
items.description:
Flags define success for each scenario and milestones decide when help is given, so progress can be measured.

  • Each flag is a specific compromise of confidentiality, integrity or availability.
  • Milestone dates are set, with the leg-up that follows if one is missed.
  • Success criteria state what evidence proves each flag.

Record: flag and milestone table; pass is each flag with criteria and an owner.

items.title: Leg-ups controlled and logged
items.description:
Leg-ups give testers access or information a patient attacker could gain, without distorting the result.

  • TIBER-EU: supplied by the control team, approved by it and the Test Manager, and logged.
  • No leg-up hands over a flag or disables a security control.
  • CBEST: de-chaining is agreed with the regulator and recorded in the report.

Record: leg-up log with reasons; pass is each approved before use.

items.title: Active testing window and oversight cadence
items.description:
Enough time and regular oversight let the red team act like a patient attacker while risk stays controlled.

  • TIBER-EU: at least 12 weeks of active testing; CBEST: about 14 weeks for the testing phase, indicatively.
  • The control team meets the red team at least weekly, and daily in critical phases.
  • Each update covers progress, flags, detections and coming risks.

Record: meeting notes; pass is no week without a control team update.

items.title: Reconnaissance objectives met within limits
items.description:
Reconnaissance refreshes the intelligence each scenario needs before the target is approached.

  • Objectives are what each scenario must know, not general collection.
  • Sources and methods stay within the agreed scope and privacy limits.
  • New exposure found is passed to the control team.

Record: findings per scenario; pass is no collection outside scope.

items.title: Initial access objectives (the in phase)
items.description:
The in phase shows whether a scenario's entry route works against the entity's defences.

  • Routes used match the approved scenario.
  • Each attempt, success or failure is logged with its time.
  • Whether the blue team noticed is recorded for the replay.
  • Attempts stop once the route is proven, without widening to other targets.

Record: outcome per route; pass is every planned route attempted or explained.

items.title: Persistence and lateral movement objectives (the through phase)
items.description:
The through phase shows whether a foothold can be kept and extended towards the flags.

  • Persistence is approved and registered for removal.
  • Movement targets only in-scope systems on the path to a flag.
  • Credentials obtained are protected and used only for the scenario.
  • Blue team detections and containment are logged against time.

Record: the path to each flag; pass is every step logged and in scope.

items.title: Actions on objectives and flags (the out phase)
items.description:
The out phase proves each flag by showing the agreed compromise is possible, not by causing it.

  • Each flag is proven with the agreed evidence, such as a marker change or a screenshot.
  • No data leaves and no service is disrupted unless the plan allows it.
  • Flags missed are recorded with the furthest point reached.

Record: flag evidence; pass is each flag captured or explained.

items.title: Red team action log kept
items.description:
A complete log of every action underpins the replay, both reports and any later question about harm.

  • Every action is logged with time, source, target and outcome.
  • Logs are protected from change and kept for future reference.
  • Logs reconcile with control team records of leg-ups and halts.
  • Times use one synchronised clock so the blue team can match them.

Record: the full log; pass is no gap in the timeline.

items.title: Blue team detections handled
items.description:
When the blue team detects the test, the control team decides the next step so the learning is not lost.

  • The control team chooses: let the response run, contain it quietly, or pause.
  • Detection time and blue team actions are logged.
  • The secrecy of the test is protected throughout.

Record: detection log; pass is each detection handled by a recorded decision.

items.title: Deviations and halts recorded
items.description:
Changes to the plan alter what the results mean, so each one is approved and recorded.

  • Deviations are approved by the control team and shared with the Test Manager under TIBER-EU.
  • Each halt records the reason, the time and how testing resumed.
  • Scenario changes are reflected in the final reports.

Record: deviation log; pass is no unrecorded change.

items.title: Red team test report delivered
items.description:
The red team report records what was done, what was achieved and why it worked.

  • TIBER-EU: due within four weeks of active testing ending; CBEST: a draft within about two weeks.
  • It covers scenarios, flags reached and missed, attack paths, deviations and leg-ups.
  • Findings carry criticality, root cause and recommendations.

Record: report version issued; pass is acceptance by the control team.

items.title: Blue team test report delivered
items.description:
Once told of the test, the blue team maps its view of events against the red team's actions.

  • The blue team is told when active testing ends, and preserves its evidence.
  • For each attack step it states what was detected, with log references.
  • TIBER-EU: due within ten weeks of active testing ending, with root causes and lessons.

Record: report on file; pass is every attack step answered.

items.title: Detection and response capability assessed
items.description:
CBEST assesses detection and response formally; elsewhere the blue team report gives the same picture.

  • CBEST: the tester completes the regulator's detection and response capability assessment.
  • It includes interviews with SOC and incident response staff after testing.
  • A qualified red team manager oversees it, and it reaches the regulator within two weeks.

Record: the submitted assessment; pass is results not vetted by the firm first.

items.title: Replay exercise held
items.description:
The replay walks the red and blue teams through both sides of the timeline together.

  • TIBER-EU: arranged by the control team within ten weeks of testing ending, once the blue team report is well advanced.
  • Each step is discussed: actions, detections, countermeasures and what more time could achieve.
  • CBEST's nearest equivalent is the review workshop with the regulator and providers.

Record: replay notes; pass is findings fed into the summary and remediation.

items.title: Purple teaming exercise held
items.description:
Purple teaming lets both teams work on the gaps the replay exposed, including scenarios not tested.

  • Strongly recommended in TIBER-EU, after the replay.
  • It ranges from tabletop discussion to technical walkthroughs of alternative scenarios.
  • Detection improvements are agreed with named owners.

Record: outputs with owners; pass is each gap with an agreed action.

items.title: Remediation plan agreed
items.description:
The remediation plan fixes root causes, not just the paths that were used.

  • Measures are prioritised with dates, owners and the risk of doing or not doing each, including detection and response.
  • TIBER-EU: due within eight weeks of the Test Manager's assessment notice.
  • CBEST: drafted on the regulator's template, finalised after a workshop and tracked under supervision.

Record: approved plan; pass is each finding mapped to an action.

items.title: Test summary report approved
items.description:
The test summary report is the entity's account of the whole test for the authority.

  • Under TIBER-EU it is written by the entity and approved by the Test Manager.
  • It covers scope, scenarios, flags, detections, leg-ups, risk measures, findings and root causes.
  • A version without sensitive detail may be requested for sharing.

Record: approved summary; pass is consistency with both team reports.

items.title: 360-degree feedback and debrief
items.description:
Feedback on how the test ran improves the next one and the providers' work.

  • TIBER-EU: the Test Manager holds a 360-degree feedback meeting, and written feedback precedes approval of the summary.
  • CBEST: the providers debrief the regulator, which keeps a debrief log.
  • Lessons on scoping, intelligence and control are recorded.

Record: feedback output; pass is lessons assigned to owners.

items.title: Attestation and follow-up
items.description:
Closure confirms the test met the framework and that remediation is tracked to the end.

  • TIBER-EU: an attestation follows approval of the summary and remediation plan, and supports mutual recognition.
  • CBEST: the regulator supervises remediation, typically over six to twelve months or longer.
  • Progress is reported until every action closes.

Record: attestation or closure letter; pass is remediation tracked to completion.

items.title: Test data and infrastructure closed down
items.description:
Providers hold sensitive data about the entity, so it is returned or destroyed as the contracts require.

  • Test infrastructure, accounts and persistence are removed and confirmed gone.
  • Data held by providers is destroyed or returned, with confirmation.
  • Logs and evidence kept for reference are stored securely with a retention date.

Record: destruction confirmations; pass is nothing held beyond its agreed date.

comp_pci_dss_11_4_v2.name: Penetration Testing for PCI DSS (v4.0.1 Requirement 11.4)
comp_pci_dss_11_4_v2.description: Coverage tracker for the penetration testing PCI DSS v4.0.1 Requirement 11.4 asks for, one item per sub-requirement with 11.4.1 split into its parts, followed by the evidence an assessor will look for. Use it to check the test, its scope and the retest evidence will stand up to an assessor; for the requirement text and testing procedures, follow the linked standard.

items.title: 11.4.1 Methodology defined, documented and implemented
items.description:
Confirms the entity, not only the tester, has a written penetration testing methodology based on industry-accepted approaches, and that this test followed it.

  • The methodology document is owned by the entity, dated and approved.
  • It names the industry-accepted approach it draws on, such as NIST SP 800-115.
  • The report states which methodology was followed and notes any deviations.

Record: methodology title, version and owner, and where the report references it; passing means a current entity methodology this test demonstrably followed.

items.title: 11.4.1 Coverage of the perimeter, critical systems and segmentation
items.description:
Checks the methodology, and this test, cover the entire cardholder data environment (CDE) perimeter and critical systems, from inside and outside the network, plus every segmentation and scope-reduction control.

  • Targets are reconciled with the entity's current PCI DSS scope and network diagrams.
  • Testing ran from both outside and inside the network.
  • Every segmentation or scope-reduction control the entity relies on was tested.

Record: a map of scope elements to tests performed; passing means nothing in scope is untested.

items.title: 11.4.1 Application-layer and network-layer testing
items.description:
Confirms both layers were tested: applications for at least the vulnerabilities listed in Requirement 6.2.4, and the network layer across components that support network functions as well as operating systems.

  • Application tests cover the attack types 6.2.4 lists for in-scope bespoke and custom software.
  • Network testing covers network devices, network services and operating systems.
  • In-scope payment pages and APIs are included.

Record: coverage per component and layer; passing means both layers are evidenced for every in-scope component.

items.title: 11.4.1 Recent threats, risk approach and retention
items.description:
Confirms the methodology covers threats and vulnerabilities experienced in the last 12 months, a documented approach to assessing and addressing exploitable findings, and retention of results.

  • The test plan shows the last 12 months' threats and vulnerabilities were considered.
  • The documented approach explains how exploitable findings are risk-ranked and addressed.
  • Test results and remediation results are kept for at least 12 months.

Record: where each element sits in the methodology; passing means all three are documented and followed.

items.title: 11.4.2 Internal penetration testing
items.description:
Confirms internal testing per the methodology at least once every 12 months and after any significant infrastructure or application upgrade or change.

  • The last two tests are no more than 12 months apart.
  • Each significant change, as the entity defines it, was followed by testing.
  • The tester is a qualified internal resource or qualified external third party with organisational independence (not required to be a QSA or ASV).

Record: test dates, change list and tester details; passing means frequency, change testing and independence are evidenced.

items.title: 11.4.3 External penetration testing
items.description:
Confirms external testing per the methodology at least once every 12 months and after any significant infrastructure or application upgrade or change.

  • The last two tests are no more than 12 months apart.
  • Each significant change to internet-facing systems was followed by testing.
  • The tester is qualified and organisationally independent (not required to be a QSA or ASV).
  • ASV scans under 11.3.2 are not presented as this test.

Record: test dates, change list and tester details; passing means frequency, change testing and independence are evidenced.

items.title: 11.4.4 Exploitable findings corrected and retested
items.description:
Confirms exploitable vulnerabilities and security weaknesses from the test are corrected in line with the entity's risk assessment under Requirement 6.3.1, and testing is repeated to verify them.

  • Each exploitable finding has a risk ranking and a fix date consistent with it.
  • Retesting repeated the conditions of the original finding.
  • Retest results show the issue is no longer exploitable, with residual items tracked.

Record: finding, ranking, fix date, retest date and result; passing means retest evidence for every exploitable finding.

items.title: 11.4.5 Segmentation testing
items.description:
Where segmentation isolates the CDE, confirms every segmentation control and method in use is tested, per the methodology, at least once every 12 months and after any change to them.

  • Results show the controls work and isolate the CDE from all out-of-scope systems.
  • Any isolation of systems with differing security levels (Requirement 2.2.3) is shown to work.
  • The tester is qualified and organisationally independent.

Record: per control: source, destination, method, date and result; passing means no out-of-scope segment reaches the CDE.

items.title: 11.4.6 Service providers: segmentation every six months
items.description:
For service providers using segmentation, confirms the 11.4.5 testing runs at least once every six months and after any change to segmentation controls or methods.

  • Test dates show no gap longer than six months.
  • Each change to segmentation controls was followed by a test.
  • Scope matches 11.4.5: all controls in use, effectiveness, isolation from out-of-scope systems and a qualified, independent tester.

Record: test dates and the segmentation change log; passing means six-monthly and change-driven tests are both evidenced.

items.title: 11.4.7 Multi-tenant service providers support customer testing
items.description:
Confirms a multi-tenant service provider supports its customers' external penetration testing under Requirements 11.4.3 and 11.4.4; this has been mandatory since 31 March 2025.

  • The provider gives evidence that 11.4.3 and 11.4.4 testing covered each customer's subscribed infrastructure, or prompt access for customers to test it.
  • Evidence, which may be redacted, still proves both requirements were met.
  • The process for customers is documented.

Record: the option used and the evidence or access process; passing means customers can get either promptly.

items.title: 12.5.2 Test scope matches the confirmed PCI DSS scope
items.description:
Assessors compare the test scope with the entity's documented scope confirmation, due at least every 12 months and on significant change (every six months for service providers under 12.5.2.1).

  • The test scope was drawn from the latest scope confirmation and data flow diagrams.
  • Systems in, connected to or able to affect the CDE, and every segmentation control, are covered.
  • Systems added since that confirmation are tested or explained.

Record: scope document date and its mapping to targets; passing means no gap between documented and tested scope.

items.title: Tester qualification and independence evidenced
items.description:
Requirements 11.4.2, 11.4.3, 11.4.5 and 11.4.6 call for a qualified internal resource or qualified external third party with organisational independence; assessors expect evidence, not assertion.

  • Qualifications (certifications, experience, training) are documented for each tester.
  • Internal testers sit outside the teams that run or administer the systems tested.
  • The report names the testers and their organisation.

Record: tester names, qualifications and reporting line; passing means qualification and independence are evidenced for every test.

items.title: A1.1.4 Multi-tenant separation tested every six months
items.description:
For multi-tenant service providers, Appendix A1 requires penetration testing at least once every six months to confirm the logical separation between customer environments, in addition to the testing under 11.4.6.

  • Tests attempt access from one customer environment to another, and to the provider's own environment.
  • Test dates show no gap longer than six months.
  • Any separation failure is corrected and retested, with evidence kept.

Record: test dates, environments tested and results; passing means no cross-customer access.

items.title: Results and remediation records retained for 12 months
items.description:
Assessors ask for the past year's reports and remediation evidence, so retention under 11.4.1 must work in practice, not only on paper.

  • Reports, retest reports and remediation records from at least the last 12 months can be produced.
  • Records show who fixed what, and when.
  • Reports are stored securely, as they describe exploitable weaknesses.

Record: where records are kept and the oldest available; passing means 12 months of results and remediation evidence on file.

items.title: Retest evidence linked to each exploitable finding
items.description:
For 11.4.4, assessors look for a retest record they can match finding by finding, not a general statement that issues were fixed.

  • Each retest entry cites the original finding identifier, the date and who retested.
  • The retest used the same method and vantage point as the original test.
  • Findings still open have a risk-based target date and an owner.

Record: the retest report or tracker extract; passing means every exploitable finding has matching, dated retest evidence.

items.title: Report traceable to every 11.4 element
items.description:
The report is the main evidence for Requirement 11.4, so it must show what was tested, how, by whom and with what result.

  • Dates, scope, test positions (inside and outside), methodology and tester details are stated.
  • Each finding states whether it was exploitable, its risk ranking and its evidence.
  • Manual testing beyond the vulnerability scans required by 11.3 is evident.
  • Segmentation results are given per control and per out-of-scope segment.

Record: the report version used for compliance; passing means each 11.4 element is traceable in it.

infra_active_directory_v2.name: Active Directory Security Review
infra_active_directory_v2.description: Coverage tracker for an Active Directory review within an internal infrastructure phase, going deeper than the internal checklist: password policy, Kerberos, delegation, privileged groups, permissions and tiering, LAPS, Group Policy, Certificate Services (the ESC classes), NTLM and relay, trusts, and audit and detection. Work through it with a domain account, keep the evidence each item names, and tick it once covered or recorded as not applicable.

items.title: Forest, domain and domain controller inventory
items.description:
Maps the forest so every later check covers every domain and domain controller, not only the one the test account sits in.

  • Domains, trusts, sites and domain controllers, including read-only ones, are listed with operating system versions and functional levels.
  • FSMO role holders and domain controllers in unexpected sites are noted.
  • Every domain controller runs a supported, patched operating system.

Record: the inventory and the test account used; passing means all domain controllers are supported, current and accounted for.

items.title: Default domain password and lockout policy
items.description:
The domain policy sets the floor for every account without a fine-grained policy.

  • Minimum length is judged against current NCSC and NIST guidance, which favour length and screening over complexity rules and routine expiry.
  • Lockout or throttling is set high enough to avoid easy denial of service and low enough to stop guessing.
  • Common and breached passwords are screened, for example with Microsoft Entra Password Protection.

Record: effective policy values against guidance; passing means long passwords, screening and lockout or throttling.

items.title: Fine-grained password policies
items.description:
Password settings objects can weaken or strengthen the policy for particular users and global security groups, and are easily overlooked.

  • Every password settings object is listed with its precedence and the users and groups it applies to.
  • No policy weakens length, lockout or history for privileged or service accounts.
  • The resultant policy is confirmed for a sample of privileged accounts.

Record: each policy, its settings and targets; passing means privileged and service accounts get the strictest policy.

items.title: Password quality audit (where authorised)
items.description:
Policy shows intent; an authorised offline audit shows what users actually chose (NIST SP 800-115 section 5.1).

  • Written authorisation covers obtaining and assessing password hashes, with secure storage and destruction agreed.
  • Results give the share of weak, reused and shared passwords, especially among privileged accounts.
  • Admins reusing their everyday password, and accounts sharing one, are identified.

Record: statistics only, no recovered passwords in the report; passing means no privileged account has a weak or reused password.

items.title: Reversible encryption and LM hash storage
items.description:
Passwords stored with reversible encryption or as LM hashes can be recovered trivially by anyone who reads the directory database.

  • Store passwords using reversible encryption is disabled in the domain policy and every fine-grained policy.
  • No account has the reversible encryption flag set.
  • Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change is enabled, and old accounts have since changed password.

Record: policies and accounts with either setting; passing means none.

items.title: Accounts without Kerberos pre-authentication
items.description:
An account set not to require Kerberos pre-authentication lets anyone request data encrypted with its password and attack it offline.

  • No enabled account has Do not require Kerberos preauthentication set.
  • Any exception has a documented reason and a long random password.
  • The flag is checked across every domain in the forest.

Record: accounts, owners and password age; passing means none.

items.title: Service accounts with service principal names
items.description:
Any domain user can request a service ticket for an account with a service principal name, so a weak password on it can be recovered offline.

  • User accounts with service principal names are listed with password age and group membership.
  • They are group managed service accounts or have long random, rotated passwords.
  • None is privileged; Microsoft Defender for Identity flags service principal names on sensitive accounts.

Record: account, SPN, privilege, password age and encryption types; passing means managed or strong passwords and no privilege.

items.title: Kerberos encryption types
items.description:
RC4 and DES keys are weaker and make offline attacks on tickets easier; Protected Users members are already limited to AES.

  • No account uses DES encryption types.
  • Accounts, especially service accounts, support AES, and the domain's supported encryption types are reviewed for RC4.
  • Accounts whose password predates AES support in the domain have been reset.

Record: accounts limited to DES or RC4 and the domain setting; passing means AES throughout.

items.title: Password age of the krbtgt account
items.description:
The krbtgt key signs every ticket in the domain, so an old key prolongs the value of any forged ticket made after a past compromise.

  • The krbtgt password last-set date is recorded for every domain, along with read-only domain controller krbtgt accounts.
  • Microsoft Defender for Identity flags a krbtgt password unchanged for more than 180 days.
  • Resets are done twice with a wait between them, as Microsoft's forest recovery guidance describes.

Record: domain and last-set date; passing means a regular reset schedule that is followed.

items.title: Unconstrained delegation
items.description:
A host trusted for unconstrained delegation receives reusable tickets from everyone who authenticates to it; if it falls, those identities can be used anywhere.

  • Only domain controllers are trusted for unconstrained delegation.
  • Any other computer or user with it is listed with its owner and reason.
  • Privileged accounts cannot be delegated (see the Protected Users item).

Record: each account trusted for unconstrained delegation; passing means domain controllers only.

items.title: Constrained delegation and protocol transition
items.description:
Constrained delegation lets a service act as users towards named services; with protocol transition it can do so without the user's own Kerberos authentication.

  • Every account with constrained delegation is listed with its target services.
  • Targets are limited to what the application needs and exclude domain controller services.
  • Protocol transition is enabled only where required.

Record: account, targets and protocol transition setting; passing means each entry is justified and narrow.

items.title: Resource-based constrained delegation
items.description:
Resource-based constrained delegation is set on the target resource, so anyone able to write that setting on a computer object can grant delegation to it.

  • Existing resource-based delegation entries are listed and justified.
  • Ordinary users and helpdesk groups cannot write delegation settings on, or take ownership of, computer objects.
  • Rights kept by the accounts that created computer objects are reviewed.

Record: resources with entries and the principals able to write them; passing means justified entries only and no broad write rights.

items.title: Highest-privilege groups
items.description:
Enterprise Admins, Domain Admins, Schema Admins and the built-in Administrators group control the forest; every member is a route to full compromise.

  • Direct and nested members of each group are listed across all domains.
  • Membership is minimal, named and justified, with Enterprise Admins and Schema Admins empty outside planned changes.
  • No service, shared or disabled account remains a member.

Record: members with owner and justification; passing means minimal, named, justified membership.

items.title: Operator and other built-in privileged groups
items.description:
Built-in operator groups and some default groups carry rights that lead to domain control, though they look minor.

  • Account Operators, Backup Operators, Server Operators and Print Operators are empty or justified.
  • DnsAdmins, Group Policy Creator Owners, Cert Publishers and Key Admins are reviewed.
  • Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access holds Everyone or Anonymous Logon only where an application still needs it.

Record: group, members and justification; passing means empty or justified.

items.title: AdminSDHolder and protected accounts
items.description:
SDProp copies AdminSDHolder's permissions onto protected accounts and groups every 60 minutes by default, so an extra entry there becomes lasting control of every privileged account.

  • The AdminSDHolder access control list matches the default, with no added users or groups.
  • Accounts still marked as protected (adminCount set) after leaving protected groups are listed, as inheritance stays off.
  • No non-sensitive account holds AdminSDHolder rights.

Record: non-default entries and orphaned protected accounts; passing means a default list and no orphans.

items.title: Administrative tiering and logon restrictions
items.description:
Domain administrators who sign in to workstations or member servers leave credentials exposed wherever those hosts fall.

  • Privileged accounts are separate from everyday ones, with no mailbox or web browsing.
  • Tier 0 accounts are denied logon to lower tiers by user rights assignment or authentication policy silos.
  • Tier 0 systems (domain controllers, CAs, identity synchronisation) are managed only from privileged access workstations.

Record: where privileged accounts actually log on, and the controls; passing means no tier 0 logons on lower tiers.

items.title: Protected Users and credential protection features
items.description:
Protected Users and host credential protections limit what an attacker can take from a compromised host.

  • Privileged users are in Protected Users after compatibility testing; service and computer accounts are not.
  • Privileged accounts are marked Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated.
  • Credential Guard and LSA protection are on for admin workstations and servers.
  • Remote administration uses Restricted Admin mode or Remote Credential Guard.

Record: membership, gaps and feature coverage; passing means privileged users are protected throughout.

items.title: Service accounts in privileged groups
items.description:
Service accounts often have old passwords, sit on many servers and cannot use MFA, so privileged membership makes them prime targets.

  • No service account is a direct or nested member of Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins or other tier 0 groups.
  • Service accounts hold only the rights their application needs, and interactive logon is denied.
  • Stale service accounts with no recent logon are disabled.

Record: account, groups, password age and last logon; passing means no privileged service accounts.

items.title: Stale, never-expiring and weakly flagged accounts
items.description:
Unused accounts and accounts exempt from password rules give attackers credentials nobody watches.

  • Enabled accounts unused for 90 days, and sensitive accounts unused for 180 days, are listed (the thresholds Microsoft Defender for Identity uses).
  • Accounts with password never expires or password not required are justified.
  • The built-in Administrator password age is checked.

Record: counts and samples per category, with owners; passing means each remaining account is justified and owned.

items.title: Hidden membership and attribute oddities
items.description:
Privilege granted through primary group or SID history does not show in normal group listings, and free-text attributes often hold passwords.

  • No account has a non-default primary group that places it in a privileged group.
  • SID history is empty except during a documented migration, and never holds privileged SIDs.
  • Description, info and similar attributes hold no passwords or hints.

Record: accounts with each condition; passing means none.

items.title: Dangerous permissions and privilege paths
items.description:
Control of privileged objects through permissions (reset password, add member, change permissions, take ownership) is a privilege path even when group membership looks clean.

  • Permissions on the domain root, privileged users and groups, and domain controller OUs are reviewed for non-admin principals.
  • Non-admins hold no write DACL, write owner, generic write or full control over sensitive groups or accounts.
  • Chained paths are traced to tier 0.

Record: each path from a non-privileged principal to tier 0, step by step; passing means no such path.

items.title: Directory replication rights
items.description:
The Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All rights let a principal request any account's password data from a domain controller.

  • Only domain controllers, built-in admin groups and documented synchronisation accounts hold both rights on the domain root.
  • Directory synchronisation servers and their service accounts are protected as tier 0.
  • Microsoft Defender for Identity's DCSync permissions assessment shows no open items.

Record: every principal holding the rights; passing means expected principals only.

items.title: Group Policy object permissions and links
items.description:
Anyone who can edit or link a GPO can run code on every computer it applies to, including domain controllers.

  • Edit and modify-security rights on GPOs reaching domain controllers, tier 0 servers or the domain root are limited to tier 0 admins.
  • Link rights on the domain, sites and sensitive OUs are restricted.
  • Scripts and installers that GPOs reference are not writable by non-admins.

Record: GPO, scope and principals with rights; passing means only tier 0 admins can change policy that reaches tier 0.

items.title: Credentials in Group Policy Preferences and SYSVOL
items.description:
Group Policy Preferences once stored passwords in SYSVOL in a form any domain user can decrypt; the MS14-025 update stopped new ones but did not remove existing ones.

  • No preference item holds a stored password (mapped drives, local users and groups, scheduled tasks, services, data sources).
  • Logon scripts and other SYSVOL and NETLOGON files hold no credentials.
  • Any credential found is checked as current or stale without using it beyond the rules of engagement.

Record: file path, account and status; passing means none.

items.title: LAPS or Windows LAPS coverage
items.description:
Unique, rotated local administrator passwords stop one local credential opening every machine.

  • All workstations and member servers are covered by Windows LAPS or legacy LAPS, with recent rotation (Microsoft Defender for Identity flags none in 60 days).
  • Domain controller DSRM passwords are managed by Windows LAPS where adopted.
  • Legacy LAPS emulation mode, which stores passwords in clear text, is temporary.

Record: coverage, exceptions and rotation evidence; passing means full coverage and recent rotation.

items.title: Access to LAPS passwords
items.description:
LAPS only helps if few people can read the stored passwords.

  • Read access to LAPS password attributes is limited to named admin groups per tier, not the whole helpdesk or Authenticated Users.
  • All extended rights and full control on computer OUs grant no unintended read access.
  • Windows LAPS password encryption is enabled where the domain supports it.

Record: principals able to read passwords per OU; passing means intended admin groups only.

items.title: Certificate Services inventory
items.description:
Active Directory Certificate Services belongs in tier 0: a CA trusted for logon can issue logon certificates for anyone.

  • Enterprise CAs, published templates, enrolment endpoints (web enrolment, enrolment web services, RPC) and their hosts are listed.
  • CA servers are administered as tier 0 and patched.
  • Templates allowing client authentication are identified for the ESC checks that follow.
