Record: CA names, hosts, templates and endpoints; passing means a complete inventory under tier 0 administration.

items.title: Certificate template weaknesses (ESC1, ESC2, ESC3)
items.description:
Covers templates that let a low-privileged requester obtain a certificate usable to authenticate as someone else.

  • ESC1: no template lets the requester supply the subject while allowing client authentication and enrolment by low-privileged users without manager approval.
  • ESC2: no template with the Any Purpose extended key usage, or none at all, is open to low-privileged enrolment.
  • ESC3: enrolment agent templates are restricted, with enrolment agent restrictions set on the CA.

Record: template, setting and who can enrol; passing means no such path.

items.title: Access control on templates, CAs and PKI objects (ESC4, ESC5, ESC7)
items.description:
Write access to a template, a CA or the PKI objects in the configuration partition lets an attacker create the weaknesses above.

  • ESC4: low-privileged principals cannot modify or own certificate templates.
  • ESC5: the CA computer object, NTAuthCertificates and the PKI containers grant no write access to non-admins.
  • ESC7: Manage CA and Manage Certificates rights on each CA are held only by tier 0 admins.

Record: object, principal and right; passing means tier 0 control only.

items.title: CA settings and certificate mapping (ESC6, ESC15)
items.description:
Some CA and domain controller settings decide whether a certificate can claim an identity it should not.

  • ESC6: no CA has the EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag set.
  • ESC15: AD CS servers carry the update for CVE-2024-49019.
  • Domain controllers enforce strong certificate mapping (KB5014754), with no override back to compatibility mode, and weak explicit mappings are replaced.

Record: CA flags, patch level and the mapping enforcement state; passing means none of these conditions remain.

items.title: Enrolment endpoints and NTLM relay (ESC8, ESC11)
items.description:
Enrolment interfaces that accept relayed NTLM let an attacker obtain a certificate for whichever account was coerced into authenticating, including domain controllers.

  • ESC8: web enrolment and enrolment web services require HTTPS with Extended Protection for Authentication, or are removed (KB5005413).
  • ESC11: the RPC enrolment interface requires packet privacy.
  • NTLM is restricted on CA servers where possible.

Record: each endpoint and its protections; passing means no endpoint accepts relayed authentication.

items.title: LM, NTLMv1 and NTLM restriction
items.description:
LM and NTLMv1 responses are weak enough to be recovered offline, and any NTLM use keeps relay possible.

  • Network security: LAN Manager authentication level is set to send NTLMv2 only and refuse LM and NTLM, on domain controllers and members.
  • NTLM auditing on domain controllers shows which systems still use NTLM.
  • NTLM is restricted for privileged accounts and towards tier 0 servers where feasible.

Record: policy values and systems still using NTLMv1; passing means NTLMv2 only, audited and shrinking.

items.title: SMB signing, LDAP signing and channel binding
items.description:
Signing and channel binding stop domain controllers and servers accepting relayed authentication.

  • Domain controllers require SMB signing (the default) and member servers require it too.
  • Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements is set to require signing.
  • Domain controller: LDAP server channel binding token requirements is set to always, after client support is checked.

Record: settings per domain controller and exceptions; passing means signing required and channel binding enforced everywhere.

items.title: Print spooler and coercion on domain controllers
items.description:
Domain controllers can be made to authenticate to another host through services such as the print spooler, which feeds relay and delegation attacks.

  • The Print Spooler service is disabled on domain controllers and other tier 0 servers.
  • Other remote interfaces able to trigger domain controller authentication are patched and filtered as Microsoft advises.
  • Outbound connections from domain controllers are limited to what they need.

Record: domain controllers with the spooler running and coercion routes found; passing means none.

items.title: Machine account quota and computer object creation
items.description:
By default any authenticated user can join up to 10 computers to the domain, creating accounts they control that feed delegation and relay attacks.

  • ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota is 0, with domain joining delegated to named groups.
  • Computer objects created by ordinary users (ms-DS-CreatorSID) are reviewed.
  • Pre-created computer accounts do not carry predictable or known passwords.

Record: the quota value and who can create computer objects; passing means 0, with joining delegated.

items.title: Domain and forest trusts and SID filtering
items.description:
Trusts extend who can authenticate; without SID filtering, a compromise in a trusted domain can carry privileged SIDs across.

  • Every trust is listed with direction, type and transitivity, and is still needed.
  • SID filtering is enabled on external and forest trusts.
  • Selective authentication is used where only some resources should be reachable, and TGT delegation across forest trusts is off.

Record: each trust and its settings; passing means only needed trusts, all filtered.

items.title: Domain controller hardening
items.description:
Domain controllers hold every credential in the domain, so anything else running on them, or with control over them, is tier 0 too.

  • Domain controllers run only the roles and agents tier 0 needs, with no web browsing or general software.
  • Their backups, virtualisation hosts and storage are protected as tier 0.
  • DSRM passwords are unique and managed.
  • Powerful user rights, such as local logon and debugging, are limited to tier 0 admins.

Record: roles, software and exceptions per domain controller; passing means a tier 0-only footprint.

items.title: Audit policy on domain controllers
items.description:
Without the right advanced audit subcategories, the attacks above leave no trace.

  • Advanced audit policy subcategories are enabled and forced to override the legacy categories.
  • Domain controllers audit credential validation, Kerberos authentication and service tickets, account and security group management and directory service changes.
  • Security log size and forwarding stop events being overwritten before collection.

Record: effective audit policy per domain controller; passing means the key subcategories are audited and forwarded.

items.title: Detection coverage for directory attacks
items.description:
Checks whether the client would notice directory abuse, using Microsoft's list of events to monitor and the test's own activity.

  • Changes to privileged groups, AdminSDHolder, GPOs, delegation settings, SID history and certificate templates raise alerts.
  • Replication requests from hosts that are not domain controllers, and unusual service ticket requests, are detected.
  • Alerts raised during the test are compared with its timeline.

Record: each test action and its detection outcome; passing means significant changes and abuse were detected.

cloud_kubernetes_v2.name: Kubernetes and Container Review (CIS, NSA and CISA)
cloud_kubernetes_v2.description: Coverage tracker for a Kubernetes cluster and its workloads, following the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark (section numbers from v1.12.0 in brackets) and the NSA and CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guidance v1.2. For EKS, AKS or GKE, mark control plane items the provider runs as provider-managed, use the provider's CIS Benchmark for nodes, and record each deviation with its evidence.

items.title: Clusters, versions and benchmark in scope
items.description:
Fixes what is reviewed and which benchmark applies.

  • Each cluster, its version, node pools and node OS are listed.
  • The control plane is marked self-managed or provider-managed (EKS, AKS, GKE).
  • The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark or the provider's own CIS Benchmark, with version, is agreed.
  • Review access (read-only cluster role, node access, cloud console) is granted.

Record: cluster inventory, benchmark and access; pass when every cluster in scope is assessed.

items.title: API server network exposure
items.description:
An API server reachable from the internet invites attack on every authentication weakness.

  • Self-managed: the API server is reachable only from management networks or an allow list.
  • EKS public endpoint off or limited by CIDR; AKS authorised IP ranges or private cluster; GKE private endpoint or authorised networks.
  • Anonymous requests from outside return no cluster information.

Record: endpoint addresses and allowed sources; pass when only management networks reach the API server.

items.title: API server authentication and anonymous access (CIS 1.2)
items.description:
Weak or anonymous authentication on the API server undermines every RBAC control behind it.

  • Anonymous authentication is off, or limited to health endpoints with no bindings for system:anonymous.
  • No static token file is configured.
  • The API server verifies kubelets with client certificates and the kubelet certificate authority.

Record: API server settings and bindings for unauthenticated users; pass when anonymous users get nothing useful.

items.title: API server authorisation, admission plugins and TLS (CIS 1.2)
items.description:
Authorisation modes and admission plugins decide whether RBAC and node limits are enforced.

  • Authorisation modes include Node and RBAC and never AlwaysAllow.
  • NodeRestriction is enabled and AlwaysAdmit is not.
  • Profiling is off, audit logging is configured and only strong TLS ciphers are allowed.

Record: API server settings against CIS 1.2; pass when deviations are justified or provider-managed.

items.title: Encryption of Secrets at rest (CIS 1.2)
items.description:
Without an encryption configuration, Secrets sit in etcd and its backups in readable form.

  • An encryption configuration covers Secrets, with a KMS v2 provider preferred over local static keys.
  • The identity provider is not first in the list, so new writes are encrypted.
  • Keys are held outside control plane hosts and rotated; managed clusters use customer keys if required.

Record: provider settings and key location; pass when Secrets are encrypted with a key kept away from etcd.

items.title: Controller manager and scheduler (CIS 1.3 and 1.4)
items.description:
These components hold powerful credentials and should expose nothing beyond the control plane host.

  • Both bind to 127.0.0.1 and have profiling off.
  • The controller manager uses separate service account credentials and rotates kubelet server certificates.
  • The service account signing key and root CA file are set and protected.

Record: component settings against CIS 1.3 and 1.4; pass when no deviation is unexplained (managed: not testable).

items.title: Control plane configuration files and PKI (CIS 1.1)
items.description:
Write access to static pod manifests, kubeconfig files or PKI keys gives full cluster control.

  • Static pod manifests, admin.conf, scheduler.conf and controller-manager.conf are root-owned, mode 600 or stricter.
  • PKI keys are mode 600; the etcd data directory is mode 700 and owned by etcd.
  • CNI configuration files are restricted in the same way.

Record: ownership and permissions found; pass when only root can read or change these files.

items.title: Protection of etcd (CIS 2)
items.description:
The etcd store holds all cluster state including Secrets; direct access bypasses the API server and RBAC.

  • Client and peer traffic use TLS with client certificate authentication, not auto-generated certificates.
  • The etcd certificate authority is separate from the cluster CA.
  • Ports for etcd are reachable only from control plane nodes; backups are encrypted and access-controlled.

Record: etcd settings, reachability and backup handling; pass when only the API server can talk to etcd.

items.title: Authentication for people (CIS 3.1)
items.description:
Personal sign-in through an identity provider keeps human access revocable.

  • People use OIDC or the provider's integration (EKS access entries, Entra ID for AKS, Google accounts for GKE).
  • No one uses client certificates, service account tokens or bootstrap tokens as a personal login.
  • Static admin credentials are disabled where possible, such as AKS local accounts.

Record: how each group authenticates and any shared credentials; pass when access is personal and revocable.

items.title: Use of cluster-admin and system:masters (CIS 5.1)
items.description:
Holders of cluster-admin have unrestricted control, and system:masters membership cannot be revoked through RBAC.

  • ClusterRoleBindings to cluster-admin are few, named and justified.
  • No user or certificate is placed in the system:masters group.
  • Bindings for system:anonymous, system:unauthenticated and system:authenticated add nothing beyond defaults.

Record: every cluster-admin binding and broad group binding; pass when each is necessary.

items.title: Wildcards, Secret access and workload creation (CIS 5.1)
items.description:
Some RBAC rights grant far more than they appear to.

  • Roles and ClusterRoles avoid wildcard verbs, resources and API groups, which also cover future types.
  • Rights to get, list and watch Secrets are limited to components that need them, as list reveals contents.
  • Rights to create pods or controllers are treated as equal to the namespace's most powerful service account.

Record: roles with these rights and their subjects; pass when each is justified.

items.title: Escalate, bind, impersonate and other escalation rights (CIS 5.1)
items.description:
Certain verbs and subresources let a subject raise its own privilege or reach nodes directly.

  • The escalate, bind and impersonate verbs are held by administrators only.
  • Rights to nodes/proxy, CSR approval, service account token creation and webhook configuration are minimal.
  • Creating PersistentVolumes, which can point at host paths, is restricted.

Record: subjects holding each right; pass when only administrators or named components have them.

items.title: Service accounts and token mounting (CIS 5.1)
items.description:
Every pod can carry an API token, so service account use decides what a compromised container can do.

  • Workloads do not use default service accounts, which hold no extra rights.
  • The automountServiceAccountToken field is false unless the pod calls the API.
  • Tokens are short-lived projected tokens; long-lived token Secrets are removed or justified.

Record: workloads with mounted tokens and their rights; pass when tokens exist only where needed.

items.title: Pod Security Standards and admission (CIS 5.2)
items.description:
Without admission policy, the right to create pods amounts to access to the node.

  • At least one policy control is active: Pod Security Admission or an equivalent policy engine.
  • Workload namespaces enforce Baseline or Restricted; Privileged is limited to system namespaces.
  • Exemptions are listed and justified, and warn or audit modes are not the only control.

Record: namespace labels or policies and exemptions; pass when every workload namespace enforces a profile.

items.title: Privileged and host-namespace workloads (CIS 5.2)
items.description:
Privileged containers and host namespaces remove most isolation between a container and its node.

  • No workload runs privileged or uses hostPID, hostIPC or hostNetwork without documented need.
  • No hostPath volumes, especially the container runtime socket or root file system; no hostPort.
  • Windows HostProcess containers are limited to agreed system workloads.

Record: each such workload with namespace, owner and reason; pass when all are justified system components.

items.title: Container security context hardening (CIS 5.2 and 5.6)
items.description:
Security context settings limit what a compromised process can do inside and beyond its container.

  • Containers run as non-root with allowPrivilegeEscalation set to false.
  • All capabilities are dropped and only needed ones added; NET_RAW and SYS_ADMIN are absent.
  • The RuntimeDefault seccomp profile applies, with read-only root file systems where possible.

Record: workloads failing each setting; pass when the Restricted profile is met or gaps are justified.

items.title: Network policies and default deny (CIS 5.3)
items.description:
Without network policies every pod can reach every other, so one compromise sees the whole cluster.

  • The CNI plugin enforces NetworkPolicy.
  • Every namespace has a default deny for ingress and egress, with explicit allow rules.
  • Sensitive namespaces (system, monitoring, data stores) accept traffic only from named sources.

Record: namespaces without policies and open paths observed; pass when traffic is limited to what workloads need.

items.title: Egress, cloud metadata and node reachability
items.description:
Pods that reach the metadata service, kubelets or the internet freely can turn one breach into wider access.

  • Pods cannot reach instance metadata unless needed (node IMDSv2 hop limit of 1 on EKS, GKE metadata server, policy).
  • Pods cannot reach kubelet or other node ports.
  • Internet egress is limited to required destinations.

Record: reachability results from an ordinary workload; pass when only intended egress succeeds.

items.title: Secrets handling (CIS 5.4)
items.description:
How Secrets reach workloads and who can read them decides how far one leak spreads.

  • Secrets are mounted as files rather than environment variables where possible.
  • Read access to Secrets is limited per namespace and per component.
  • High-value secrets use an external store; none sit in ConfigMaps, images or manifests in source control.

Record: delivery methods and secrets found in the wrong place; pass when secrets are scoped and stored properly.

items.title: Kubelet authentication and authorisation (CIS 4.2)
items.description:
The kubelet API can run commands in pods and read their data, so every caller must be checked.

  • Kubelet anonymous authentication is off and a client CA file is set.
  • The kubelet authorisation mode is Webhook, not AlwaysAllow.
  • The read-only port is disabled (set to 0).

Record: kubelet settings per node pool and any port open without credentials; pass when all callers are checked.

items.title: Worker node files and other kubelet settings (CIS 4.1 to 4.3)
items.description:
Node configuration files and kubelet options set certificates, limits and defaults for every pod on the node.

  • Kubelet service, kubeconfig, config and CA files are root-owned, mode 600 or stricter.
  • Certificate rotation is on, strong TLS ciphers are set and a pod PID limit applies.
  • RuntimeDefault seccomp is the kubelet default; kube-proxy metrics bind to localhost.

Record: node settings against CIS 4.1 to 4.3; pass when deviations are justified.

items.title: Node operating system and access
items.description:
Nodes share one kernel across all their containers, so node hardening sets the floor for isolation.

  • Nodes run a minimal or container-optimised OS, patched on a regular cycle.
  • SSH or remote access to nodes is off, or limited to logged emergency use.
  • Node cloud identities hold only what node agents need.

Record: node images, patch age and access paths; pass when nodes are current and not routinely accessed.

items.title: Admission control and policy enforcement
items.description:
Admission control enforces rules RBAC cannot, and weak webhook settings let requests slip through.

  • Required rules are enforced by ValidatingAdmissionPolicy or admission webhooks.
  • Security webhooks fail closed, and selectors do not exempt workload namespaces.
  • Only cluster administrators can change webhook configurations or policy objects.

Record: admission policies, failure policies and exemptions; pass when policy cannot be sidestepped by configuration.

items.title: Image provenance and registries (CIS 5.5)
items.description:
Clusters should run only images from trusted sources, unchanged since they were built.

  • Images come from approved registries, enforced at admission.
  • Images are referenced by digest or immutable tag, with signatures verified at admission where adopted.
  • Image pull secrets are scoped per namespace and not shared widely.

Record: registries in use and how they are enforced; pass when untrusted images cannot be admitted.

items.title: Image vulnerability scanning and content
items.description:
Images often carry vulnerable packages, build tools and leftover secrets into production.

  • Images are scanned in the pipeline and registry, and running images are rescanned as advisories appear.
  • Base images are minimal and current, without shells or package managers where not needed.
  • Image layers hold no credentials, keys or unshipped source code.

Record: scan coverage, critical findings in running images and secrets found; pass when critical issues have fix dates.

items.title: Runtime threat detection
items.description:
Runtime detection spots shells in pods, odd processes and escapes that reviews miss.

  • Runtime detection covers every node pool (GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring, Defender for Containers, Container Threat Detection).
  • Alerts cover interactive shells in containers, privileged pod creation and access to sensitive node files.
  • Alerts reach a monitored queue with an owner.

Record: detection coverage and an example alert path; pass when all nodes are monitored and alerts are handled.

items.title: Kubernetes audit policy and log handling (CIS 3.2)
items.description:
Audit logs are the only record of who read Secrets, opened shells in pods or changed RBAC.

  • The audit policy records Secret, RBAC, exec and token requests, with at least Metadata for Secrets.
  • Logs leave the cluster for a store its administrators cannot alter, with agreed retention.
  • High-risk events (RBAC changes, exec, anonymous requests) raise alerts.

Record: audit policy, destination and retention; pass when key security events are kept off the cluster.

items.title: Managed control plane logging
items.description:
On managed services the provider runs the API server, so its logs must be switched on and routed.

  • EKS control plane logging is on for at least the api, audit and authenticator log types.
  • AKS diagnostic settings send kube-audit or kube-audit-admin logs to a workspace.
  • GKE audit logs are retained in Cloud Logging, with Data Access logs on where required.

Record: log types on per cluster and their destination; pass when audit and authentication logs are kept.

items.title: Exposed dashboards and web consoles
items.description:
Cluster web consoles often run with powerful service accounts and are exposed for convenience.

  • The Kubernetes Dashboard, now archived and unmaintained, is removed or replaced.
  • Any console requires personal sign-in and acts with the user's own rights, not a shared admin token.
  • Consoles are not published through public ingress or load balancers.

Record: consoles found, how they are reached and their identity; pass when none gives anonymous or shared admin access.

items.title: Add-ons and their exposed endpoints
items.description:
Monitoring, GitOps, mesh and ingress add-ons run with high privilege and expose their own APIs.

  • Each add-on is a supported version and its service account rights are least privilege.
  • Add-on metrics, admin and debug endpoints are not reachable from untrusted pods or the internet.
  • Tools that apply manifests (GitOps controllers, CI agents) are limited to their target namespaces.

Record: add-ons, versions, rights and endpoints; pass when none gives an unauthenticated path to control.

items.title: Services, ingress and external exposure
items.description:
LoadBalancer and NodePort services and ingress rules decide which workloads the outside world reaches.

  • Every externally reachable service and ingress is intended and documented.
  • Ingress terminates TLS with current settings; internal services use internal load balancers.
  • Services do not set externalIPs unless required, since these can capture cluster traffic.

Record: exposed services with hostnames and ports; pass when exposure matches intent.

items.title: Namespaces and multi-tenancy (CIS 5.6)
items.description:
Namespaces are the main administrative boundary, but a weak one without RBAC, policy and node placement.

  • Workloads are split by namespace per team, environment or trust level; the default namespace is unused.
  • Tenants of different trust do not share nodes (taints, node pools or sandboxed runtimes).
  • Tenant RBAC is namespaced, with no cluster-wide rights.

Record: namespace layout, shared nodes and cross-tenant rights; pass when isolation matches the trust model.

items.title: Resource quotas and limits
items.description:
Without limits one workload or tenant can starve the cluster of CPU, memory, storage or process IDs.

  • Namespaces have ResourceQuota objects for compute, storage and object counts.
  • LimitRange sets defaults, and containers declare requests and memory limits.
  • A pod PID limit applies on nodes.

Record: namespaces without quotas and unbounded workloads; pass when every workload namespace is bounded.

items.title: Pod access to cloud identities
items.description:
Pod-level cloud identities replace node credentials, but broad trust turns a pod breach into cloud access.

  • Pods use EKS Pod Identity or IRSA, Microsoft Entra Workload ID, or Workload Identity Federation for GKE.
  • Each mapping trusts one namespace and service account only.
  • Cloud roles reachable from pods are least privilege.

Record: service account to cloud role mappings and rights; pass when no pod can assume broad cloud privilege.

items.title: Version support and upgrades
items.description:
Unsupported Kubernetes versions and add-ons stop getting security fixes.

  • The cluster runs one of the three minor releases the project maintains, or one the provider still supports.
  • Node versions are within the supported skew of the control plane.
  • An upgrade process exists and deprecated APIs in use are tracked.

Record: control plane, node and add-on versions with end-of-support dates; pass when all are supported.

people_social_engineering_v2.name: Social Engineering and Phishing Assessment
people_social_engineering_v2.description: Coverage tracker for a social engineering or phishing phase, from authorisation and legal review through campaign control and measurement to a debrief that blames no one, drawing on the PTES pre-engagement guidance and the NCSC's phishing guidance. Tick an item when it is agreed or done and its record is filed; nothing here covers how to build lures or infrastructure.

items.title: Written authorisation from the right person
items.description:
Social engineering targets people as well as systems, so authority must come from someone who can speak for both.

  • A senior signatory with authority over the staff and systems in scope signs.
  • The authorisation names the channels, dates, target groups and testing firm.
  • Staff of contractors or partners are covered only with their own employer's consent.

Record: the signed authorisation; pass is every target group covered by it.

items.title: Legal and HR review
items.description:
Simulated attacks touch employment law and staff trust, and the NCSC advises checking with HR before running them.

  • HR confirms results will not be used for discipline and raises any union or works council points.
  • Legal reviews impersonation, call recording and interception questions for each channel.
  • The review covers every country where targeted staff work.

Record: review notes and sign-off; pass is no open legal question at launch.

items.title: Privacy review and data protection
items.description:
Campaign data is personal data about staff, so UK GDPR principles govern what is collected and kept.

  • The lawful basis and the privacy information for staff are confirmed with the client's data protection lead.
  • Only data needed for the agreed measures is collected (data minimisation).
  • Retention, access and deletion dates are set (storage limitation).
  • The need for a data protection impact assessment is considered and recorded.

Record: privacy decision record; pass is a deletion date for every data set.

items.title: Objectives and measures agreed
items.description:
Counting only clicks rewards silence; the NCSC advises treating reports as a sign of success.

  • The aim is stated: reporting culture, technical controls, process checks or awareness.
  • Measures are fixed in advance: delivery, opens, clicks, submissions, reports and time to report.
  • Baselines from earlier campaigns are noted if comparison is wanted.

Record: agreed objectives and measures; pass is each measure defined before launch.

items.title: Channels, dates and times in scope
items.description:
Each channel reaches people differently and carries its own risk, so each is authorised separately.

  • Email, phone, SMS and in-person approaches are each marked in or out of scope.
  • Sending windows avoid times the client excludes, such as pay day or year end.
  • Only company-issued accounts and numbers are targeted unless consent covers personal ones.

Record: channel schedule; pass is no activity outside it.

items.title: Target list approved
items.description:
Who receives the campaign changes both the risk and the results, so the client approves the list.

  • Named people or groups are approved, with the source of each address or number.
  • Exclusions are applied, such as staff on leave or known to be vulnerable.
  • Shared mailboxes and distribution lists are included or excluded deliberately.

Record: approved list and exclusions; pass is no message to anyone not on it.

items.title: Pretexts approved in writing
items.description:
PTES expects pretexts that reflect real attacks yet suit a workplace, approved before use.

  • Each pretext and its variants are approved in writing.
  • Themes likely to distress, such as health, bereavement, pay or redundancy, are excluded.
  • No real third party is impersonated without its agreement.

Record: approved pretext set; pass is no unapproved content sent.

items.title: Campaign infrastructure inventoried and controlled
items.description:
Domains, numbers and pages used for the test must be known, protected and removed afterwards.

  • Every domain, sender address, phone number and landing page is listed with an owner.
  • Access to campaign systems is limited to named testers.
  • A takedown date is agreed for each item.

Record: the inventory; pass is every item traceable to this engagement.

items.title: Coordination with mail, security and service desk teams
items.description:
Who knows about the test, and what filtering changes are made, decide what the results actually measure.

  • Trusted contacts who know are named, and nobody else is told.
  • Any allow-listing is recorded, as it removes filtering from the measure.
  • The service desk route for worried staff leads to a contact who knows.

Record: coordination record; pass is no undisclosed filtering exception.

items.title: Submissions recorded without keeping passwords
items.description:
Capturing real passwords adds risk without adding evidence; the fact of a submission is enough.

  • Pages log a submission event, and entered passwords are never stored or passed on.
  • Any username kept is needed for a measure and stored encrypted.
  • Captured data is reviewed before launch to confirm nothing secret persists.

Record: a signed-off configuration check; pass is no secret recoverable from any store.

items.title: End-to-end test run before launch
items.description:
A test run proves tracking and safety controls work before any member of staff receives anything.

  • Approved test recipients receive each message variant.
  • Every event type (delivery, open, click, submission, report) is recorded correctly.
  • Clocks across tracking systems are checked to agree.
  • The stop mechanism is tested.

Record: test run results; pass is every event type and the stop confirmed.

items.title: Delivery measured
items.description:
Delivery shows which messages reached people and which controls stopped the rest.

  • Sent, delivered, bounced and quarantined counts are recorded per variant.
  • Messages blocked by controls are credited to those controls.
  • Whether external-sender or warning banners were shown is noted.
  • Delivery times are kept for the time-to-report measure.

Record: delivery table; pass is every message accounted for.

items.title: Opens and clicks measured with their limits
items.description:
Opens and clicks are noisy measures that need care before any conclusion is drawn.

  • Open tracking is treated as approximate, since images are often blocked.
  • Automated clicks by security scanners are separated from human ones.
  • Results are counted per group, not per person.

Record: open and click figures with caveats; pass is no figure without its limits stated.

items.title: Submissions measured
items.description:
Submissions show how far a message would succeed against the client's other controls.

  • Submissions are counted per group and per message variant.
  • Any attachment used carries only a harmless marker that records opening.
  • The share of submitters who then reported is recorded.

Record: submission figures with times; pass is every event timestamped.

items.title: Reports to the security team and time to report
items.description:
The NCSC treats reporting as a sign of success, so measure it as carefully as clicks.

  • Reports through the client's button, mailbox or desk are counted per group.
  • Time from delivery to first report, and to the security team acting, is recorded.
  • A report made after clicking counts as a positive outcome.

Record: reporting figures and times; pass is reports shown alongside clicks.

items.title: Security team response measured
items.description:
The response to the first report shows whether the organisation could stop a real campaign.

  • Actions after the first report are logged: investigation, blocking, removal, warning.
  • The time of each action is recorded.
  • Whether the team recognised the campaign as a test, and how, is noted.
  • Escalations are deconflicted so that no real incident process runs on.

Record: response timeline; pass is each action timed.

items.title: Vishing calls where in scope
items.description:
Phone pretexts test verification procedures live, so calls need tighter limits than email.

  • Call scripts, numbers to call and the caller identity shown are approved.
  • Calls are recorded only if lawful and agreed; otherwise notes are made straight after.
  • Callers never ask for a real password to be read out, and end the call if someone is distressed.
  • Measures: verification steps followed, information disclosed, call reported.

Record: call log with outcomes; pass is every call within its script.

items.title: Smishing messages where in scope
items.description:
Text messages reach phones that mix work and home, so scope and consent matter more.

  • Only approved numbers, normally company-issued phones, receive messages.
  • The sender name and message content are approved.
  • Links lead only to agreed pages with the same no-password controls as email.
  • Clicks, submissions and reports are measured as for email.

Record: message log; pass is no message to an unapproved number.

items.title: Stop conditions agreed and tested
items.description:
A campaign must be stoppable within minutes when something goes wrong.

  • Stop triggers are agreed: staff distress, a real incident, wrong recipients, media interest, a client request.
  • Sending pauses and pages go offline on instruction.
  • A client contact is reachable throughout.

Record: each stop with time and reason; pass is the stop tested before launch.

items.title: Staff welfare looked after
items.description:
Some staff react strongly to being targeted, and how they are supported reflects on the client.

  • A support route exists for anyone worried or upset.
  • Staff who report or ask questions are thanked, not questioned.
  • Concerns raised during the campaign reach the client contact the same day.

Record: welfare contacts and actions; pass is every concern answered.

items.title: Results reported without blaming individuals
items.description:
The NCSC warns that blaming users does not change why they click and discourages reporting.

  • Results are given by team, role or site, never as named lists.
  • Reporting is shown alongside clicks and submissions.
  • Recommendations target controls and process: filtering, MFA, reporting routes and verification steps.

Record: reviewed report; pass is no individual identifiable.

items.title: Debrief that blames no individual
items.description:
A supportive debrief turns the campaign into learning rather than distrust.

  • Staff are told about the exercise if the client wishes, with the reasons for it.
  • The signs that gave each pretext away are shared, and reporters are thanked.
  • Managers receive group results, not names.
  • Staff are reminded how to report and what happens after a report.

Record: debrief material; pass is HR approval of it before use.

items.title: Close-down and data deletion
items.description:
Close-down removes what the campaign created and the data it gathered.

  • Pages, sending services and numbers are taken down on the agreed date.
  • Domains are kept or released as agreed, so that no one else can reuse them.
  • Collected data is deleted, and deletion is confirmed to the client.

Record: close-down record; pass is every inventory item closed.

people_physical_v2.name: Physical Security Assessment
people_physical_v2.description: Coverage tracker for a physical security phase, from authorisation letters and safety through perimeter, entry points, reception, staff behaviour, access control, monitoring and secure areas to evidence handling, with controls compared against UK NPSA guidance. Tick an item when it is assessed and recorded; items cover observation and review, never defeating locks, passes or alarms.

items.title: Authorisation letter carried by every tester
items.description:
The letter protects a tester who is challenged, so it must stand up to scrutiny on the spot.

  • It is signed by someone with authority over the sites and names each tester, who carries photo ID.
  • It states the sites, dates, times and permitted activities.
  • It gives client contacts reachable in every testing window, plus a number that can be checked independently.

Record: a copy per tester; pass is every tester carrying a current letter.

items.title: Client contacts able to confirm the testers
items.description:
A letter only helps if someone answers when staff, guards or police call to check it.

  • Named contacts know the testers' names and the testing windows.
  • Contacts are reachable out of hours if testing runs then.
  • A verification reference is agreed for these calls.

Record: contact list tested before testing; pass is a call answered within minutes.

items.title: Authority over every site and area
items.description:
The client may not control the whole building, so others with rights over it must agree.

  • Landlords, shared building managers and security contractors consent where needed.
  • Shared areas, neighbours and other tenants are identified and either excluded or agreed.
  • Whether the guarding company's management is told is decided deliberately.

Record: consent per site; pass is no area tested without it.

items.title: Rules of engagement for physical testing
items.description:
Written rules set what testers may do, so that every action can be defended afterwards.

  • Permitted activities, times and areas are listed.
  • Forced entry, damage, climbing and hazardous areas are ruled out unless agreed in writing.
  • Testers stop and comply as soon as security staff or police challenge them.

Record: signed rules; pass is every tester briefed on them.

items.title: Safety risk assessment
items.description:
Physical testing carries real safety risks for testers, staff and the public.

  • Hazards are assessed for each site: machinery, roofs, laboratories, construction, traffic, lone working.
  • Testers never run, hide in unsafe places or carry anything that could look threatening.
  • First aid and emergency arrangements are known for each site.

Record: risk assessment per site; pass is no unassessed hazard.

items.title: Process when challenged, detained or police attend
items.description:
A calm, rehearsed response protects testers and staff when a test is discovered.

  • Testers identify themselves, show the letter and call the client contact.
  • Whether local police are told in advance is decided with the client.
  • Each challenge is logged with the time, who challenged and how it ended.

Record: challenge log; pass is every challenge ended safely.

items.title: Sites, buildings and areas in scope
items.description:
A precise scope keeps testers out of areas they have no authority to enter.

  • Each site, building, floor and zone is marked in or out of scope.
  • Secure areas are listed explicitly, with whether entry may be attempted.
  • Remote sites, car parks and shared entrances are addressed explicitly.
  • Out-of-scope areas are marked on the plans testers carry.

Record: the scope plan; pass is all activity inside it.

items.title: Hostile reconnaissance view assessed
items.description:
NPSA describes hostile reconnaissance as the planning stage of an attack; assess what it would yield, within limits.

  • What the client publishes (photos, floor plans, virtual tours, staff details) is reviewed.
  • Site observation is from public places and avoids recording members of the public.
  • Whether the observation was noticed or challenged is recorded.

Record: observations with sources; pass is little of use to a hostile.

items.title: Perimeter condition and coverage
items.description:
The perimeter is the first chance to deter, detect and delay, so assess it from outside without causing damage.

  • Fences, gates, barriers and signs are intact, with no gaps or climbing aids.
  • Lighting and vegetation leave no unobserved approach.
  • Perimeter detection exists, and its alerts reach someone who acts.

Record: photographs of gaps with locations; pass is a continuous, monitored perimeter.

items.title: Entry points observed
items.description:
Every way into a building is a possible route, and observation shows how each is used day to day.

  • Doors, fire exits, loading bays, car park links and roof or plant access are listed.
  • Doors left open, propped or unalarmed are recorded, not forced.
  • How each entry point is monitored is noted.

Record: entry point log with times; pass is each one controlled and monitored.

items.title: Reception and visitor management
items.description:
Reception decides who comes in, so its checks are tested against its own procedure.

  • Visitors are checked against an expected appointment, and the host confirms.
  • Identity is verified, and visitor passes are visible, dated and distinct from staff passes.
  • Escort rules are applied, and passes are collected on exit.

Record: each approach and its outcome; pass is no unverified entry.

items.title: Contractors, couriers and deliveries
items.description:
People in work clothes or carrying parcels are often trusted, so check how they are verified.

  • Contractor arrivals are checked against expected work and an approver.
  • Couriers are kept to delivery points and not admitted further.
  • Post and parcels are received in a controlled area.

Record: observations and approaches; pass is verification every time.

items.title: Staff challenge and reporting behaviour
items.description:
Vigilant staff who notice and report are central to NPSA guidance on disrupting hostile reconnaissance.

  • Whether staff challenge people without visible passes is recorded.
  • Whether concerns reach security, and how quickly, is noted.
  • Results are reported by area or team, never by name.

Record: challenge rate per area; pass is a prompt challenge and report.

items.title: Tailgating susceptibility observed
items.description:
Tailgating shows whether access control holds up against politeness; observe first and attempt only if agreed.

  • People following others through controlled doors or turnstiles are observed at busy times.
  • Any attempt is a polite follow, never forced, and stops at the first challenge.
  • Counts of attempts, successes and challenges are kept, without names.

Record: tailgating log with times; pass is a challenge or refusal at each door.

items.title: Access control system reviewed
items.description:
The access control system is reviewed with the client's administrators rather than defeated.

  • Credential technology and reader types are identified from records and inspection.
  • Door forced and held-open alarms, time schedules and anti-passback are configured.
  • Leavers' and lost credentials are revoked promptly, and audit logs are kept.

Record: configuration evidence; pass is settings that match policy.

items.title: Pass issue, display and return
items.description:
Passes only work as a control if they are issued carefully and worn visibly.

  • Passes carry a photo and are issued only after identity checks.
  • Passes are worn visibly, as policy requires.
  • Temporary and visitor passes are returned, and lost passes are reported.
  • Unreturned passes are cancelled in the access control system the same day.

Record: observations and issue records; pass is policy followed throughout.

items.title: Doors, locks and key control
items.description:
Door and key condition decides whether physical barriers hold, so inspect them without manipulation.

  • Doors close and latch, and fire doors are not wedged open.
  • A key register exists, and master keys are controlled.
  • Locks on secure areas match the protection those areas need.

Record: photographs and key register review; pass is closed, controlled doors.

items.title: CCTV coverage and monitoring
items.description:
Cameras help only if they cover key areas and someone watches or reviews the images.

  • Coverage of entrances, perimeters and secure areas is assessed.
  • Image quality supports identification where it is needed.
  • Whether the control room noticed the testers is checked against the timeline.

Record: coverage notes and detection times; pass is testers seen and acted on.

items.title: Intruder alarm and response
items.description:
An alarm is measured by the response it brings, not by its presence.

  • Alarm zones, setting procedures and who responds are reviewed.
  • Any activation is agreed in advance and never caused by defeating the system.
  • Whether an alarm receiving centre monitors the system, and whom it calls, is confirmed.
  • Response time and actions are recorded.

Record: alarm records against the timeline; pass is a timely, correct response.

items.title: Security officers and patrols
items.description:
Officers turn detection into action, so their vigilance and procedures are assessed.

  • Patrol patterns and assignment instructions are reviewed.
  • Officers check the authorisation letter properly when they challenge testers.
  • The response to suspicious behaviour follows procedure.

Record: observations with times; pass is officers who challenge and verify.

items.title: Secure areas
items.description:
Server rooms, communications rooms, plant rooms and records stores need tighter control than general space.

  • Access is limited to an authorised list that is reviewed.
  • Doors are kept shut and entry is logged.
  • Unescorted access by visitors or contractors is recorded.
  • Network and communications cabinets in shared spaces are locked.

Record: access records and observations; pass is authorised entry only.

items.title: Clear desk and clear screen
items.description:
Information left out is easy to take, so record what is exposed without removing it.

  • Sensitive papers, passwords on notes and unlocked screens are noted.
  • Unattended laptops and removable media are noted.
  • Printers and meeting rooms are checked for documents left behind.
  • Photographs avoid personal data and faces.

Record: counts per area; pass is nothing sensitive left exposed.

items.title: Disposal of documents and media
items.description:
Waste routes are a quiet leak, so check how confidential material leaves the building.

  • Confidential waste bins are locked and emptied by an approved contractor.
  • General and recycling bins hold no sensitive documents.
  • Destruction meets an accepted standard, such as BS EN 15713.

Record: observations and contracts; pass is no sensitive material in open waste.

items.title: Unattended network points and devices
items.description:
Live network points and unattended devices in public areas can turn physical access into network access.

  • Network points in reception, meeting rooms and corridors are noted.
  • Whether a point is live is checked only if the rules of engagement allow it.
  • Unattended printers, kiosks and other devices are noted.

Record: locations and status; pass is public points disabled.

items.title: Out-of-hours conditions
items.description:
Security often relaxes out of hours, when guards, cleaners and contractors are the only people present.

  • Lighting, locking and alarm setting are observed within authorised windows.
  • Cleaners and contractors keep doors closed and passes visible.
  • An out-of-hours keyholder and response arrangement is in place.

Record: observations with times; pass is out-of-hours controls as strong as daytime ones.

items.title: Detection and response timeline
items.description:
Matching every action to what security saw gives the real measure of detection.

  • Every tester action is logged with its time and location.
  • The log is compared afterwards with CCTV, guard and alarm records.
  • Missed detections are reported as gaps in controls, not failures of individuals.

Record: the matched timeline; pass is every action accounted for.

items.title: Evidence handling and privacy
items.description:
Photographs and recordings can capture people and secrets, so keep only what the report needs.

  • Images avoid the public and staff faces where possible.
  • Evidence is encrypted at rest, with access limited.
  • Each image is logged with the time, place and finding it supports.
  • Deletion happens on an agreed date and is confirmed.

Record: evidence log; pass is no image kept beyond its date.

items.title: Items taken or left accounted for
items.description:
Markers left, or items taken as proof, must be tracked so nothing is lost or misread.

  • Each marker or item has a log entry with time and location.
  • Items are returned and markers removed at the end.
  • Nothing of value is removed unless agreed in writing.
  • Markers hold no client data and are clearly marked as test items.

Record: item log; pass is every item returned or removed.

items.title: Debrief without blame
items.description:
Results should improve controls and culture, not single out the people who were tested.

  • Findings are framed around process, training and design.
  • Staff who challenged or reported are recognised.
  • Individuals are not named in the report.
  • Each recommendation names its control owner, such as facilities, security or HR.

Record: reviewed report; pass is the client agreeing no individual is identifiable.

dev_iot_istg_v2.name: IoT Device Testing (OWASP ISTG)
dev_iot_istg_v2.description: Coverage tracker for an IoT device following the OWASP IoT Security Testing Guide test case catalogue, with one item per component category (or pair of categories) naming its ISTG test case IDs. Agree the physical (PA-1 to PA-4) and authorisation (AA-1 to AA-4) access levels first, mark items outside them as not applicable, and record the result of each test case.

items.title: ISTG-PROC to ISTG-UI Components and access levels agreed
items.description:
The ISTG attacker model decides which components and test cases apply.

  • Device parts are mapped to the ISTG device model components, from processing units to user interfaces.
  • The highest physical (PA-1 remote to PA-4 invasive) and authorisation (AA-1 to AA-4) levels are agreed.
  • Permission to open, modify or damage units, and the number of samples, is confirmed in writing.

Record: component map, agreed levels and sample serials; pass when each later item is marked in or out of scope.

items.title: ISTG-PROC-AUTHZ Access to the processing unit
items.description:
Even with PA-4 access, processor debug and programming must need authorisation. Test cases ISTG-PROC-AUTHZ-001 and ISTG-PROC-AUTHZ-002.

  • 001: debug and programming access to the processing unit is locked or authenticated.
  • 002: a low-privileged session cannot reach restricted processor functions.
  • Debug lock and fuse states are recorded from documentation or observation.

Record: access routes tried, lock state and result; pass when access needs the intended authorisation level.

items.title: ISTG-PROC-LOGIC and ISTG-PROC-SIDEC Instruction handling and side-channel resistance
items.description:
Covers ISTG-PROC-LOGIC-001 and ISTG-PROC-SIDEC-001 on instruction misuse and side-channel leakage.

  • Undocumented or misused instructions do not leave the device in an unknown or insecure state.
  • The processor model is checked for published speculative execution and similar flaws.
  • Resistance to timing analysis and glitching is assessed where in scope and equipment allows.

Record: processor model, known issues and observed behaviour; pass when no weakness is found or each is mitigated.

items.title: ISTG-MEM-INFO Information exposed by memory contents
items.description:
Memory read with PA-4 access can expose code and data. Test cases ISTG-MEM-INFO-001 to ISTG-MEM-INFO-005.

  • 001 to 003: no source code, implementation detail or ecosystem detail (hosts, accounts, keys) useful to an attacker.
  • 004: user data cannot be read by an unauthorised person.
  • 005: binaries use mitigations such as PIE, NX, stack canaries, RELRO and FORTIFY_SOURCE.

Record: chips read, content found and missing mitigations; pass when nothing sensitive is readable in clear form.

items.title: ISTG-MEM-SCRT and ISTG-MEM-CRYPT Secrets and cryptography in memory
items.description:
Covers ISTG-MEM-SCRT-001 and ISTG-MEM-CRYPT-001: secrets on memory chips must not be in plain text, and stored data must use current algorithms.

  • No passwords, private keys or tokens are stored in plain text.
  • Encrypted regions use algorithms and settings that are sound today.
  • Keys protecting stored data are held in secure hardware, not beside the data.

Record: secrets found (redacted) and algorithms identified; pass when stored secrets have current protection.

items.title: ISTG-FW-INFO Information disclosed by the firmware
items.description:
Firmware images show how a device works and what it talks to. Test cases ISTG-FW-INFO-001 to ISTG-FW-INFO-003.

  • 001: no source code or debug material ships in the image.
  • 002: implementation details (algorithms, authentication design, paths) are noted for later tests.
  • 003: configuration exposes no ecosystem details such as back-end hosts, accounts or certificates.

Record: image source, version and notable disclosures; pass when the image reveals nothing that weakens the ecosystem.

items.title: ISTG-FW-CONF Outdated and unnecessary software in firmware
items.description:
Firmware bundles an operating system and packages that age quickly. Test cases ISTG-FW-CONF-001 and ISTG-FW-CONF-002.

  • 001: package, library and kernel versions are identified and checked against vulnerability databases.
  • 002: tools and services the device does not need (debug servers, shells, compilers) are absent.
  • Any vendor software bill of materials matches what is found.

Record: component list with versions and known vulnerabilities; pass when components are current and minimal.

items.title: ISTG-FW-SCRT Secrets in firmware
items.description:
Secrets in firmware are shared by every unit, so one extraction can expose the whole fleet. Test cases ISTG-FW-SCRT-001 to ISTG-FW-SCRT-003.

  • 001: public storage areas hold no passwords, keys or tokens.
  • 002: restricted storage areas hold no secrets in plain text.
  • 003: no hard-coded credentials or keys appear in binaries or scripts.

Record: each secret (redacted), where found and whether unique per device; pass when none is found or each is unique and protected.

items.title: ISTG-FW-CRYPT Cryptography used in firmware
items.description:
Test case ISTG-FW-CRYPT-001: data stored by or in the firmware must use algorithms adequate today.

  • Encrypted segments are found and their algorithms identified where possible.
  • Source, configuration and binaries are checked for deprecated algorithms, modes or short keys.
  • Findings are judged against a current cryptography guideline named in the report.

Record: algorithms, key lengths and the guideline used; pass when no weak primitive protects sensitive data.

items.title: ISTG-FW[INST]-AUTHZ and ISTG-FW[INST]-INFO Access to the running firmware and user data
items.description:
Covers ISTG-FW[INST]-AUTHZ-001, ISTG-FW[INST]-AUTHZ-002 and ISTG-FW[INST]-INFO-001; ISTG-FW cases also apply.

  • AUTHZ-001: no route to the running firmware (shell, SSH, debug access) works without the intended authorisation.
  • AUTHZ-002: a low-privileged account cannot reach root or restricted functions.
  • INFO-001: user data on the device cannot be read without authorisation.

Record: access routes, privilege reached and data exposed; pass when access and data match the intended level.

items.title: ISTG-FW[INST]-CRYPT Bootloader signature verification
items.description:
Test case ISTG-FW[INST]-CRYPT-001: secure boot protects the device only if each boot stage checks the next before running it.

  • The device verifies the bootloader signature during boot and refuses an invalid one.
  • The chain of trust continues to the kernel and root file system.
  • Verification keys are in read-only or fused storage, and debug overrides are disabled.

Record: boot chain stages and verification evidence; pass when modified boot components are rejected.

items.title: ISTG-FW[UPDT]-AUTHZ Authorisation to update firmware
items.description:
Test case ISTG-FW[UPDT]-AUTHZ-001: only authorised parties may start a firmware update, locally or remotely.

  • Every update route (web interface, app, cloud push, USB, serial) needs the intended authorisation.
  • Authorisation cannot be skipped by calling the update function directly.
  • Update events are logged on the device or back end.

Record: update routes and the authorisation each needs; pass when no unauthorised route starts an update.

items.title: ISTG-FW[UPDT]-CRYPT-001 and ISTG-FW[UPDT]-CRYPT-004 Update signing and signature checks
items.description:
Updates must be signed with a strong algorithm, and the device must check the signature before installing.

  • 001: update packages carry a signature made with a current algorithm and key size.
  • 004: the device verifies the signature and rejects modified or unsigned packages.
  • The verification key cannot be replaced through configuration.

Record: signature scheme and the device response to an altered package; pass when only correctly signed packages install.

items.title: ISTG-FW[UPDT]-CRYPT-002 and ISTG-FW[UPDT]-CRYPT-003 Update encryption and delivery
items.description:
Updates may need encryption to protect their contents, and must travel over a channel that protects integrity.

  • 002: where the vendor requires encrypted packages, a sound algorithm is used.
  • 003: updates arrive over a protected channel, such as TLS with server certificate validation.
  • The download location cannot be redirected through user-controlled settings without checks.

Record: transport, ciphers and certificate checks; pass when updates cannot be read or altered in transit.

items.title: ISTG-FW[UPDT]-LOGIC Rollback protection
items.description:
Test case ISTG-FW[UPDT]-LOGIC-001: if older firmware can be installed, fixed vulnerabilities come back.

  • The device refuses validly signed but older versions, unless a controlled exception exists.
  • Version counters are stored where they cannot be reset.
  • Recovery or factory images do not bypass the rule.

Record: versions tried and the outcome; pass when downgrade is refused.

items.title: ISTG-DES-AUTHZ Access to data exchange services
items.description:
Network services on the device (web APIs, MQTT, CoAP, proprietary protocols) must enforce authorisation. Test cases ISTG-DES-AUTHZ-001 and ISTG-DES-AUTHZ-002.

  • 001: every service and function needs authentication unless meant to be public.
  • 002: a low-privileged user cannot reach admin functions or other users' data.
  • Default or shared credentials are not accepted.

Record: services, functions and the access each allowed; pass when access matches the intended levels.

items.title: ISTG-DES-INFO Information disclosed by services
items.description:
Banners, errors and responses can reveal internals, ecosystem details and user data. Test cases ISTG-DES-INFO-001 to ISTG-DES-INFO-003.

  • 001: disclosed versions, paths and algorithms are noted for later tests.
  • 002: responses expose no back-end hosts, cloud accounts or other devices.
  • 003: user data is not returned to unauthorised callers.

Record: disclosures with the request that caused them; pass when nothing sensitive comes back without authorisation.

items.title: ISTG-DES-CONF Outdated software and unneeded functions in services
items.description:
Services should run current software and offer only what the device needs. Test cases ISTG-DES-CONF-001 and ISTG-DES-CONF-002.

  • 001: service software and library versions are checked against vulnerability databases.
  • 002: debug, test or legacy functions reachable over the network are absent or disabled.
  • Listening ports match the documented services.

Record: listening services, versions and unneeded functions; pass when all are current and required.

items.title: ISTG-DES-SCRT and ISTG-DES-CRYPT Secrets and cryptography in data exchange
items.description:
Covers ISTG-DES-SCRT-001 and ISTG-DES-CRYPT-001: services must not hand out secrets, and their traffic must use sound cryptography.

  • SCRT-001: no service returns keys, passwords, tokens or Wi-Fi credentials without need.
  • CRYPT-001: sensitive traffic uses current protocols and cipher suites.
  • Algorithms seen in headers and messages are judged against a current guideline.

Record: secrets exposed and protocol findings; pass when secrets stay protected.

items.title: ISTG-DES-LOGIC Business logic of data exchange
items.description:
Test case ISTG-DES-LOGIC-001: the device must detect and handle requests that skip or reorder workflow steps.

  • Multi-step flows (pairing, provisioning, firmware update) cannot be completed out of order.
  • Limits and state checks (counters, rates, modes) are enforced on the device or back end.
  • Unexpected sequences leave the device in a safe, known state.

Record: workflows reviewed and any deviations accepted; pass when deviations are rejected.

items.title: ISTG-DES-INPV Input validation in data exchange
items.description:
Embedded services often pass input to shells or parsers, so it must be validated. Test cases ISTG-DES-INPV-001 and ISTG-DES-INPV-002.

  • 001: data outside the expected structure, type or range is rejected.
  • 002: input is never run as code or operating system commands.
  • Malformed input does not crash or hang the service.

Record: inputs tested and behaviour seen; pass when invalid input is rejected safely.

items.title: ISTG-INT-AUTHZ Access through internal interfaces
items.description:
Board-level interfaces such as JTAG, SWD or SPI (PA-4) must not give unauthorised access. Test cases ISTG-INT-AUTHZ-001 and ISTG-INT-AUTHZ-002.

  • 001: debug and programming interfaces are disabled, locked or authenticated.
  • 002: access gained through an interface does not exceed the intended level.
  • Test points and headers are identified and documented.

Record: interfaces found, their state and access reached; pass when none gives unauthorised control.

items.title: ISTG-INT-INFO Information on internal interfaces
items.description:
Internal bus traffic and output can disclose implementation detail, ecosystem detail and user data. Test cases ISTG-INT-INFO-001 to ISTG-INT-INFO-003.

  • 001: debug output and bus traffic reveal no more implementation detail than is public.
  • 002: no back-end addresses, credentials or certificates cross internal buses in clear form.
  • 003: user data on internal buses is protected.

Record: interfaces observed and data seen; pass when nothing sensitive is exposed.

items.title: ISTG-INT-CONF Configuration of internal interfaces
items.description:
Interface software should be current, with debug functions off in production. Test cases ISTG-INT-CONF-001 and ISTG-INT-CONF-002.

  • 001: software reachable through the interface (bootloader, debug monitor) is current.
  • 002: development features and unused interfaces are disabled on production units.
  • Production and development hardware revisions are told apart.

Record: interface software versions and enabled functions; pass when production units expose only what is needed.

items.title: ISTG-INT-SCRT and ISTG-INT-CRYPT Secrets and cryptography on internal interfaces
items.description:
Covers ISTG-INT-SCRT-001 and ISTG-INT-CRYPT-001: secrets must not be readable over internal interfaces, and protection must be sound.

  • SCRT-001: no keys, passwords or certificates can be read through internal interfaces.
  • CRYPT-001: secrets passed between chips (such as processor to secure element) use current algorithms.
  • Keys are not sent in clear form at start-up or during provisioning.

Record: secrets observed (redacted) and algorithms; pass when secrets stay protected.

items.title: ISTG-INT-LOGIC and ISTG-INT-INPV Logic and input handling on internal interfaces
items.description:
Covers ISTG-INT-LOGIC-001, ISTG-INT-INPV-001 and ISTG-INT-INPV-002: components on internal buses must handle odd sequences and data safely.

  • Out-of-sequence commands do not put the device in an unsafe state.
  • Malformed data on the interface is rejected.
  • Input is never run as code or commands.

Record: inputs and sequences tried and outcomes; pass when the device stays in a safe state.

items.title: ISTG-INT[I2C] I2C bus access, data and invalid input
items.description:
Covers ISTG-INT[I2C]-AUTHZ-001, ISTG-INT[I2C]-INFO-001 to ISTG-INT[I2C]-INFO-003 and ISTG-INT[I2C]-INPV-001.

  • Bus components are identified and ignore commands from an added, unauthorised device.
  • Bus traffic and EEPROM contents hold no keys, credentials or sensitive settings in clear text.
  • EEPROM write protection works; invalid or out-of-range transactions are handled safely.

Record: components, data seen and EEPROM protection; pass when nothing sensitive is readable or writable.

items.title: ISTG-INT[UART]-AUTHZ Serial console and bootloader access
items.description:
Test cases ISTG-INT[UART]-AUTHZ-001 and ISTG-INT[UART]-AUTHZ-002 on serial console and bootloader access.

  • 001: the console gives no unauthenticated shell, and login cannot be skipped via boot options.
  • 002: autoboot cannot be interrupted to a bootloader prompt, or the prompt needs authentication.
  • Bootloader commands that read or write flash or load code are off in production.

Record: console state, privilege and bootloader protection; pass when serial access gives no control.

items.title: ISTG-INT[UART]-INFO and ISTG-INT[UART]-INPV Serial output and command handling
items.description:
Covers ISTG-INT[UART]-INFO-001, ISTG-INT[UART]-INFO-002 and ISTG-INT[UART]-INPV-001.

  • INFO-001: UART pins and settings are identified, including unpopulated test points.
  • INFO-002: boot and runtime output holds no credentials, keys, Wi-Fi details or provisioning data.
  • INPV-001: restricted command menus cannot be escaped to run arbitrary commands.

Record: captured output (redacted) and command handling results; pass when nothing sensitive prints and commands stay restricted.

items.title: ISTG-PHY-AUTHZ Access through physical interfaces
items.description:
External ports such as USB, Ethernet, card slots and service connectors must enforce authorisation. Test cases ISTG-PHY-AUTHZ-001 and ISTG-PHY-AUTHZ-002.

  • 001: no port gives access to functions or data without the intended authorisation.
  • 002: access through a port cannot be raised to higher privilege.
  • Service or maintenance modes reached through ports are protected.

Record: ports, functions reached and authorisation needed; pass when access matches the intended level.

items.title: ISTG-PHY-INFO Information through physical interfaces
items.description:
Physical ports can reveal implementation detail, ecosystem detail and user data. Test cases ISTG-PHY-INFO-001 to ISTG-PHY-INFO-003.

  • 001: device descriptors, file systems and diagnostic output reveal no more than intended.
  • 002: no back-end hosts, accounts or certificates are exposed through ports.
  • 003: user data cannot be read through a port, or from removable media, without authorisation.

Record: disclosures per port; pass when nothing sensitive is exposed.

items.title: ISTG-PHY-CONF Configuration of physical interfaces
items.description:
Software behind physical ports should be current, and unneeded ports disabled. Test cases ISTG-PHY-CONF-001 and ISTG-PHY-CONF-002.

  • 001: drivers and services behind each port are current.
  • 002: unused ports and functions (such as USB device modes or network boot) are disabled.
  • Removable media is not run or imported automatically.

Record: enabled ports and functions with versions; pass when only needed functions are active.

items.title: ISTG-PHY-SCRT and ISTG-PHY-CRYPT Secrets and cryptography on physical interfaces
items.description:
Covers ISTG-PHY-SCRT-001 and ISTG-PHY-CRYPT-001: ports must not disclose secrets, and data across them must use sound algorithms.

  • SCRT-001: no keys or credentials are readable through a port.
  • CRYPT-001: data exchanged over ports that carries secrets uses current algorithms.
  • Configuration export files hold no clear-text secrets.

Record: secrets observed (redacted) and algorithms used; pass when secrets are protected.

items.title: ISTG-PHY-LOGIC and ISTG-PHY-INPV Logic and input handling on physical interfaces
items.description:
Covers ISTG-PHY-LOGIC-001, ISTG-PHY-INPV-001 and ISTG-PHY-INPV-002: data and sequences arriving through ports must be validated.

  • Out-of-order or unexpected port sequences leave the device in a safe state.
  • Malformed data from ports or removable media is rejected.
  • Input from ports is never run as commands or code.

Record: inputs tested and behaviour seen; pass when invalid input is handled safely.

items.title: ISTG-WRLS-AUTHZ Access through wireless interfaces
items.description:
Wi-Fi, Bluetooth Low Energy, Zigbee, LoRa, cellular and NFC are reachable from a distance (PA-2). Test cases ISTG-WRLS-AUTHZ-001 and ISTG-WRLS-AUTHZ-002.

  • 001: pairing or joining needs the intended credential, and no function is open before it.
  • 002: a paired low-privileged party cannot reach admin functions.
  • Pairing windows are short and need user action.

Record: interfaces, pairing methods and access reached; pass when unpaired or unauthorised parties get no access.

items.title: ISTG-WRLS-INFO Information disclosed over the air
items.description:
Broadcasts and radio traffic can reveal implementation detail, ecosystem detail and user data. Test cases ISTG-WRLS-INFO-001 to ISTG-WRLS-INFO-003.

  • 001: advertisements and service lists reveal no more than needed.
  • 002: radio traffic exposes no back-end details or network credentials.
  • 003: user data cannot be read from traffic or unauthenticated characteristics.

Record: disclosures captured per interface; pass when no sensitive data is readable without authorisation.

items.title: ISTG-WRLS-CONF Configuration of wireless interfaces
items.description:
Radio firmware and stacks should be current, and unneeded radios or modes off. Test cases ISTG-WRLS-CONF-001 and ISTG-WRLS-CONF-002.

  • 001: wireless chipset firmware and protocol stacks are current and checked for known flaws.
  • 002: unused radios, setup access points and legacy modes are disabled after provisioning.
  • Default network names and keys are unique per device or changed at setup.

Record: radios, modes and stack versions; pass when only needed radios run current software.

items.title: ISTG-WRLS-SCRT and ISTG-WRLS-CRYPT Secrets and cryptography over the air
items.description:
Covers ISTG-WRLS-SCRT-001 and ISTG-WRLS-CRYPT-001: wireless links must protect secrets and use current security modes.

  • SCRT-001: keys, Wi-Fi credentials and tokens are never exposed in clear form, provisioning included.
  • CRYPT-001: links use current modes, such as WPA3 or WPA2 with AES, and LE Secure Connections for Bluetooth LE.
  • Legacy pairing and fixed keys are refused.

Record: security modes and any secrets seen; pass when links use current modes and expose nothing.

items.title: ISTG-WRLS-LOGIC and ISTG-WRLS-INPV Logic and input handling over the air
items.description:
Covers ISTG-WRLS-LOGIC-001, ISTG-WRLS-INPV-001 and ISTG-WRLS-INPV-002: radio messages must be validated and workflows enforced.

  • Commands sent out of sequence or replayed are rejected.
  • Malformed frames or messages do not crash the device or its radio stack.
  • Received data is never run as commands or code.

Record: messages tested and device behaviour; pass when invalid or replayed input is rejected safely.

items.title: ISTG-UI-AUTHZ Access to user interfaces
items.description:
Web interfaces, companion apps and on-device screens and buttons must all enforce authorisation. Test cases ISTG-UI-AUTHZ-001 and ISTG-UI-AUTHZ-002.

  • 001: interfaces need authentication, with no default or shared credentials.
  • 002: users cannot reach admin functions or other users' data.
  • Reset and recovery need physical presence or strong verification.

Record: interfaces, roles and access reached; pass when each role gets only its intended functions.

items.title: ISTG-UI-INFO Information disclosed by user interfaces
items.description:
Interfaces can disclose implementation detail, ecosystem detail and user data. Test cases ISTG-UI-INFO-001 to ISTG-UI-INFO-003.

  • 001: version pages, errors and client-side code reveal no more than needed.
  • 002: no back-end hosts, keys or account details are visible.
  • 003: user data is shown only to authorised users.

Record: disclosures per interface; pass when nothing sensitive appears without authorisation.

items.title: ISTG-UI-CONF Configuration of user interfaces
items.description:
Interface software should be current and expose only required functions. Test cases ISTG-UI-CONF-001 and ISTG-UI-CONF-002.

  • 001: web server, framework and companion app versions are current.
  • 002: test, debug and hidden menus are removed or protected.
  • Security settings (session timeout, password change at first use) are on by default.

Record: interface components, versions and extra functions; pass when only needed functions are present.

items.title: ISTG-UI-SCRT and ISTG-UI-CRYPT Secrets and cryptography in user interfaces
items.description:
Covers ISTG-UI-SCRT-001 and ISTG-UI-CRYPT-001: interfaces must not reveal secrets and must use sound cryptography.

  • SCRT-001: stored passwords, keys and Wi-Fi credentials cannot be viewed or retrieved.
  • CRYPT-001: web interfaces use HTTPS with current TLS, and apps validate certificates.
  • Exported backups and configuration files are encrypted or omit secrets.

Record: secrets reachable and protocol findings; pass when no interface reveals secrets.

items.title: ISTG-UI-LOGIC and ISTG-UI-INPV Logic and input handling in user interfaces
items.description:
Covers ISTG-UI-LOGIC-001, ISTG-UI-INPV-001 and ISTG-UI-INPV-002: device web interfaces often pass input to system commands.

  • Setup, reset and update workflows cannot be completed out of order.
  • Input outside the expected type, length or range is rejected.
  • Input is never run as code or operating system commands.

Record: inputs and workflows tested with outcomes; pass when invalid input and sequences are rejected.

dev_thick_client_v2.name: Thick Client Application Testing
dev_thick_client_v2.description: Coverage tracker for a desktop (thick client) application and its back end, covering architecture, installation, binaries, local data, traffic, server-side enforcement, updates and the local attack surface, with OWASP Desktop App Security Top 10 (2021) and CWE references where they apply. Work through each item with the client installed and run as a standard user, and keep the evidence each item names.

items.title: Architecture and trust boundaries
items.description:
Shows what runs on the user's machine, what it talks to and where trust sits.

  • Client technology is known (.NET, Java, native code, Electron or another embedded browser).
  • Back-end endpoints, protocols and any direct database or file share links are listed.
  • Elevated components (services, drivers, helpers) are identified.
  • Security decisions made on the client are noted for later items.

Record: a data flow diagram with trust boundaries; pass when every interface is listed.

items.title: Two-tier clients talking straight to a database
items.description:
When the client connects straight to the database, the database must enforce every rule.

  • Each user has a personal database login, not one shared account embedded in the client.
  • Database permissions limit users to their application role, through views or stored procedures.
  • The connection is encrypted and the server certificate is validated.

Record: how the client signs in to the database and that login's effective rights; pass when bypassing the client grants nothing extra.

items.title: Three-tier clients and the application server API
items.description:
In a three-tier design the server API is the real boundary, and it can be called without the client.

  • Every operation the client uses needs authentication and checks the caller's role on the server.
  • Undocumented or admin operations found in the client are also protected on the server.
  • Server errors reveal no stack traces, queries or internal hostnames.

Record: the API inventory and how each operation was verified; pass when the server enforces every rule itself.

items.title: Installer and installation location
items.description:
Installers run elevated, so where they write decides whether users can tamper with privileged code.

  • The installer package is signed.
  • The application installs to a protected folder such as Program Files.
  • Elevated install, repair and update steps use no files from user-writable locations.
  • No trusted root certificates, firewall exceptions or services are added without need.
