Record: install path and installer actions; pass when no elevated step trusts user-writable content.

items.title: Installed file and folder permissions
items.description:
If standard users can change the application's code or settings, they can run code as whoever starts it.

  • Install folders, executables, DLLs, plug-ins and scripts are writable only by administrators.
  • Shared data folders (such as under ProgramData) hold no code or settings that privileged processes trust.
  • Standard users cannot modify settings that change behaviour.

Record: access control lists for each location; pass when standard users cannot change code or trusted settings.

items.title: DLL and library search order
items.description:
A library loaded from a folder a standard user can write to lets that user run code in the application.

  • The application and installer load no DLLs from user-writable folders, the current directory or PATH.
  • Libraries load by full path or with safe search flags (SetDefaultDllDirectories).
  • Java, .NET and Electron clients load no plug-ins, assemblies or modules from writable paths.

Record: library loads from unsafe locations; pass when every library resolves to a protected folder.

items.title: Binary exploit mitigations
items.description:
Compiler and linker protections make memory corruption bugs much harder to turn into code execution.

  • Executables and DLLs are built with ASLR (DYNAMICBASE, plus HIGHENTROPYVA for 64-bit) and DEP (NXCOMPAT).
  • Control Flow Guard and buffer security checks (/GS) are on for native code.
  • Bundled third-party native libraries meet the same standard.

Record: mitigation flags per binary; pass when every native binary has ASLR and DEP and gaps are justified.

items.title: Code signing of binaries and scripts
items.description:
Signatures let users and endpoint controls confirm that code came from the vendor unchanged.

  • All executables, DLLs, drivers, installers and scripts carry a valid Authenticode signature from the vendor.
  • Signatures are timestamped and use SHA-256 or stronger.
  • The application checks signatures of plug-ins or components it loads at runtime, where supported.

Record: unsigned or invalidly signed files; pass when every shipped binary verifies to the vendor.

items.title: Secrets and keys in binaries
items.description:
Anything compiled into the client can be extracted by any user, so embedded secrets are effectively public (CWE-798).

  • Binaries, assemblies and bundled scripts hold no passwords, API keys, connection strings or private keys.
  • Keys protecting local data or traffic are not hard-coded (CWE-321).
  • Obfuscation is not relied on to hide secrets.

Record: each secret found (redacted), where and what it grants; pass when none exists or each is useless without server checks.

items.title: Secrets in configuration files
items.description:
Configuration files often hold connection strings and service credentials in clear text.

  • Configuration holds no clear-text passwords, tokens or connection strings with credentials.
  • Protected values use a platform mechanism such as per-user DPAPI, not a key stored beside them.
  • Files with sensitive settings are readable only by the user or service that needs them.

Record: files with sensitive values and their permissions; pass when no credential is recoverable by another local user.

items.title: Stored credentials and session tokens
items.description:
Remember-me features and cached sessions let anyone with access to the profile reuse the user's identity.

  • Passwords are not saved; any stored token sits in the OS credential store or user-scoped DPAPI.
  • Stored tokens expire and are invalidated on the server at logout.
  • Offline sign-in, if offered, keeps no reversible passwords or weak hashes.

Record: where credentials or tokens are kept and how; pass when another user or a copied profile cannot reuse them.

items.title: Local storage of application data
items.description:
Local databases, caches and exports often hold personal or business data outside the server's controls.

  • Local databases, caches, temporary files and exports with sensitive data are encrypted or minimised.
  • They sit in per-user locations whose permissions exclude other users.
  • Temporary files are deleted after use and at logout.

Record: each local store with data types and protection; pass when sensitive data is protected and limited to its user.

items.title: Sensitive data in memory and crash dumps
items.description:
Secrets kept in memory longer than needed can be read from process memory, page files or crash dumps.

  • Passwords and keys are cleared from memory after use, not kept for the whole session.
  • Decrypted data and credentials do not persist after logout.
  • Crash dumps and diagnostic bundles capture no secrets, or are protected and short-lived.

Record: secrets seen in memory or dumps and when; pass when exposure is limited to the moment of use.

items.title: Sensitive data in logs and diagnostics
items.description:
Client logs are rarely protected and often capture tokens, queries and personal data (CWE-532).

  • Logs and trace files hold no passwords, tokens, keys or full personal records.
  • Users cannot switch on debug or verbose logging that exposes sensitive detail.
  • Log files are readable only by the user and administrators.

Record: log locations and sensitive entries; pass when logs reveal nothing that helps reuse an identity or session.

items.title: Traffic interception and protocols
items.description:
Thick clients often use non-HTTP or proprietary protocols, so all traffic must be mapped (OWASP DA7).

  • Every connection is identified, including database, file share, licence and update traffic.
  • No credentials or sensitive data travel in clear text (CWE-319).
  • Proprietary protocols do not rely on obscurity or home-made encryption.

Record: each endpoint with protocol and protection; pass when all sensitive traffic uses standard encryption.

items.title: TLS and certificate validation
items.description:
A client that accepts any certificate hands its traffic to anyone who can intercept it (CWE-295).

  • Server certificates are checked for chain, expiry and hostname; no custom callback accepts everything.
  • Only TLS 1.2 or later is negotiated.
  • Pinning, if used, cannot be switched off through user-editable settings.

Record: behaviour when shown an untrusted or mismatched certificate; pass when the client refuses to connect.

items.title: Authorisation enforced on the server
items.description:
Hiding or disabling functions in the client does not stop a user calling them directly (CWE-602).

  • Hidden, disabled or role-restricted functions are refused by the server for users without the role.
  • Record identifiers sent by the client cannot be changed to reach other users' or tenants' data.
  • Read-only and masked fields are enforced on the server.

Record: each check with role and result; pass when the server rejects every request beyond the user's rights.

items.title: Input handling and injection through the client
items.description:
Data from the client, imported files and server replies must be treated as untrusted wherever it is parsed or queried.

  • Server-side validation does not rely on checks made in the client.
  • Queries use parameters; two-tier clients never put user input into dynamic SQL (CWE-89).
  • Imported files and messages are not deserialised with unsafe formatters such as BinaryFormatter (CWE-502).

Record: inputs tested and results; pass when malformed input is rejected without side effects.

items.title: Authentication and session handling
items.description:
Some thick clients authenticate locally and then trust themselves, or keep sessions alive indefinitely (CWE-603).

  • The server, not the client, decides whether authentication succeeded.
  • Session tokens are random, expire after inactivity and are revoked at logout.
  • Sign-in has lockout or throttling, and MFA applies where policy requires it.

Record: the authentication flow and session lifetimes; pass when no client-side change yields a session.

items.title: Use of cryptography
items.description:
Weak or home-made cryptography offers little once its keys and algorithms are read from the binary (OWASP DA4).

  • Current algorithms are used (AES-GCM, SHA-256 or stronger); MD5, SHA-1, DES and ECB mode serve no security purpose.
  • Keys are generated or protected by the platform, not derived from constants.
  • Random values for tokens and keys come from a cryptographic generator.

Record: algorithms and key handling found; pass when no security function relies on weak or embedded keys.

items.title: Update mechanism integrity
items.description:
An auto-updater runs downloaded code, often with high privilege, so its checks decide who controls every client (CWE-494).

  • Update metadata and packages are fetched over validated TLS.
  • The updater verifies package signatures before installing, not just the transport.
  • Older versions cannot be forced on the client, and the update service runs no user-supplied files.

Record: update channel, verification steps and updater privilege; pass when only current, vendor-signed packages install.

items.title: Inter-process communication exposure
items.description:
Named pipes, local ports, COM objects and URI handlers let other local processes, or web pages, drive the application.

  • Named pipes and shared memory have access control lists that exclude other users.
  • Local TCP or HTTP listeners bind to loopback and require authentication.
  • Custom URI schemes and file associations validate their arguments before acting.

Record: each IPC endpoint with permissions and authentication; pass when none accepts unauthorised commands.

items.title: Registry keys and permissions
items.description:
Registry keys under the local machine hive often control what privileged components load or run.

  • Keys used by services, COM registrations, start-up entries or plug-in paths are not writable by standard users.
  • No secrets are stored in the registry in clear text.
  • Per-user keys do not change how privileged components behave.

Record: key paths with weak permissions or sensitive values; pass when none can be abused by a standard user.

items.title: Privileged services shipped with the client
items.description:
Services and tasks installed with the client often run as LocalSystem, a common route to administrator.

  • Each service runs as the least privileged account that works.
  • Service paths are quoted and point to protected folders; service permissions stop users reconfiguring them.
  • Commands the service accepts from users are authorised and validated.

Record: services and tasks with account, paths and access rights; pass when no standard user can change or abuse them.

items.title: Privilege the client runs with
items.description:
A client that needs administrator rights for daily use turns every flaw in it into an administrator-level flaw (OWASP DA6).

  • The client runs as a standard user and does not ask for elevation in normal use.
  • Tasks needing elevation are split into a separate, narrowly scoped component.
  • The client does not disable or weaken operating system security settings to work.

Record: privilege level in use and any elevation prompts; pass when normal use needs no administrator rights.

items.title: Licensing and feature checks done on the client
items.description:
Licence and entitlement checks run on the client can be altered by its user, so they must not guard paid features or data.

  • The server confirms entitlements before serving restricted features or data.
  • Licence files, trial dates and feature flags stored locally are signed or checked on the server.
  • Offline grace periods are limited and logged.

Record: where licence decisions are made and what client changes affect them; pass when unlicensed use gains no protected server function.

items.title: Embedded browsers and web content
items.description:
Electron, CEF or WebView2 clients can turn a web content flaw into code execution through an open native bridge.

  • Only trusted HTTPS origins load in-app; other links open in the system browser.
  • Node integration is off, context isolation and sandboxing on, and host objects expose only what is needed.
  • Developer tools and remote debugging are off in production builds.

Record: framework, settings and exposed native functions; pass when untrusted content cannot reach native code.

items.title: Bundled components and runtimes
items.description:
Thick clients ship runtimes and libraries the vendor must patch, and old ones carry known flaws (OWASP DA9).

  • Bundled runtimes (Java, .NET, Chromium) and libraries (such as OpenSSL) are listed with versions.
  • None has known exploitable flaws without a fix plan, and none is out of support.
  • The vendor provides a component inventory or software bill of materials.

Record: component list with versions and known issues; pass when all are supported and patched.

items.title: Error handling and malformed input
items.description:
Crashes and verbose errors on malformed files, replies or messages point to memory safety bugs and leak detail (OWASP DA8).

  • Malformed files, server replies and IPC messages are handled without crashing.
  • Errors shown or logged reveal no stack traces, queries or secrets.
  • Unhandled exceptions fail closed rather than leaving functions unlocked.

Record: crashes or disclosures with the input type that caused them; pass when the client degrades safely.

items.title: Security event logging on the server
items.description:
Client logs can be altered by the user, so the server must record security events from client activity (OWASP DA10).

  • Sign-ins, failures, privilege changes and access to sensitive records are logged with user and source.
  • Rejected requests that sidestep client controls are logged and can raise alerts.
  • Logs exclude secrets and keep personal data to what is needed.

Record: events tested and whether each reached the server logs; pass when the test activity can be reconstructed.

items.title: Uninstall residue
items.description:
Uninstalling should remove the client's code, services and secrets; leftovers keep privileged components and credentials around.

  • Services, scheduled tasks, drivers and start-up entries are removed.
  • Stored credentials, tokens, keys and cached data are deleted, or the user is told they remain.
  • Certificates added to trust stores and firewall rules are removed.

Record: files, keys and settings left after uninstall; pass when nothing sensitive or privileged remains.

run_kickoff_v1.name: Engagement kick-off and readiness
run_kickoff_v1.description: Runbook for the kick-off call and the readiness checks that come before any testing. Use it in the week before the start date to confirm authorisation, rules of engagement, contacts, access and the go or no-go decision.

items.title: Confirm scope and authorisation are signed
items.body:
Before booking the kick-off, the engagement lead checks that the contract or statement of work, the scope schedule and the written authorisation to test are signed and consistent. Testing without consent from someone entitled to give it can be an offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990.

  • The signatory has authority over every listed asset, or the owner's written consent is attached.
  • Targets are listed exactly, with dates, and exclusions are written down.

Done when: signed copies are filed and every planned target traces to the signed scope.

items.title: Hold the kick-off call
items.body:
The engagement lead runs a call at least three working days before testing with the client's technical contact, the risk owner and the testers, plus any hosting or managed service provider involved. It turns the signed scope into a shared plan.

  • Walk through objectives, targets, approach, timeline and any scenarios.
  • Capture constraints: fragile systems, out-of-hours needs and compliance drivers.
  • Confirm reporting needs, such as the rating scheme and the report date.

Done when: minutes listing decisions and open actions are sent within one working day.

items.title: Agree the rules of engagement
items.body:
The engagement lead and the client agree in writing how testing will behave, so testers never have to guess mid-test. The rules go in the engagement file and every tester is briefed.

  • Permitted and prohibited activities, including denial of service and social engineering.
  • How far to go once an issue is confirmed, and limits on touching live data.
  • Account lockout tolerance, and whether protective controls are allow-listed.
  • What to do on finding a prior compromise or illegal material.

Done when: the client has approved the rules and each tester has confirmed reading them.

items.title: Exchange contacts and an emergency route
items.body:
Both sides name who to call and when, because a critical finding or an outage needs a person, not a shared mailbox. The engagement lead builds the contact sheet and tests it.

  • Firm: the engagement lead, a deputy and each tester.
  • Client: technical contact, deputy, risk owner and an emergency contact reachable throughout every testing window, each with two contact methods.
  • The SOC or managed security provider, so alerts can be checked against testing.

Done when: the sheet is shared with everyone named on it and the emergency number has been tested.

items.title: Fix testing windows and time zones
items.body:
The engagement lead records exactly when testing may run, in the client's local time and in UTC, so nobody misreads a window across time zones or a clock change.

  • Dates, daily start and stop times, and any out-of-hours or weekend work.
  • Blackout periods such as releases, month end, trading peaks and bank holidays.
  • Change freezes, and who confirms on the day that a window is still open.

Done when: the client has confirmed the window schedule in writing and it is in the test plan.

items.title: Declare and allow-list source addresses
items.body:
The engagement lead sends the client every address testing will come from, so the client can recognise the traffic, allow-list it where agreed and tell a real attack apart from the test.

  • List static egress, VPN and any cloud-hosted testing addresses.
  • Agree whether testing runs through protective controls or with them allow-listed, and record why.
  • Pass the list to the SOC or managed provider.
  • Declare any new address before it is used.

Done when: the client confirms the addresses are recorded and any allow-listing is in place.

items.title: Receive accounts, data and access
items.body:
The testers confirm before day one that everything they need has arrived through a secure channel and works, so testing time is not lost to access problems.

  • Test accounts for each role in scope, ideally two per role, with MFA arranged.
  • Documentation, API definitions, application builds and test data.
  • VPN, jump host, network port or desk space for internal work.
  • Named client staff who can fix access faults during testing.

Done when: every account and access route has been tried and any fault reported to the client.

items.title: Confirm the environment and its safeguards
items.body:
The engagement lead confirms with the client what environment is being tested and what protects it if something goes wrong, because the answer changes how carefully testers work.

  • Production or not; if not, how closely it matches production.
  • Recent, restorable backups and who can restore them.
  • Change freezes, fragile components and rate limits to respect.
  • Automated emails, payments or alerts that tests could trigger.

Done when: the environment and its safeguards are recorded in the test plan.

items.title: Agree communication and status updates
items.body:
The engagement lead agrees how information moves during the test, so sensitive details never travel in clear text and the client always knows what is happening.

  • The day-to-day channel, and the secure route for findings, evidence and credentials.
  • Start and end-of-day messages and any status meetings.
  • The escalation route and target times for critical findings.
  • The draft report date and how it will be delivered.

Done when: the arrangements are recorded and both sides have used the channel once.

items.title: Make the go or no-go decision
items.body:
On the last working day before testing, the engagement lead reviews readiness and decides whether testing starts as planned. Starting without authorisation, tested contacts or working access risks harm and wasted days.

  • Check that each earlier step is complete.
  • If anything is missing, decide no-go, agree a new date with the client and record the reason.
  • If go, confirm the start time to the testers and the client contact.

Done when: the decision, its time and who agreed it are recorded in the engagement file.

run_credentials_v1.name: Test accounts and credentials
run_credentials_v1.description: Runbook for requesting, receiving, storing, using and retiring the test accounts and secrets a client provides, and for handling credentials found during testing. Use it from the first account request until the client confirms everything is disabled.

items.title: Request the right accounts
items.body:
The engagement lead asks the client for accounts that match the roles in scope, so access controls can be tested properly and every account is easy to trace in the client's logs.

  • At least two accounts per role, to test access between users of the same role.
  • Names that identify the firm and the test, so they stand out in logs.
  • An expiry date set at the end of the engagement.
  • No access to real customer data beyond what testing needs.

Done when: the request has been sent with a list of roles.

items.title: Receive them through a secure channel
items.body:
The engagement lead makes sure credentials arrive only through an agreed secure route. Credentials sent in plain email or chat are treated as exposed from the moment they arrive.

  • Use the firm's secure portal, the client's password-sharing tool, or an encrypted file with the passphrase sent separately.
  • If credentials arrive insecurely, ask the client to reset them and send them again securely.
  • Confirm receipt to the client.

Done when: every credential has arrived through a secure route.

items.title: Store them in the firm's vault
items.body:
Credentials go straight into the firm's approved vault, in a folder for the engagement, so access to them is controlled and logged.

  • Only testers assigned to the engagement can open the folder.
  • Never keep credentials in notes, tickets, chat, scripts or report drafts.
  • Record in the vault which role and environment each account belongs to.

Done when: all credentials for the engagement are in the vault and nowhere else.

items.title: Set up MFA and recovery
items.body:
Where accounts need MFA, the tester registers it on a firm-managed device, never a personal phone, so access can be withdrawn cleanly at the end of the engagement.

  • Record which device holds which registration.
  • Keep recovery codes in the vault, not on the device.
  • Agree with the client what happens if a device is lost or a code stops working.

Done when: MFA works for every account that needs it and the registrations are listed in the vault.

items.title: Check the accounts before day one
items.body:
The tester signs in with each account before testing starts and confirms it has the role and data the test plan expects, so faults are fixed before they cost testing time.

  • Change any first-use passwords and store the new values in the vault.
  • Report missing accounts or wrong permissions to the client at once.
  • Note any account shared with other users at the client.

Done when: every account works with its expected role.

items.title: Use accounts only in scope
items.body:
Testers use client accounts only against in-scope systems and only for the agreed purpose, because the authorisation covers the targets, not everything an account can reach.

  • Single sign-on may open other applications; do not use them unless they are in scope.
  • Change account security settings only as far as testing needs.
  • Log which account was used for which activity.

Done when: the activity log shows each account used only on in-scope targets.

items.title: Share safely within the team
items.body:
Testers share access through the vault, never by pasting credentials into chat or email, so every use can be traced.

  • Agree who uses which account, so concurrent sessions do not interfere with each other or with results.
  • When a tester leaves the engagement, remove their vault access.
  • Ask the client to rotate anything a departing tester could have copied, where the rules of engagement require it.

Done when: the vault access list matches the current team.

items.title: Handle credentials found during testing
items.body:
When a tester finds credentials, keys or tokens, for example in files, code, configuration or responses, they handle them as sensitive evidence.

  • Record where they were found and what they appear to grant.
  • Store them in the vault, not in notes.
  • Use them only if the rules of engagement allow, and only against in-scope systems.
  • Escalate live, high-privilege secrets through the critical finding runbook.

Done when: each find is recorded and the client knows about any live secret.

items.title: Deal with lock-outs and suspected exposure
items.body:
If an account locks, stops working or may have been exposed while in the firm's care, the tester tells the engagement lead, who informs the client the same day.

  • Ask the client to reset or reissue the account.
  • If exposure is possible, ask for immediate revocation and rotation.
  • Do not keep retrying a locked account.

Done when: the account is restored or replaced and the event is in the activity log.

items.title: Retire everything at the end
items.body:
At close-out, the engagement lead lists every account, key, token, certificate, VPN profile and MFA registration given or created, and asks the client in writing to disable or remove them all.

  • Ask the client to rotate any credentials found during testing.
  • Remove MFA registrations from firm devices.
  • Delete the vault folder once the client confirms.

Done when: the client has confirmed in writing that everything is disabled.

run_third_party_v1.name: Third-party and hosting provider permissions
run_third_party_v1.description: Runbook for confirming that everyone with a stake in the targets allows the test, from cloud providers to managed service, hosting, CDN, WAF and SaaS providers. Use it during scoping, and again whenever a target turns out to be hosted or run by someone else.

items.title: Map who owns and runs each target
items.body:
The engagement lead lists everyone involved in each target, from the client's answers and records, before any testing starts.

  • The owner, and where the target is hosted: cloud, data centre or shared hosting.
  • Who operates or monitors it, such as a managed service provider or SOC.
  • Services in front of it, such as a CDN, WAF or DDoS protection.
  • SaaS platforms and identity providers involved.

Done when: every target has an owner and provider list in the scope record.

items.title: Check each cloud provider's policy
items.body:
The engagement lead reads the current testing policy of each cloud provider involved, because the client's consent does not override the provider's terms.

  • AWS: listed services need no prior approval; denial of service outside its simulation policy, flooding and Route 53 zone walking are prohibited.
  • Microsoft: only your own tenants and assets; no denial of service.
  • Google Cloud: no notice needed, but its acceptable use policy applies.

Done when: each policy and the date it was read are recorded.

items.title: Confirm the client's rights over each asset
items.body:
The engagement lead confirms the client holds the cloud accounts, tenancies or contracts the targets sit in. A provider's permission only covers resources that its own customer controls.

  • Resources in a supplier's account need that supplier's consent.
  • On multi-tenant platforms, testing is limited to the client's own configuration and data.

Done when: each asset is matched to an account or contract the client controls, or to a recorded consent.

items.title: Get managed service provider agreement
items.body:
Where a managed service provider runs or monitors the targets, the engagement lead obtains its written agreement, or confirms that its contract with the client allows testing.

  • Tell it the dates and source addresses, unless measuring its detection is an agreed objective.
  • Agree who it calls if it sees the test.
  • Confirm it will check with the client before blocking or reporting test traffic as an attack.

Done when: the provider's agreement and contact are on file.

items.title: Clear hosting, CDN and WAF providers
items.body:
The engagement lead checks the terms of hosting providers, and of CDN or WAF services in front of the targets, because test traffic passes through their platforms.

  • Shared hosting usually needs the host's permission, since other customers share the infrastructure.
  • Agree whether testing goes through the CDN or WAF, or to the origin with allow-listing.
  • Test only the client's configuration, never the provider's platform.

Done when: each provider's position is recorded.

items.title: Deal with SaaS vendors
items.body:
Testing a SaaS application the client uses means testing the vendor's system, so the vendor's permission or published testing policy decides what is possible.

  • Check whether the vendor allows customer testing, and on what conditions.
  • Without permission, limit the work to reviewing the client's own settings, users and permissions through its normal administrative access.

Done when: each SaaS target is recorded as permitted, limited to configuration review or excluded.

items.title: Record written consent
items.body:
The engagement lead files every consent with the engagement, so the chain of authorisation can be shown to anyone who asks, including the provider itself.

  • Consent names the targets, dates, activities and source addresses.
  • Keep the provider's own reply or form, not only the client's word that consent exists.
  • Note any conditions, such as notice periods or banned techniques.

Done when: every third party on the map has a recorded position.

items.title: Know what is never tested without the owner
items.body:
Testers are briefed on what is always off limits unless its owner has agreed in writing.

  • Providers' underlying infrastructure, management planes and shared services.
  • Other tenants and customers, and their data.
  • Provider staff, through social engineering.
  • Denial of service against shared infrastructure.
  • ISP, DNS registrar, payment and identity provider systems the client does not own.

Done when: each tester has confirmed the restrictions that apply to their targets.

items.title: Report provider vulnerabilities properly
items.body:
If testing reveals a flaw in a provider's own service, the tester stops once it is identified and tells the engagement lead.

  • Tell the client, and agree who will report it.
  • Use the provider's vulnerability reporting route, such as MSRC for Microsoft.
  • If data belonging to someone else is reached, stop, report it and keep none of it.

Done when: the flaw has been reported through the provider's route and a copy of the report is filed.

items.title: Recheck when new targets appear
items.body:
The engagement lead repeats this runbook whenever a new target, a new provider or a hosting change appears during the engagement, since permissions do not carry over automatically.

  • Treat new third-party assets through the scope change runbook first.
  • Update the provider map.
  • Brief testers on any new restrictions before they touch the target.

Done when: the provider map matches the final scope.

run_testing_day_v1.name: Starting and ending a testing day
run_testing_day_v1.description: Runbook for the routine that opens and closes every testing day. Use it daily so that all activity is authorised, logged and traceable, and the client always knows what is running and what was found.

items.title: Confirm authorisation and today's window
items.body:
Each tester checks, before sending any traffic, that today's work is still authorised, because scope and windows can change after the test plan is written.

  • Today falls within the signed dates and the agreed daily window.
  • No client message has paused testing, added a freeze or changed scope.
  • The targets planned for today are in the current scope record.
  • The engagement lead and the client contact are reachable.

Done when: the tester has noted the check and its time in the activity log.

items.title: Check the testing platform
items.body:
The tester prepares the testing machine and network path before starting, because a wrong clock or an undeclared source address makes any later investigation much harder.

  • The approved testing build is up to date and its disk is encrypted.
  • The clock is synchronised, so log times line up with the client's logs.
  • Traffic leaves from a declared source address.
  • No data from another client is present on the machine.

Done when: the source address and clock check are written at the top of today's log.

items.title: Announce the start
items.body:
The tester or the engagement lead tells the client contact, through the agreed channel, that testing is starting. This lets the client link any alert or fault to the test straight away instead of treating it as an attack.

  • Who is testing, and from which source addresses.
  • Which targets and activities are planned, flagging high-volume work such as discovery or automated scanning.
  • The planned finish time.

Done when: the message is sent and, where the rules of engagement require it, acknowledged.

items.title: Keep the activity log as you work
items.body:
Each tester keeps a running log written at the time, not reconstructed later. It is the record used to answer an outage query, to separate test traffic from a real attack and to support the report.

  • Each entry: timestamp with time zone, source address, target, activity and outcome.
  • Note anything unexpected, such as errors, slow responses or lockouts.
  • Keep the log in the engagement folder, never on a personal device.

Done when: every testing activity of the day has a matching log entry.

items.title: Work to the plan and the agreed rates
items.body:
Testers follow the test plan in its agreed order, at the rates agreed with the client, and tick coverage as they go so gaps show early rather than on the last day.

  • Keep request rates and parallel jobs within the agreed limits.
  • Watch how targets respond and slow down at the first sign of strain.
  • Update the phase checklist as each area is covered.
  • Raise blockers, such as locked accounts or lost access, at once.

Done when: the day's planned areas are covered, or the reason they were not is logged.

items.title: Check in during the day
items.body:
The tester and the engagement lead hold short check-ins at agreed times, and after any significant event, so problems are dealt with while there is still time to act on them.

  • Progress against the plan, and any change of approach.
  • Candidate high or critical findings that may need escalation.
  • Blockers that need the client, such as access or accounts.
  • Whether tomorrow's plan still stands.

Done when: each check-in and its outcome is noted in the activity log.

items.title: Stop when a stop condition is met
items.body:
Any tester stops active testing at once if a stop condition is met, then follows the matching runbook. Nobody restarts until the engagement lead and the client have agreed it.

  • Degraded service or an outage on any target.
  • Signs of a real compromise by someone else.
  • Unexpected sensitive data, such as special category personal data.
  • An out-of-scope asset, or a client request to pause.

Done when: the stop time, the reason and the people told are recorded in the activity log.

items.title: Finish and announce the end
items.body:
The tester stops all activity before the window closes, confirms nothing is still running, then tells the client that testing has ended for the day.

  • Confirm no scans, scheduled jobs or open sessions remain active.
  • Remove temporary files or accounts created today, or list them for later removal.
  • Send the end message through the agreed channel.

Done when: the end time is logged and the client has received the message.

items.title: Send the end-of-day summary
items.body:
The engagement lead, or the lead tester, sends the client contact a short summary so the client can follow progress and act on anything urgent.

  • Areas covered today and the plan for tomorrow.
  • Blockers and what is needed from the client.
  • Significant findings at headline level only; detail goes through the secure route.
  • Any test artefacts still in place.

Done when: the summary is sent and a copy is filed with the engagement.

items.title: Secure the day's evidence
items.body:
Before logging off, each tester moves the day's evidence into the firm's approved, encrypted engagement store, so nothing sensitive is left loose on a laptop overnight.

  • Screenshots, captured requests and responses, notes and the activity log.
  • Redact secrets and personal data that are not needed as evidence.
  • Clear working copies from local folders as the firm's policy requires.

Done when: today's evidence is in the engagement store and the checklist shows today's coverage.

run_scope_change_v1.name: Scope changes and out-of-scope discoveries
run_scope_change_v1.description: Runbook for when testing reveals assets outside the signed scope, or the client asks to add or remove targets. Use it before interacting with anything new, so every target tested stays authorised in writing.

items.title: Stop at the boundary
items.body:
When a tester meets an asset that may not be in scope, such as a hostname, an address outside the listed ranges, a linked service or another tenant, they stop interacting with it immediately. Scope is a legal boundary, not a guide.

  • Send no further requests to the asset.
  • Do not follow links or credentials into it.
  • Carry on only with work that is clearly in scope.

Done when: interaction has stopped and the time is in the activity log.

items.title: Record the discovery
items.body:
The tester records what was seen and how it was found, so the engagement lead can judge it without anyone touching the asset again.

  • Identifiers such as the hostname, address or URL.
  • How it came to light, for example a link, a DNS record or a name on a certificate.
  • Why it seems related to the client, and any data already seen.

Done when: the discovery is in the engagement log with the minimum evidence needed to describe it.

items.title: Check ownership against the scope
items.body:
The engagement lead compares the asset with the signed scope and reviews public ownership information, such as address registration or DNS, without testing it. Never assume the client owns something because it carries the client's name.

  • Is it inside a listed range or domain?
  • Could it belong to a supplier, cloud provider, SaaS vendor or another tenant?

Done when: the lead's view on ownership and relevance is recorded in the engagement log.

items.title: Raise it with the client
items.body:
The engagement lead tells the client contact about the asset and why it matters, for example because it connects to or holds data from in-scope systems. The decision belongs to the client's risk owner.

  • Ask the client to confirm who owns it.
  • Set out the options: add it to scope, with any effect on time and cost, or leave it out and record it as a limitation.

Done when: the client has given a decision and it is recorded.

items.title: Get written approval before testing
items.body:
No testing of a new asset starts until written approval arrives from the person who signed the original authorisation, or someone with equal authority. A technical contact's verbal agreement is not enough.

  • The approval names the asset, the dates and the activities.
  • Where a third party owns it, that party's consent is attached.
  • Any change to effort or price is agreed as a contract variation.

Done when: the signed approval is filed with the engagement.

items.title: Update the scope record
items.body:
The engagement lead issues the scope record and test plan as a new version, so every tester works from the same list of targets.

  • Record the change, its date and the approval reference.
  • Brief every tester and update the phase checklists.
  • Ask the client to update allow-lists and to tell its SOC or managed provider.

Done when: the new scope version is issued and every tester has acknowledged it.

items.title: Handle client-requested changes
items.body:
When the client asks during testing to add targets, remove them or move dates, the engagement lead applies the same discipline as for a discovery.

  • Ask for the request in writing from someone with authority.
  • Assess the effect on effort, coverage and the report date.
  • Removals take effect immediately; additions wait for written approval.

Done when: the change is approved, recorded and reflected in the test plan.

items.title: Treat third-party assets with care
items.body:
If the asset belongs to a supplier, a host or a SaaS vendor, testers never test it without that owner's permission, even when the client agrees.

  • Pass anything seen without testing to the client, so it can inform the owner.
  • Agree with the client whether the firm may contact the owner directly.
  • Follow the third-party permissions runbook for any consent.

Done when: the client has been told and any onward notification is agreed.

items.title: Report scope decisions
items.body:
The report shows what was tested, what changed and what was left out, so readers understand the limits of the results.

  • The final scope, with each change, its date and its approval.
  • Assets found but not tested, listed as limitations or observations.
  • Why those assets matter to the client's risk.

Done when: the scope section of the draft report reflects every scope decision made during the engagement.

run_service_impact_v1.name: Unexpected impact or an outage during testing
run_service_impact_v1.description: Runbook for when a target slows down, errors or fails while testing is running, whether or not the test caused it. Use it the moment impact is noticed or reported, and follow it through to an agreed restart and the report.

items.title: Stop all testing at once
items.body:
As soon as any tester notices impact, or is told about it, every tester stops active traffic against every target, not only the one affected. Waiting to be sure can turn a slowdown into an outage.

  • Cancel running and scheduled jobs and close open sessions.
  • Do not retry requests to see whether the service recovers.
  • Note the exact stop time in the activity log.

Done when: no test traffic is leaving any tester's machine and the stop time is logged.

items.title: Notify the client and the engagement lead
items.body:
The tester tells the engagement lead immediately, and the lead phones the client's technical contact within 15 minutes, moving to the emergency contact if needed. The client should hear it from the firm first.

  • What was running, against which target, from which address and since when.
  • What was observed, and when.
  • That all testing has stopped.

Done when: a named person at the client knows and the time of the call is recorded.

items.title: Preserve your logs and timestamps
items.body:
Each tester saves an untouched copy of everything that shows what they did, because the client will need it to establish the cause.

  • The activity log, tool output and captured requests for the period.
  • The testing machine's time zone and any clock offset.
  • Copies stored in the engagement store, with the originals left unedited.

Done when: the preserved copies are filed and listed in the incident note.

items.title: Help the client establish cause
items.body:
The engagement lead gives the client a timeline of test activity to set against its own monitoring, and works with the client to find the cause. Be open that the test may be responsible.

  • Identify the last test actions before the impact began.
  • Consider other causes too, such as a change, load or an unrelated fault.
  • Put conclusions in writing only once the facts support them.

Done when: the client and the firm have an agreed account of the likely cause.

items.title: Support recovery, not repair
items.body:
The client restores the service. Testers do not change client systems to fix the problem, which could make things worse and would go beyond the authorisation to test.

  • Tell the client about anything the test created that may need removing, such as records, files or accounts.
  • Stay available to answer questions during recovery.
  • Keep the activity log open and record each contact with the client.

Done when: the client confirms the service is restored and stable.

items.title: Report it inside the firm
items.body:
The engagement lead reports the event through the firm's internal incident process on the same day, so management, quality and any insurance obligations are handled properly.

  • Summarise the timeline, the impact and the likely cause.
  • Flag any contractual or insurance notification that may be needed.
  • Note lessons for the firm's methodology and tooling.

Done when: the internal report is logged with a reference number.

items.title: Agree resumption criteria
items.body:
The engagement lead and the client agree in writing what must be true before testing restarts, and what will be done differently.

  • The service is confirmed stable, and the cause is understood or accepted.
  • Changes such as lower rates, excluding the fragile component, a different window or a non-production copy.
  • Who approves the restart, and a new end date if testing time was lost.

Done when: the client has approved the criteria in writing.

items.title: Restart under the changed conditions
items.body:
Testers restart only once the criteria are met, announce it to the client as they would a new day's start, and watch the affected system closely.

  • Apply the new limits from the very first request.
  • Check in with the client contact after the first hour.
  • Stop again at the first sign of strain and repeat this runbook.

Done when: testing has run for an agreed period without further impact.

items.title: Record it in the report
items.body:
The report describes the event factually, because a system that fails under ordinary test traffic tells the client something about its resilience.

  • What happened, when, the likely cause and how it was resolved.
  • Any weakness it shows, such as missing rate limits or resource controls, as a finding or observation.
  • Coverage lost, and any limit this places on the results.

Done when: the event and its effect on coverage are in the draft report.

run_critical_finding_v1.name: Escalating a critical finding during testing
run_critical_finding_v1.description: Runbook for reporting a finding that cannot wait for the report, such as an easily abused exposure or evidence of an existing compromise. Use it the moment a tester suspects a critical issue, before testing continues.

items.title: Recognise what counts as critical
items.body:
The tester compares the issue with the escalation criteria agreed at kick-off. When in doubt, treat it as critical and let the engagement lead decide.

  • Unauthenticated access from the internet to systems, administrative functions or sensitive data.
  • Exposed secrets or credentials that grant wide access.
  • Access to another customer's or tenant's data.
  • A flaw known to be actively exploited, on an exposed system.
  • Signs of a prior or ongoing compromise.

Done when: the tester has decided whether the criteria are met and logged the time.

items.title: Stop and confirm
items.body:
The tester stops interacting with the affected component and confirms the issue with the least further access, so the escalation is accurate and no extra harm is done.

  • Recheck that the asset is in scope.
  • Rule out a false positive, with a second tester checking where one is available.
  • Capture only the evidence needed and view no more data than proves the point.
  • Do not alter or remove anything left by a suspected intruder.

Done when: the issue is confirmed or discarded, with the evidence saved.

items.title: Tell the engagement lead at once
items.body:
The tester phones the engagement lead straight away rather than waiting for the next check-in. The lead owns the decision to escalate and all contact with the client about it.

  • Give the asset, the issue, how it was confirmed and when.
  • Agree what the client needs to hear and any interim advice.
  • If the lead cannot be reached within 15 minutes, call the deputy lead.

Done when: the lead has confirmed the escalation, or recorded why it is not needed.

items.title: Notify the client within the agreed time
items.body:
The engagement lead phones the client's technical contact within the time agreed at kick-off, typically within an hour of confirmation, then follows up in writing through the secure channel.

  • If the contact does not answer, work down the contact sheet to the emergency contact.
  • For signs of compromise, advise the client to start its incident response process.
  • Leave no detail in voicemail or plain email.

Done when: a named person at the client has been told by phone and the time is logged.

items.title: Share details through a secure channel
items.body:
The engagement lead sends a short written notice through the agreed secure route, so the client can act without waiting for the report.

  • The affected asset, what the issue is and its likely impact.
  • When it was found and how it was confirmed, at methodology level.
  • Interim mitigation the client could apply now.
  • Exposed secrets referred to by location, never copied into the notice.

Done when: the notice is delivered through the secure route and a copy is filed with the engagement.

items.title: Confirm receipt and ownership
items.body:
The engagement lead obtains an explicit acknowledgement, because an unread notice is not an escalation, and notes who at the client now owns the response.

  • Record the name of the person who acknowledged it and the time.
  • Agree who the firm will update, and how often.
  • If no acknowledgement arrives within the agreed time, escalate to the next contact and the risk owner.

Done when: a named person at the client has acknowledged receipt in writing.

items.title: Agree whether testing continues
items.body:
The engagement lead and the client decide together what happens to testing next, and the client's decision is recorded in writing.

  • Options: continue elsewhere, pause the affected component or pause all testing.
  • Where a compromise is suspected, pause by default so test traffic does not confuse the investigation.
  • Any fix applied during testing is noted for later verification.

Done when: the decision, who made it and when are recorded, and every tester has been told.

items.title: Support the client without taking over
items.body:
The firm helps the client respond but does not act on the client's systems beyond the agreed testing, which would go beyond the authorisation.

  • Provide an extract of the activity log and the source addresses, so test traffic can be separated from anything else.
  • Answer technical questions about the finding.
  • Attempt no fix or clean-up for the client unless separately instructed in writing.

Done when: the client confirms it has what it needs from the firm.

items.title: Record the escalation
items.body:
The engagement lead writes up the escalation in the engagement record on the same day, so the timeline can be shown to the client, an auditor or an insurer.

  • Times found, confirmed, lead told, client told and acknowledged.
  • People involved, channels used and what was shared.
  • The decision on testing and any later updates.

Done when: the escalation entry is complete and the evidence is in the engagement store.

items.title: Carry it into the report
items.body:
The tester writes the finding up in full in the report, with the escalation timeline, so the report matches what the client was told during testing.

  • Include the notification dates and any interim mitigation advised.
  • State whether a fix made during testing was verified, and how.
  • Agree with the client how a suspected prior compromise is described.

Done when: the finding and its timeline are in the draft report and have passed peer review.

run_client_data_v1.name: Handling client data and evidence
run_client_data_v1.description: Runbook for collecting, storing, sharing and destroying client data and test evidence. Use it from kick-off to close-out so the firm meets its contract and its UK GDPR duties when it handles personal data for the client.

items.title: Confirm the data terms before testing
items.body:
The engagement lead checks that the contract covers how the firm handles client data. Where the firm processes personal data on the client's behalf, UK GDPR Article 28 requires written processor terms.

  • What evidence may be kept, and in what form.
  • Where it may be stored, who may access it and for how long.
  • Return or destruction at the end, and how that is confirmed.

Done when: the terms are confirmed and summarised in the engagement file.

items.title: Collect the minimum
items.body:
Testers gather only what proves a finding, which keeps both the risk and the later clean-up small. Data minimisation applies to testers as much as to the client.

  • Prove access with counts, structure or one redacted record, not a download.
  • Do not copy data sets off client systems.
  • Stop and tell the engagement lead on reaching special category data or large volumes of personal data.

Done when: the evidence for each finding is the least that proves it.

items.title: Redact before evidence leaves the working area
items.body:
The tester redacts sensitive values in evidence before it goes into drafts or is shared, keeping just enough to prove the point.

  • Names, email addresses, account numbers and other personal data.
  • Passwords, keys, tokens and session identifiers, partly masked.
  • Screenshots, image metadata and file names, not only text.

Done when: evidence in the engagement store is redacted and a second person has checked it at peer review.

items.title: Encrypt data at rest
items.body:
Everything that holds client data is encrypted, so a lost laptop or drive does not become a personal data breach.

  • Full-disk encryption on every testing machine.
  • An encrypted engagement store, with a separate folder per engagement.
  • Removable media only if encrypted and approved.
  • Test virtual machines encrypted, or rebuilt between clients.

Done when: the engagement lead has confirmed encryption on every device and store used for the engagement.

items.title: Encrypt data in transit
items.body:
Data moves between the firm and the client only through approved encrypted routes, in both directions, so nothing sensitive crosses the internet in clear text.

  • Use the firm's secure portal, or an encrypted archive with the passphrase sent by a different channel.
  • Never attach evidence or reports to plain email.
  • Do not use personal messaging apps or personal file-sharing accounts.

Done when: every transfer on the engagement has used an approved route.

items.title: Store only in approved locations
items.body:
Client data lives only in the firm's approved engagement repository and on managed testing machines, so the firm always knows where all of it is.

  • No copies on personal devices or in personal cloud storage.
  • No uploading client data to online tools or AI services unless they are approved and covered by the contract.
  • Tool output and notes stay in the engagement folder.

Done when: all engagement data sits in approved locations only.

items.title: Control and log access
items.body:
The engagement lead limits access to the engagement folder to the people working on it, and reviews the list whenever the team changes.

  • Testers, the peer reviewer, the QA reviewer and the engagement lead only.
  • Access removed when someone leaves the engagement.
  • The store's access log kept for the retention period.

Done when: the access list matches the current team and the review is noted in the engagement file.

items.title: Handle a data incident
items.body:
If client data is lost, sent to the wrong person or exposed, whoever notices tells the engagement lead and the firm's data protection lead at once. As a processor, the firm must tell the client without undue delay (UK GDPR Article 33).

  • Contain it: recall messages, revoke links and ask recipients to delete.
  • Give the client the facts it needs to decide whether to report to the ICO, which, where required, is due within 72 hours of the client becoming aware.

Done when: the client has been told and the incident is recorded.

items.title: Apply the retention period
items.body:
When the final report is delivered, the engagement lead diarises the destruction date the contract sets and tells the client what will be kept, and until when.

  • Separate what the firm keeps, such as the final report, from raw evidence.
  • Return client-supplied material that has to go back.
  • Note any legal hold that suspends destruction.

Done when: the destruction date is diarised and the client has been told.

items.title: Destroy securely and certify
items.body:
On the due date, the engagement lead has all remaining client data securely deleted and confirms it to the client with a certificate.

  • Delete from the engagement store, testing machines and any backups as policy allows.
  • Use the firm's approved secure deletion method.
  • The certificate states what was destroyed, when, how and by whom.

Done when: the certificate is issued to the client and a copy is filed.

run_reporting_qa_v1.name: Writing, reviewing and delivering the report
run_reporting_qa_v1.description: Runbook for turning test results into a report the client can act on, through technical peer review and quality assurance to secure delivery of the draft and final versions. Use it from the last testing day until the client accepts the final report.

items.title: Set the structure before writing
items.body:
The engagement lead sets up the report template and the rating scheme agreed at scoping, so every writer works to one shape.

  • Executive summary: engagement context, overall position, how findings combine, and good practice seen.
  • Scope, method, dates, testers and limitations.
  • Findings in severity order, then appendices for evidence, coverage and version history.
  • Rating scheme: the agreed CVSS version, or CHECK levels where CHECK applies.

Done when: the template is ready for the engagement.

items.title: Write each finding to a standard
items.body:
Each tester writes up their findings in the same structure, so the client can act on any one of them in isolation.

  • Title, affected assets and a plain description.
  • How it was confirmed, in enough detail for the client's team to reproduce it at methodology level.
  • Evidence, impact in business terms and likelihood.
  • Severity with its rationale, then remediation and references.

Done when: every confirmed issue in the activity log has a complete write-up.

items.title: Calibrate severity
items.body:
The lead tester checks that ratings are consistent and defensible, because severity drives the client's priorities and budgets.

  • Apply the agreed scheme the same way to similar issues, and compare with the firm's ratings guide.
  • For CVSS, record the version and the full vector with each score.
  • Rate chained issues on their combined effect.
  • Document and justify any rating that departs from the scheme's result.

Done when: every rating has a recorded rationale.

items.title: Check evidence quality and redaction
items.body:
The writer checks that each finding's evidence proves it and exposes nothing it should not.

  • Screenshots are legible, cropped to the point and labelled with the asset and time.
  • Secrets, tokens and personal data are redacted.
  • No material from another client or engagement appears anywhere, including file properties.
  • Host and asset names match the scope record.

Done when: every finding has clean and sufficient evidence.

items.title: Write remediation the client can act on
items.body:
The writer gives advice specific enough to assign and to verify, rather than general advice to follow good practice.

  • The setting, version, design change or control to apply.
  • A short-term mitigation where the full fix will take time.
  • The root cause, where several findings share one.
  • How the client can confirm the fix has worked.

Done when: each finding has remediation that an engineer could start work on.

items.title: Run a technical peer review
items.body:
A second tester who did not write the section reviews it for technical accuracy before it goes to quality assurance.

  • Check reproducibility, severity, false positives and missing context.
  • Compare coverage with the phase checklists and the test plan.
  • Track comments, so each one is resolved or answered.

Done when: the peer reviewer signs off with no open technical comments.

items.title: Run quality assurance
items.body:
A QA reviewer checks the whole report as the client will read it, independently of the testers.

  • Scope and dates match the signed scope, and limitations are stated.
  • The executive summary matches the findings and their ratings.
  • Client name, UK English, formatting and numbering are consistent.
  • The version number and classification marking are correct.

Done when: QA sign-off is recorded with the reviewer's name and the date.

items.title: Issue the draft securely
items.body:
The engagement lead issues the report marked as a draft, with a version number, through the agreed secure channel and only to the named recipients.

  • Use the secure portal, or an encrypted file with the passphrase sent separately.
  • Confirm that the named recipient has received it.
  • Invite factual corrections and comments by an agreed date.

Done when: receipt of the draft is confirmed and recorded.

items.title: Handle client comments
items.body:
The engagement lead logs each client comment and the firm's response, so every change to the report can be traced.

  • Correct factual errors.
  • Change a rating only on evidence, such as a proven compensating control, and record why.
  • Do not remove a finding because the client disagrees; record the disagreement or the client's risk acceptance.

Done when: every comment has a recorded response.

items.title: Issue the final version
items.body:
The engagement lead issues the final report with its version history and records who received it, so there is no doubt which version is authoritative.

  • Use the same secure route as for the draft.
  • Ask the client to discard earlier drafts.
  • Keep the final report in the engagement record for the agreed retention period.

Done when: the final version is delivered and the delivery is recorded.

run_readout_v1.name: Readout and debrief meeting
run_readout_v1.description: Runbook for the meeting that walks the client through the report and agrees what happens next. Use it once the draft or final report has been issued, ideally within two weeks of delivery.

items.title: Book it with the right people
items.body:
The engagement lead schedules the readout and invites the people who must understand the findings and act on them.

  • Client: technical owners, the security lead and the risk owner or sponsor.
  • Anyone who will carry out fixes, such as developers or a managed provider.
  • Firm: the engagement lead and the testers behind the critical and high findings.
  • Allow 60 to 90 minutes and send the agenda in advance.

Done when: the meeting is booked and the agenda is sent.

items.title: Prepare the material
items.body:
The engagement lead prepares a short pack that tells the story of the test without needing the full report open on screen.

  • Scope, overall position, and the critical and high findings.
  • Themes and root causes, plus good practice observed.
  • No secrets or exploitable detail in any pack that is not protected.
  • A list of the findings the client has questioned.

Done when: a second consultant has reviewed the pack.

items.title: Open with context
items.body:
The engagement lead starts by restating what was tested and how, so everyone reads the findings in the right light.

  • Scope, dates and approach, for example authenticated or unauthenticated testing.
  • What was not tested, and why.
  • How severity was rated.
  • Any events during testing, such as escalations or outages.

Done when: attendees accept the context and nobody is surprised by the scope.

items.title: Walk through critical and high findings
items.body:
The testers explain each critical and high finding in turn, at a level that both technical owners and managers can follow.

  • What it is and how it was found, at methodology level.
  • Which assets are affected, and what an attacker could do with it.
  • How it combines with other findings.
  • The recommended fix, and any short-term mitigation.

Done when: each one is understood by the person who will own its fix.

items.title: Draw out root causes and themes
items.body:
The engagement lead groups findings by what lies behind them, which helps the client fix causes rather than symptoms one by one.

  • For example patch management, secure development, identity hygiene or configuration management.
  • Controls that worked well, not only failures.
  • Where the client's own vulnerability management should have found an issue first.

Done when: the themes are agreed and recorded.

items.title: Agree remediation priorities
items.body:
The client decides priorities and owners, and the firm advises. Risk decisions belong to the client's risk owner, not to the testers.

  • Advise on order: critical exposures first, then quick wins, then root causes.
  • Give each action an owner, a priority and a target date.
  • Note actions that depend on suppliers or third parties.

Done when: the client has a draft action plan with owners and dates.

items.title: Take questions and record disputes
items.body:
The engagement lead records every question and its answer, and settles disagreements on evidence rather than opinion.

  • For disputed findings, agree what evidence the client will send, and by when.
  • Record any risk acceptance as the client's decision, with the name of the person who made it.
  • Note follow-up questions the firm has to answer.

Done when: each open question has an owner and a date.

items.title: Agree next steps and retest timing
items.body:
Before the meeting closes, the engagement lead confirms what happens next and who does it.

  • When fixes are expected, and when the retest will run.
  • Which findings the retest will cover.
  • Whether the report needs reissuing after comments.
  • Who else should be told, such as a regulator, insurer or supplier.

Done when: next steps and the retest window are agreed in the meeting.

items.title: Send the meeting notes
items.body:
The engagement lead sends notes within two working days through the secure channel, so agreements made in the room are not lost.

  • Actions, owners and dates, and the agreed retest window.
  • Answers to questions raised, and any follow-ups owed by the firm.
  • A request for feedback on the engagement.

Done when: the notes are sent and filed with the engagement.

run_retest_v1.name: Retesting remediated findings
run_retest_v1.description: Runbook for verifying a client's fixes against the original findings and updating the report. Use it when the client confirms remediation is complete and asks for the retest agreed in the contract.

items.title: Confirm what was fixed and how
items.body:
The engagement lead asks the client for a list of the findings it believes are fixed, so the retest checks the right things in the right places.

  • For each finding: what changed, such as a patch, configuration or code change, and when.
  • Which assets the fix was applied to.
  • Findings the client has formally accepted as risks.
  • Changes since the test, such as new addresses or hosts.

Done when: the client's remediation list is on file.

items.title: Agree the retest scope and authorisation
items.body:
The engagement lead agrees the retest scope in writing. A retest checks the original findings; it is not a new test, and anything wider needs its own scope.

  • The findings to retest and the assets they affect.
  • Dates, windows, accounts and source addresses.
  • Authorisation that covers the retest dates.

Done when: written authorisation for the retest is filed with the engagement.

items.title: Prepare from the original evidence
items.body:
The tester, ideally the one who found each issue, reviews the original method, conditions and evidence before retesting, so the comparison is like for like.

  • The role, account, asset version and preconditions used.
  • Check that the accounts still work and the environment matches.
  • Note any finding that can no longer be reached as before.

Done when: each finding has a retest note saying how it will be checked.

items.title: Test each finding the same way
items.body:
The tester repeats the original method under the original conditions, then checks close variants, to see whether the fix addresses the cause or only the example reported.

  • Other parameters, endpoints, hosts or roles of the same kind.
  • Before and after evidence for each finding.
  • Stay within the agreed retest scope.

Done when: every finding in scope has been retested, or the reason it could not be is logged.

items.title: Record the outcome
items.body:
The tester gives each finding a single outcome, with evidence and the retest date.

  • Remediated: no longer reproducible by the original method or its variants.
  • Part remediated: some instances or conditions remain, or the impact is reduced.
  • Not remediated: still reproducible.
  • Risk accepted: formally accepted by the client.
  • Not retested: with the reason.

Done when: every finding has an outcome and supporting evidence.

items.title: Reassess severity where partly fixed
items.body:
Where a fix reduces an issue but does not remove it, the tester re-rates it with a rationale and keeps the original rating visible, so the client can see the progress made.

  • Explain what the fix changed and what it did not.
  • Recommend what remains to be done.
  • Have the lead tester check the new rating.

Done when: each part-remediated finding has a revised rating and rationale.

items.title: Record new issues noticed
items.body:
If the retest reveals a new issue, such as a regression or a weakness the fix introduced, the tester records it with the same rigour as any other finding.

  • Flag it as found during the retest.
  • Escalate it if it meets the critical criteria.
  • Send anything beyond the retest scope through the scope change runbook.

Done when: new issues are written up or referred to the engagement lead.

items.title: Update the report and version history
items.body:
The tester updates the report so it shows the current status alongside the original findings, rather than replacing them.

  • Add the retest outcome, date and tester to each finding.
  • Add a retest summary to the executive summary.
  • Increase the version number and add an entry to the version history.

Done when: the updated report is ready for peer review.

items.title: Review and deliver
items.body:
The retest results go through peer review and quality assurance like the original report, then are delivered securely.

  • The peer reviewer checks each outcome against its evidence.
  • Deliver through the agreed secure route and confirm receipt.
  • Tell the client which actions remain open.

Done when: the updated report is delivered and receipt is recorded.

run_closeout_v1.name: Engagement close-out and clean-up
run_closeout_v1.description: Runbook for closing an engagement cleanly: removing what testing left behind, revoking access, returning or destroying data and capturing lessons. Use it after the last testing activity, and finish it before the engagement is marked complete.

items.title: List every artefact left in place
items.body:
The engagement lead and the testers build a list, from the activity logs, of everything the test created or changed on client systems.

  • Accounts, files, uploads and records created in applications.
  • Scheduled tasks, services, configuration changes and any agents placed with approval.
  • Test emails, tickets and markers.
  • The location and owner of each item.

Done when: the artefact list is complete and checked against the activity logs.

items.title: Remove artefacts and revert changes
items.body:
Testers remove what they created while they still have authorised access, and confirm each removal.

  • Revert configuration changes to their recorded original state.
  • Mark items only the client can remove, such as records that need administrator deletion.
  • Leave client logs that show test activity untouched.

Done when: each item on the list is marked as removed or left for the client.

items.title: Confirm clean-up with the client in writing
items.body:
The engagement lead sends the client the artefact list, showing what was removed and what the client must remove itself, and asks for written confirmation.

  • Give removal dates and the locations of remaining items.
  • Include the list as an appendix to the report.
  • Agree a date by which the client will remove what remains.

Done when: the client has confirmed the clean-up position in writing.

items.title: Ask for accounts and secrets to be disabled
items.body:
The engagement lead asks the client in writing to disable or delete everything issued for the test, following the credentials runbook.

  • Test accounts, API keys, certificates and MFA registrations.
  • Credentials found during testing, which should be rotated.
  • Accounts created during testing, if the testers could not remove them.

Done when: the client confirms each item is disabled, deleted or rotated.

items.title: Revoke the firm's access
items.body:
The engagement lead asks the client to remove every route the firm had into its environment, and the firm removes its own side.

  • VPN profiles, jump hosts, remote desktops and cloud roles.
  • The firm's source addresses on allow-lists.
  • Hardware left on site, collected or returned.
  • Testers delete local connection profiles.

Done when: the client confirms revocation and the firm holds no working access.

items.title: Return or destroy client data
items.body:
The engagement lead returns client-supplied material and arranges destruction of engagement data on the date the contract sets, following the client data runbook.

  • Diarise the destruction date.
  • Issue a destruction certificate when it is done.
  • Keep only what the contract allows, such as the final report.

Done when: material is returned and destruction is scheduled or certified.

items.title: Clean testing machines
items.body:
Each tester removes engagement data and client-specific settings from their testing machines and virtual machines, so nothing carries into the next engagement.

  • Delete local evidence, notes and captures once the engagement store has them.
  • Remove client VPN profiles, certificates and host entries.
  • Rebuild or revert test virtual machines.

Done when: each tester has confirmed their machines are clean.

items.title: Hold a lessons-learned review
items.body:
The engagement lead runs a short internal review within two weeks of the final report, so the next engagement benefits from this one.

  • What went well and what did not, across scoping, access, timing and communication.
  • Effort used against the estimate.
  • Changes needed to checklists, runbooks or templates.

Done when: lessons and resulting actions are recorded with owners.

items.title: Request client feedback
items.body:
The engagement lead asks the client for feedback on the engagement and the report, and handles any complaint through the proper route.

  • Use the firm's feedback form or a short call.
  • Log any complaint through the firm's complaints process.
  • Share feedback with the testers involved.

Done when: feedback has been requested and anything received is filed.

items.title: Close the engagement record
items.body:
The engagement lead checks that every runbook and checklist for the engagement is complete, then marks the engagement closed.

  • Final report delivered and readout held.
  • Clean-up, access revocation and data actions confirmed.
  • Retention dates set and any retest window noted.

Done when: the engagement is marked complete with nothing outstanding.

run_web_assessment_v1.name: Running a web application and API assessment
run_web_assessment_v1.description: Runbook for running a web application and API test from preparation to validated findings, ordered around the OWASP WSTG categories and the OWASP API Security Top 10 2023. Use it to plan the work, keep coverage recorded and make sure every reported issue has been confirmed.

items.title: Prepare and confirm access
items.body:
The tester confirms, before testing starts, everything needed to cover the application fully and safely.

  • In-scope hostnames, URLs and environments, and any excluded functions.
  • Accounts for every role, two per role, and how MFA works for them.
  • API definitions, such as OpenAPI files or GraphQL schemas.
  • Whether a WAF is allow-listed, and the agreed request rate.
  • Functions that send email or SMS, or take payments.

Done when: access works for every role and the constraints are noted in the test plan.

items.title: Map the application and its roles
items.body:
The tester uses every function as each role and records what the application exposes (WSTG-INFO). The map becomes the test plan for the rest of the phase.

  • Pages, endpoints, parameters, uploads, workflows and integrations.
  • A role and permission matrix from the documentation, checked against what is observed.
  • Technologies and frameworks in use, and information leaked in comments, metadata and headers.

Done when: the application map and the role matrix are saved with the engagement.

items.title: Review configuration and deployment
items.body:
The tester checks how the application and its platform are configured (WSTG-CONF) and how data in transit is protected (WSTG-CRYP).

  • TLS versions, cipher suites and certificate validity.
  • Security headers, such as Content-Security-Policy and Strict-Transport-Security.
  • Permitted HTTP methods, default and backup files, and exposed admin interfaces.
  • Cloud storage and subdomains linked to the application.

Done when: each configuration check is marked passed or failed, with evidence.
