items.title: Cover the unauthenticated surface first
items.body:
The tester assesses everything reachable without signing in, since it is open to anyone on the internet (WSTG-IDNT and WSTG-ATHN).

  • Registration and account provisioning.
  • Login, password reset and username enumeration.
  • Lockout and rate limiting on authentication.
  • Public API endpoints, and protected content reachable without a session.

Done when: every unauthenticated entry point has been covered and recorded.

items.title: Test authentication and sessions
items.body:
The tester checks how users prove who they are and how their sessions are kept (WSTG-ATHN and WSTG-SESS).

  • Credential handling, password policy, remember-me and MFA enforcement on every route.
  • Session token randomness, and the Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite cookie attributes.
  • Idle and absolute timeouts, and invalidation on logout and password change.
  • Session fixation and cross-site request forgery protection.

Done when: each check has a recorded result for each role.

items.title: Test authorisation across roles and objects
items.body:
The tester works through the role matrix to confirm access controls hold (WSTG-ATHZ), as broken access control is one of the most common high-impact web findings.

  • Each privileged function requested by a lower-privileged role.
  • Object identifiers swapped between users of the same role, and across tenants.
  • Path traversal and file inclusion conditions.

Done when: every cell of the role matrix has a recorded result.

items.title: Test input handling and errors
items.body:
The tester checks how each input vector is validated and encoded (WSTG-INPV), and what error responses reveal (WSTG-ERRH).

  • The injection classes relevant to the stack, such as SQL, command, template and XML.
  • Reflected and stored cross-site scripting.
  • Server-side request forgery from URL and file inputs.
  • Stack traces or internal detail in error responses.

Done when: every mapped input has been covered for the classes relevant to it.

items.title: Test client-side behaviour
items.body:
The tester reviews what runs in the browser (WSTG-CLNT), where modern applications hold much of their logic and state.

  • DOM-based issues, and unsafe handling of URL fragments and cross-window messages.
  • Open redirects, the cross-origin resource sharing policy and framing protection.
  • Sensitive data kept in browser storage.
  • Third-party scripts and how their integrity is assured.

Done when: client-side checks are recorded for each major page type.

items.title: Test business logic
items.body:
The tester uses their understanding of what the application is for to find misuse that automated tools cannot (WSTG-BUSL).

  • Workflow steps skipped or taken out of order.
  • Limits on how often a function can be used.
  • Prices, quantities or other values the server should check.
  • Timing and race conditions on single-use actions.
  • Uploads of unexpected file types.

Done when: each key workflow has been examined and the result recorded.

items.title: Test the APIs against the API Top 10
items.body:
The tester covers each API endpoint against the OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 (API1:2023 to API10:2023), and any GraphQL service against WSTG-APIT.

  • Authentication on every endpoint (API2), and object, property and function level access per role (API1, API3, API5).
  • Resource limits and sensitive business flows (API4, API6).
  • Request forgery and misconfiguration (API7, API8).
  • Old versions and undocumented hosts (API9), and trust in third-party APIs (API10).

Done when: each endpoint has a result for every relevant risk.

items.title: Validate every candidate issue
items.body:
The tester confirms each candidate issue by hand before it becomes a finding. Automated output is a lead, not a result.

  • Reproduce the issue at least twice.
  • Establish its real impact using the least data possible.
  • Check whether other instances share the same issue.
  • Discard false positives, and note why.

Done when: every candidate is confirmed or discarded with a recorded reason.

items.title: Record as you go
items.body:
The tester records each confirmed issue on the day it is found and keeps coverage current, so the report reflects the testing actually done.

  • Affected URLs, parameters and roles, with evidence and timestamps.
  • Reproduction notes at methodology level.
  • The phase checklist ticked per WSTG category and API risk.
  • Areas not tested, and why, recorded as limitations.

Done when: the activity log, evidence and checklist all match the work done.

run_internal_assessment_v1.name: Running an internal infrastructure and Active Directory assessment
run_internal_assessment_v1.description: Runbook for an internal network and Active Directory test, from getting connected to reaching the agreed objectives without disrupting the business. Use it to pace discovery safely, cover the directory review and record privilege paths as evidence.

items.title: Get connected and record your position
items.body:
The tester connects through the agreed route, whether an on-site port, VPN, jump host or a supplied device, and records where on the network the test starts.

  • The segment or VLAN, the address assigned and how it was assigned.
  • Whether network access control stopped an unknown device.
  • Confirm the client knows the device's address and hardware identifier.

Done when: the starting position is recorded in the activity log.

items.title: Agree safety limits first
items.body:
The tester confirms the limits that protect the business before any active work, because internal networks hold fragile systems and account lockouts affect real users.

  • The domain lockout threshold and observation window, and a margin to stay well below them.
  • Fragile systems to avoid or treat gently, such as OT, medical devices, telephony, printers and legacy servers.
  • Windows for heavier work, and who to call.

Done when: the limits are written into the test plan.

items.title: Discover hosts at an agreed rate
items.body:
The tester finds live hosts subnet by subnet, starting gently and watching for any sign of strain on hosts or links.

  • Work through the in-scope ranges in the agreed order.
  • Keep to the agreed rate and level of parallel work.
  • Stop at once if a host or link misbehaves, and follow the impact runbook.
  • Record coverage per subnet.

Done when: every in-scope subnet has a recorded coverage result.

items.title: Inventory services and versions
items.body:
The tester builds an inventory of what each host runs, which shapes the rest of the test and the patching findings.

  • Server and workstation operating systems, flagging any out of support.
  • Management interfaces, including baseboard management controllers and network device consoles.
  • Databases, file shares, printers and voice systems.

Done when: the inventory is saved and unsupported systems are flagged.

items.title: Review name resolution and legacy protocols
items.body:
The tester checks for network settings that would let one compromised host capture or relay the credentials of others.

  • LLMNR, NBT-NS and mDNS in use, and how WPAD is handled.
  • SMBv1 enabled, or SMB signing not required.
  • LDAP signing and channel binding not enforced.
  • NTLMv1 still permitted.

Done when: each setting has a recorded state, with the hosts affected.

items.title: Check credential hygiene
items.body:
The tester looks for credential weaknesses that give an easy way in, within the rules of engagement.

  • Default credentials on devices, tested at low volume where allowed.
  • Shared local administrator passwords, and whether LAPS is deployed.
  • Credentials stored in file shares, scripts and Group Policy files.
  • Any password audit only as agreed, with results reported in aggregate.

Done when: each check has a recorded result.

items.title: Review the directory
items.body:
Starting from a standard domain user, as agreed for an assumed-breach test, the tester reviews Active Directory configuration against current guidance.

  • Privileged group membership, stale accounts and passwords that never expire.
  • Service accounts with old passwords, and accounts without Kerberos pre-authentication.
  • Unconstrained and resource-based delegation, and the machine account quota.
  • Certificate templates, permissions on privileged objects, Group Policy and trusts.

Done when: each review area has a recorded result.

items.title: Map privilege paths
items.body:
The tester maps the relationships that lead from the starting account to the most privileged assets, so the client sees how small weaknesses chain together.

  • Group nesting, permissions on objects, logged-on sessions, local administrator rights and delegation.
  • End points include domain controllers, certificate services and identity synchronisation servers.
  • Each path recorded link by link.

Done when: the shortest and most likely paths are documented.

items.title: Pursue the agreed objectives
items.body:
The tester validates the chosen path towards each agreed objective, such as domain administrator equivalence or access to a named system, only as far as needed to prove it.

  • Prefer read-only proof, such as group membership or a directory listing.
  • Make directory changes only if agreed and reversible, and log each one.
  • Do not extract business data to prove access.

Done when: each objective is proven, or recorded as not reached, with evidence.

items.title: Check segmentation and detection
items.body:
The tester checks whether the network limits where an attacker can go, and whether the client noticed the activity.

  • Reachability from user networks to server, management, OT and backup networks.
  • Firewall rules between segments, compared with the client's intended design.
  • Alerts raised by the SOC, where detection is in scope.

Done when: segmentation results and detection notes are recorded.

items.title: Record evidence and clean up
items.body:
Before the phase ends, the tester completes the evidence and removes what the test created, while access still exists.

  • Evidence per finding, with hosts, accounts and timestamps.
  • Changes, files and accounts created, each reverted or listed for the client.
  • Coverage per subnet and per directory review area, with limitations.

Done when: the clean-up list is complete and the evidence is in the engagement store.

run_external_assessment_v1.name: Running an external infrastructure assessment
run_external_assessment_v1.description: Runbook for testing an organisation's internet-facing infrastructure, from confirming ownership of every address to validated findings. Use it to order the work and keep discovery, validation and evidence traceable.

items.title: Confirm targets and ownership
items.body:
The tester confirms that every in-scope address, range and hostname belongs to the client before sending any traffic. Cloud addresses can be reassigned, so they are rechecked at the start of the test.

  • Each target traces to the signed scope.
  • Registration, DNS or cloud account records support the client's ownership.
  • Hosted or provider-run addresses have third-party consent.

Done when: every target is confirmed, or raised with the engagement lead.

items.title: Agree source addresses and protections
items.body:
The tester confirms the test will come from declared addresses, and that the client knows whether its protective controls will see the traffic.

  • Source addresses declared and, where agreed, allow-listed on the IPS, WAF or DDoS service.
  • The testing window and the agreed rate.
  • The SOC or managed provider told, unless detection is being measured.

Done when: the arrangements are noted at the top of the activity log.

items.title: Gather passive information
items.body:
The tester builds a picture of the external footprint from public sources before any active work, which often reveals assets the client has forgotten.

  • DNS records, certificate transparency logs and search engine results.
  • Public code repositories and documents that expose hostnames or secrets.
  • Unlisted assets go to the scope change runbook, not into testing.

Done when: the footprint is recorded and compared with the signed scope.

items.title: Discover hosts and services at an agreed rate
items.body:
The tester identifies live hosts and listening services across all in-scope addresses, at the rate agreed with the client.

  • The full TCP port range, and the common UDP services.
  • Coverage per address, including filtered and unreachable results.
  • A comparison with the services the client expects to expose.

Done when: every in-scope address has a recorded discovery result.

items.title: Identify and fingerprint services
items.body:
The tester establishes what each open service is and which version it runs, which drives the rest of the assessment.

  • Remote access and VPN portals, SSH and RDP.
  • Administrative and management interfaces.
  • Databases, file transfer and mail services.
  • End-of-life or unsupported software.

Done when: each open port has a service, a version and an owner noted.

items.title: Review encryption and certificates
items.body:
The tester checks how each service protects data in transit, and records weak configurations as findings.

  • TLS versions offered, with SSL, TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 recorded as findings.
  • Cipher suites, key sizes, and certificate validity, chain and hostname match.
  • HSTS on web services.
  • Key exchange and host key algorithms on SSH.

Done when: every encrypted service has a recorded result.

items.title: Check email and DNS posture
items.body:
The tester reviews the controls that stop the client's domains being spoofed and its DNS leaking information.

  • SPF, DKIM and DMARC records, and whether DMARC enforces quarantine or reject.
  • Mail servers that relay mail for unauthorised senders.
  • Name servers that allow zone transfers to any host.
  • DNS records pointing at cloud resources that no longer exist.

Done when: each in-scope domain has recorded results.

items.title: Assess exposed authentication
items.body:
The tester checks every exposed login point, staying within the lockout limits agreed with the client.

  • MFA on VPN, remote access, webmail and admin portals.
  • Lockout and rate limiting on repeated failures.
  • Username enumeration through responses or timing.
  • Default credentials, tested only where the rules of engagement allow.

Done when: each login point has a recorded result.

items.title: Validate vulnerabilities
items.body:
The tester confirms each candidate vulnerability rather than reporting scanner output, and stops once exposure is proven.

  • Check versions against vendor advisories, allowing for backported fixes.
  • Give priority to flaws on CISA's list of known exploited vulnerabilities.
  • Escalate critical exposures at once through the critical finding runbook.
  • Discard false positives, with a reason.

Done when: every candidate is confirmed or discarded.

items.title: Record evidence and coverage
items.body:
The tester records each finding and the overall coverage, so the report shows what was and was not tested.

  • For each finding: host, port, service, evidence and timestamps.
  • A coverage table for every in-scope address.
  • Limitations, such as hosts that were down or filtered.

Done when: evidence and coverage are in the engagement store and the phase checklist is up to date.

run_cloud_review_v1.name: Running a cloud configuration review
run_cloud_review_v1.description: Runbook for a read-only configuration review of an AWS, Azure or Google Cloud estate against the provider's CIS Benchmark and the provider's own guidance. Use it from setting up access to removing it, so findings are complete, validated and traceable.

items.title: Agree scope and check the provider policy
items.body:
The engagement lead confirms exactly which parts of the estate are in scope, and checks the provider's testing policy for anything beyond reading configuration.

  • The organisation, accounts, subscriptions or projects, and regions.
  • Shared and landing zone services, and who owns them.
  • Any active testing in the review, checked against the provider's policy.

Done when: the scope lists every account, subscription or project by its identifier.

items.title: Set up read-only access
items.body:
The client creates a dedicated identity for the review with read-only rights across the scope, so the review cannot change anything.

  • AWS: the SecurityAudit and ViewOnlyAccess managed policies.
  • Azure: Reader at the agreed scope, plus read-only directory access in Microsoft Entra ID.
  • Google Cloud: Viewer and Security Reviewer at organisation or folder level.
  • MFA or federation, an expiry date and, where possible, a source address restriction.

Done when: the identity exists and its credentials are in the firm's vault.

items.title: Check the access before starting
items.body:
The tester confirms the identity can read everything in scope and cannot write, by reviewing its role assignments rather than attempting changes.

  • List resources in every in-scope account and region.
  • Record anything denied, for example by an organisation policy, as a limitation.
  • Confirm no write, delete or permission-changing rights are attached.

Done when: access is confirmed as read-only and complete, or the gaps are recorded.

items.title: Build the inventory
items.body:
The tester lists what exists across the estate, because resources nobody knows about are often the weakest.

  • Accounts, subscriptions or projects, and the regions in use.
  • Compute, storage, databases, serverless functions and containers.
  • Networks, identities and keys.
  • A comparison with the client's expected list, noting unknown resources.

Done when: the inventory is saved and unknown resources have been raised with the client.

items.title: Review against the benchmark
items.body:
The tester assesses configuration against the CIS Benchmark for the provider, recording the version used, and against the provider's own security guidance.

  • Identity, logging, monitoring, networking, storage and database settings.
  • A pass or fail for each recommendation, with evidence.
  • Automated results checked by hand, never copied straight into findings.

Done when: every applicable recommendation has a recorded result.

items.title: Review identity and privilege paths
items.body:
The tester works out who can do what, since identity is the main control surface in the cloud.

  • The number of administrators, and MFA on privileged, root and break-glass accounts.
  • Old access keys, unused identities and wildcard permissions.
  • Cross-account trust, federation and workload identities.
  • Identities that could grant themselves more access, for example by editing policies or assigning roles.

Done when: privileged identities and escalation paths are documented.

items.title: Review data exposure and network access
items.body:
The tester checks what is reachable from the internet and which data could be exposed.

  • Public storage, snapshots and machine images.
  • Databases and management ports open to the internet in security groups or firewall rules.
  • Encryption at rest, customer-managed keys where policy requires them, and key access policies.
  • Private endpoints where the design expects them.

Done when: each exposure check has a result for every account.

items.title: Review logging and detection
items.body:
The tester checks that the client would see misuse of its cloud estate, and keep the evidence.

  • Audit logging, such as AWS CloudTrail, the Azure activity log or Google Cloud Audit Logs, in every account and region.
  • Log retention, and protection from deletion.
  • Threat detection services, such as Amazon GuardDuty or Microsoft Defender for Cloud, enabled and alerting.

Done when: logging and detection coverage is recorded for every account.

items.title: Validate findings
items.body:
The tester confirms each finding against the live configuration and its context before reporting it.

  • Take account of compensating controls, such as organisation policies or private networking.
  • Check exceptions the client has documented.
  • Rate each finding by real exposure, not by a tool's default severity.

Done when: every finding is confirmed or discarded with a recorded reason.

items.title: Record evidence
items.body:
The tester records enough for the client to find and fix each issue without repeating the review.

  • Resource identifier, account and region.
  • The setting's value, a timestamp and the benchmark recommendation number.
  • Exported configuration or screenshots, with secrets redacted.

Done when: every finding has its evidence in the engagement store.

items.title: Remove access
items.body:
When the review ends, the engagement lead asks the client to delete the review identity and its role assignments, and to confirm this in writing.

  • Delete stored credentials from the vault once removal is confirmed.
  • Delete exported configuration data on the agreed retention date.
  • Record the removal in the engagement file.

Done when: the client has confirmed the identity is removed.

run_mobile_assessment_v1.name: Running a mobile application assessment
run_mobile_assessment_v1.description: Runbook for testing an iOS or Android application and the APIs behind it, using the OWASP MASVS control groups and the MASTG. Use it to receive builds and devices, order the static and dynamic work, and confirm results on the store build.

items.title: Receive builds and confirm versions
items.body:
The tester confirms which builds are being tested and records them, because results only hold for the build that was tested.

  • Android and iOS packages, with version and build numbers.
  • A test build, ideally without anti-tamper protections, plus the store build.
  • A hash of each file received.
  • Which backend environment each build talks to.

Done when: the build register is filed with the engagement.

items.title: Prepare test devices
items.body:
The tester prepares firm-managed devices that are used only for testing and hold no personal data.

  • OS versions covering the newest and the oldest the app supports.
  • A rooted or jailbroken device for internal checks, and a stock device.
  • Emulators or simulators only where they give reliable results.
  • The firm's interception certificate installed only where it is needed.

Done when: the devices are ready and recorded in the build register.

items.title: Confirm accounts and backend scope
items.body:
The tester confirms the accounts and backend systems in scope, since the app's traffic may reach services the client does not own.

  • Test accounts for each role.
  • API hosts in scope, and the source addresses testing will use.
  • Third-party SDK and analytics endpoints excluded unless agreed.

Done when: the backend target list is agreed in writing with the client.

items.title: Carry out the static review
items.body:
The tester unpacks and decompiles the app to review its contents and configuration without running it (MASVS-STORAGE, MASVS-CRYPTO, MASVS-CODE and MASVS-PLATFORM).

  • Permissions, exported components, URL schemes and backup settings.
  • App Transport Security exceptions, or cleartext traffic settings.
  • Hard-coded secrets, keys and endpoints.
  • Third-party libraries with known vulnerabilities, and cryptography choices.

Done when: each static check has a recorded result.

items.title: Carry out the dynamic review
items.body:
The tester runs the app on a device, using every function as each role, to see how it behaves with real data (MASVS-STORAGE and MASVS-PLATFORM).

  • Sensitive data in files, databases, preferences and logs.
  • Use of the iOS Keychain or Android Keystore for secrets.
  • Data in screenshots, the app switcher, the clipboard and backups.
  • Deep link and WebView handling.

Done when: each dynamic check has a recorded result.

items.title: Inspect network traffic
items.body:
The tester routes the app's traffic through an intercepting proxy to check how it is protected in transit (MASVS-NETWORK).

  • All traffic uses TLS, and certificate validation works.
  • Pinning behaviour, where the client expects pinning.
  • Sensitive data placed in URLs, headers or bodies where it should not be.

Done when: traffic from every function has been reviewed and the results recorded.

items.title: Test authentication and sessions
items.body:
The tester checks how the app and its backend authenticate users and maintain sessions (MASVS-AUTH).

  • Biometric unlock tied to a cryptographic operation, not just a local true or false result.
  • How tokens are stored, and how long they last.
  • Logout and expiry enforced by the server.
  • Step-up authentication for sensitive actions.

Done when: each check has a recorded result.

items.title: Test the backend APIs
items.body:
The tester assesses the APIs the app calls as an API test, against the OWASP API Security Top 10 2023, because the most serious mobile findings often sit on the server.

  • Object and function level access between roles and users.
  • Excess data in responses, and rate limits.
  • Endpoints found in the app that the interface never uses.

Done when: every endpoint the app uses has been covered.

items.title: Assess resilience and privacy where in scope
items.body:
Where the client has asked for it, the tester assesses the app's protection against tampering (MASVS-RESILIENCE) and its handling of personal data (MASVS-PRIVACY).

  • Root and jailbreak detection, debugger and tamper detection, and obfuscation, on the store build.
  • Data collected, compared with what the privacy notice and store listing declare.
  • Personal data shared with third-party SDKs.

Done when: results are recorded for each requested area.

items.title: Compare the store build with the test build
items.body:
The tester checks whether findings from the test build hold on the build that users actually install.

  • Protections present in the store build.
  • Debug features, test endpoints and verbose logging absent.
  • Differences recorded and reflected in each finding.

Done when: each finding states which builds it affects.

items.title: Validate, record and clean up
items.body:
The tester confirms each issue on a device and records it, then clears the devices so nothing carries into the next engagement.

  • Evidence per finding, with build number, OS version and device.
  • Remove the app, test data and certificates from the devices, and reset them.
  • Delete builds and captures on the agreed retention date.

Done when: the evidence is filed and the devices are reset.

run_wireless_assessment_v1.name: Running an on-site wireless assessment
run_wireless_assessment_v1.description: Runbook for an on-site assessment of an organisation's Wi-Fi, from authorisation and the site survey to configuration checks, rogue access point investigation and evidence. Use it to plan the visit and make sure only the client's own networks and devices are tested.

items.title: Confirm authorisation and the network list
items.body:
The engagement lead obtains the client's list of its own wireless networks and written authorisation for the sites and dates, because nearby networks belong to others and must never be tested.

  • Network names, known access point identifiers and controllers.
  • Sites, buildings and floors, and outdoor areas for leakage checks.
  • Landlord or shared-building consent where needed.

Done when: the list and the authorisation are filed, and copies travel with the tester.

items.title: Plan the visit
items.body:
The tester agrees the practical details with the site contact before travelling, so the visit runs smoothly and safely.

  • Arrival time, the reception process and an escort for restricted areas.
  • Areas and times allowed, including outside the building.
  • Equipment to be brought, declared to site security.
  • A phone number for the site contact throughout the visit.

Done when: the site contact has confirmed the visit plan.

items.title: Survey passively first
items.body:
The tester listens without connecting to anything, building a picture of the radio environment across the 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz bands.

  • All visible networks, including hidden ones, with their security modes.
  • Which networks belong to the client, matched by name and known identifiers.
  • Neighbouring networks recorded only as context, never examined further.

Done when: the survey is saved with locations and times.

items.title: Match against the authorised inventory
items.body:
The tester compares what was observed with the client's list, to find gaps in either direction.

  • Client networks on the list but not seen, and seen but not on the list.
  • Networks imitating the client's network names.
  • Unknown access points that may be connected to the client's wired network.

Done when: each discrepancy is recorded for follow-up with the client.

items.title: Review encryption and authentication modes
items.body:
For each client network, the tester records how it is secured and judges it against current good practice.

  • WPA3-Personal with SAE, WPA3-Enterprise, or WPA2 with AES.
  • WPA3 transition mode, TKIP, WEP or open networks, each noted.
  • Protected Management Frames required, optional or off.
  • Wi-Fi Protected Setup enabled or disabled.

Done when: every client network has a recorded configuration.

items.title: Review enterprise authentication
items.body:
For 802.1X networks, the tester checks that users' credentials are only ever presented to the genuine authentication server.

  • EAP methods in use: certificate-based EAP-TLS, or password-based methods such as PEAP.
  • Client devices validate the server certificate, its issuer and its name.
  • Users cannot accept an unknown certificate when prompted.

Done when: results are recorded for each enterprise network and each managed device type.

items.title: Assess shared keys and guest access
items.body:
The tester reviews networks that use a shared key or serve guests, as agreed in the rules of engagement.

  • Key length and complexity, how the key is shared and whether it changes when staff leave.
  • The guest portal, terms of use and time limits.
  • Guest isolation from corporate networks, and between guest devices.

Done when: results are recorded for each shared-key and guest network.

items.title: Check segmentation from each network
items.body:
Using the authorised credentials for each network, the tester checks what a connected device can reach.

  • Corporate, server and management networks reachable from guest or device networks.
  • Management interfaces of controllers and access points.
  • Client isolation within each network.

Done when: reachability from each network is recorded with evidence.

items.title: Investigate rogue devices
items.body:
For each suspected rogue access point, the tester gathers what the client needs to deal with it, without disconnecting or interfering with it.

  • Locate it by signal strength and photograph where it is.
  • With the client's network team, check whether it connects to the wired network.
  • Report it to the client contact on the same day.

Done when: each suspected rogue is located, or recorded as not found.

items.title: Measure signal leakage
items.body:
The tester records how far the client's networks reach beyond its premises, where anyone could pick them up.

  • Signal readings at the perimeter, in car parks and streets, and in shared areas.
  • Readings marked on a site plan, with times.
  • A comparison with what the business needs.

Done when: leakage readings are recorded for each site.

items.title: Record evidence and leave cleanly
items.body:
The tester finishes the visit by securing the evidence and leaving nothing behind.

  • Screenshots and exports with time, location, network name and identifier.
  • Delete captured traffic not needed as evidence, as it may hold staff or neighbours' data.
  • Collect all equipment, sign out and tell the site contact the visit has ended.

Done when: the evidence is in the engagement store and the client knows the visit is over.

run_phishing_campaign_v1.name: Running an authorised phishing campaign
run_phishing_campaign_v1.description: Runbook for planning, running and reporting an authorised phishing simulation that measures reporting as well as clicks and harms no one. Use it from the first approvals to the no-blame debrief; it covers process only, not how to build lures or infrastructure.

items.title: Get the approvals
items.body:
The engagement lead obtains written authorisation from a sponsor with authority over the staff and systems involved, and confirms HR and legal have agreed. The NCSC notes that simulations carry legal risk, especially where staff could be penalised for clicking.

  • HR and legal sign-off, and any staff representative body consulted.
  • The client's IT and security leads informed.

Done when: signed authorisation and HR and legal approval are on file.

items.title: Complete a privacy review
items.body:
The engagement lead and the client review the personal data the campaign will process before any is collected. The client decides the lawful basis and whether a data protection impact assessment is needed.

  • Collect only names, work addresses and interaction events.
  • Never store passwords or other values that staff type in.
  • Agree retention, the deletion date and who sees results.

Done when: the privacy review is recorded and approved by the client.

items.title: Agree objectives and measures
items.body:
The engagement lead agrees with the client what the campaign is for and how success is measured, so the results drive improvement rather than blame.

  • Reports to the security team, and time to the first report, as headline measures.
  • Clicks and submissions as supporting measures.
  • Results by team or site, never by named individual.

Done when: objectives and measures are recorded in the engagement file.

items.title: Approve the pretexts
items.body:
The sponsor and HR approve each pretext and landing page in writing before it is used.

  • No distressing themes, such as pay, redundancy, health, bereavement or discipline.
  • No impersonation of a real organisation or brand without its agreement.
  • No offers of money, prizes or benefits.
  • A copy of every approved message and page kept on file.

Done when: every pretext has written approval on file.

items.title: Approve the target list
items.body:
The client supplies and approves the list of recipients. The firm does not build the list from public sources unless that is an agreed objective.

  • Only the client's own domains and work addresses.
  • Exclusions for people on leave, recently bereaved, unwell or under investigation, and anyone else the client names.
  • A named approver for the final list.

Done when: the approved list and its exclusions are filed.

items.title: Agree sending windows and coordination
items.body:
The engagement lead agrees when messages go out and who at the client knows about the campaign.

  • Staggered sends within working hours, avoiding the client's peak periods.
  • Mail and security teams told, or not, according to the objectives, with any filtering exceptions recorded.
  • A test send to approved recipients before launch.

Done when: the schedule is approved and the test send has worked end to end.

items.title: Monitor the campaign live
items.body:
A named campaign owner at the firm watches the campaign throughout each sending window and stays reachable by the client contact.

  • Delivery, reports and the security team's response.
  • Messages forwarded outside the approved list.
  • Technical faults and anything behaving unexpectedly.

Done when: each sending window has been monitored and notable events are logged.

items.title: Stop when a stop condition is met
items.body:
The campaign owner stops sending and disables links at once if a stop condition is met, then tells the client contact.

  • Messages reach people outside the approved list or outside the organisation.
  • The client, HR or legal asks for a stop.
  • Staff distress, complaints or media attention.
  • A real incident at the client, or data collected beyond what was agreed.

Done when: the stop time, the reason and the client notification are logged.

items.title: Handle replies and reports
items.body:
The campaign owner handles replies and reports through the agreed route, so staff are supported and nobody is drawn into a conversation with the test.

  • Staff who report the message get the client's normal positive acknowledgement.
  • Replies and worried staff are passed to the client contact.
  • Concerns are acknowledged on the same day.

Done when: every reply and concern has been routed and logged.

items.title: Measure without keeping credentials
items.body:
The campaign owner records only that events happened, never what was entered, and checks this both before launch and at the end.

  • Event type and time for each pseudonymised recipient.
  • Typed values discarded on receipt and absent from all logs.
  • Results aggregated by team or site.

Done when: results are aggregated and a check has confirmed no credentials were kept.

items.title: Debrief without blame
items.body:
The engagement lead reports at the level of teams, processes and controls, and presents reporting behaviour alongside clicks.

  • How quickly staff reported, and how the security team responded.
  • Technical controls observed, such as filtering, DMARC and MFA.
  • Recommendations for making reporting quick and easy.
  • No individual named for discipline.

Done when: the debrief is held and the report has passed review.

items.title: Close down and delete data
items.body:
The engagement lead closes the campaign completely and confirms it to the client in writing.

  • Take down sending domains, landing pages and accounts used for the campaign.
  • Delete campaign data on the agreed date.
  • Offer the client a supportive message to staff explaining the exercise.

Done when: the client has written confirmation of close-down and data deletion.

run_physical_assessment_v1.name: Running an authorised physical assessment
run_physical_assessment_v1.description: Runbook for planning and running an authorised physical security assessment safely, from the authorisation letter to the debrief. Use it for every site visit; it covers conduct and process only, not techniques for defeating locks, badges or alarms.

items.title: Confirm authority for every site
items.body:
The engagement lead obtains written authorisation from someone with authority over each site, plus consent from any landlord, managing agent or security contractor where the client does not control the premises.

  • Sites, buildings, floors and areas in scope, with dates and times.
  • Prohibited actions, such as forced entry, damage, and entering hazardous or excluded areas.
  • Approved objectives, such as reaching a named room.

Done when: authorisation and consents for every site are filed.

items.title: Prepare the authorisation letter
items.body:
The engagement lead prepares a letter for each tester to carry, so anyone who stops them can verify the test quickly.

  • Signed by the authoriser, naming each tester, the sites and the dates.
  • At least two verification contacts at the client, reachable throughout the testing window.
  • Each tester carries the letter and photo ID.
  • The verification contacts hold the tester list.

Done when: letters are issued and the verification contacts have been test-called.

items.title: Plan for safety
items.body:
The engagement lead completes a risk assessment for each visit, because people's safety comes before any objective.

  • Testers work in pairs, or with a remote colleague on scheduled check-ins.
  • Site hazards, such as roofs, construction areas and machinery, are excluded.
  • Out-of-hours visits have extra controls.
  • Emergency numbers and first aid arrangements are known to everyone.

Done when: the risk assessment is approved and shared with the team.

items.title: Agree the stop and challenge procedure
items.body:
The team agrees in advance exactly what happens if a tester is challenged, stopped or detained.

  • Stay calm and comply; never run, resist or argue.
  • Say you are a tester and show the letter if the situation escalates, or when security staff or police ask.
  • Ask for a verification contact to be called.
  • Whether local police are told beforehand is the client's decision.

Done when: every tester can state the procedure from memory.

items.title: Brief the team and the client
items.body:
Before each visit, the engagement lead briefs the testers and the small group of client staff who know about the test.

  • Objectives, approved routes, prohibited areas, roles and timings.
  • How the client's security control room will confirm the test if it raises an alarm.
  • How testers and the engagement lead stay in contact throughout.

Done when: the brief has been held and recorded.

items.title: Conduct yourself properly on site
items.body:
Testers behave professionally throughout and keep strictly to the agreed scope.

  • Cause no damage, and never interfere with safety equipment or fire exits.
  • Do not touch personal belongings, or read personal data beyond noting that it is exposed.
  • Treat staff and members of the public with courtesy.
  • Leave if anyone's safety is at risk.

Done when: the visit ends with no conduct issues, or any issue is logged.

items.title: Capture evidence proportionately
items.body:
Testers record enough to support the report without capturing more than is needed.

  • Timestamped photographs of access points, exposures and markers.
  • Faces of staff and the public avoided where possible.
  • Notes of times and locations, and of who challenged and when.
  • A log of items taken and markers left.

Done when: the evidence log matches the visit timeline.

items.title: Stop when a stop condition is met
items.body:
Testers stop at once and contact the engagement lead if a stop condition is met, whatever progress has been made.

  • An injury, a safety hazard or damage.
  • Police attend, or a real security incident occurs.
  • A member of staff or the public becomes distressed.
  • The client asks for a stop.

Done when: testing has stopped, the verification contact has been told and the reason is logged.

items.title: Account for items and leave cleanly
items.body:
Before leaving, testers account for everything taken or left, and tell the client the visit is over.

  • Retrieve markers, or report exactly where they are.
  • Return any items taken as proof, and any visitor passes.
  • Sign out where the site requires it.

Done when: every item is accounted for and the client knows testing has ended.

items.title: Debrief the client
items.body:
The engagement lead holds a short debrief with the client contact on the same day, then reports in full.

  • What was achieved, set against a timeline of detection and response.
  • Good challenges by staff recognised, with no one named for discipline.
  • Recommendations on controls, procedures and training.
  • Evidence stored encrypted and deleted on the agreed date.

Done when: the debrief is held and its notes are filed.

run_red_team_ops_v1.name: Running a red team operation
run_red_team_ops_v1.description: Runbook for running a red team operation under white team control, from deconfliction and risk management to closure with the blue team. Use it for intelligence-led and objective-based operations; it covers process only, not tradecraft.

items.title: Stand up the white team
items.body:
The client sponsor forms a small white team that knows about the operation and controls it (CBEST calls this the Control Group). The blue team is not told.

  • A white team lead with authority to pause or stop the operation.
  • A few trusted agents, and the firm's red team lead.
  • Confidentiality agreed by everyone involved.
  • A contact sheet reachable at all hours during the operation.

Done when: white team members, roles and contacts are recorded.

items.title: Agree objectives and flags
items.body:
The white team and the red team lead agree what the operation sets out to show, based on threat intelligence or scenarios the client has chosen.

  • Objectives tied to realistic threats against important business services.
  • Flags defined as verifiable proof, such as a marker file on a named system.
  • A test plan approved by the white team, and by the regulator where one is involved.

Done when: the approved test plan is filed.

items.title: Set the risk management plan
items.body:
The white team owns a risk assessment, completed before the operation starts and kept current throughout. It sets out what must never happen.

  • Systems and services that must not be affected.
  • Prohibited actions, such as destructive changes, denial of service and removal of real sensitive data.
  • Limits on social engineering and physical activity.
  • Who can approve exceptions.

Done when: the white team has approved the risk management plan.

items.title: Agree deconfliction
items.body:
The white team lead and the red team lead agree how to tell red team activity from a real attack quickly, so real response effort is not wasted and real threats are not missed.

  • The red team shares its infrastructure, accounts and activity times with the white team lead only.
  • A target time to check an alert, such as 30 minutes.
  • Rules that stop a detection being escalated to police or regulators before it is checked.

Done when: the deconfliction process is written down and has been tested.

items.title: Define stop conditions
items.body:
The white team and the red team agree the conditions that pause or end the operation at once. In CBEST, the Control Group can order a temporary halt.

  • Signs of a real attacker in the environment.
  • Impact on operations or on safety.
  • Reaching third-party systems or highly sensitive data.
  • A legal concern, or a request from the white team.

Done when: the stop conditions and the halt procedure are written into the plan.

items.title: Run the operation within the plan
items.body:
The red team works within the approved plan. Any change of approach or target needs the white team's approval first.

  • Request leg-ups through the white team and record the reason; in CBEST they are agreed with the regulator and recorded in the report.
  • Escalate critical vulnerabilities to the white team.
  • Pause whenever a stop condition is met.

Done when: the active phase ends on its planned date, or at an earlier point the white team approves.

items.title: Update the white team daily
items.body:
The red team lead gives the white team lead a short update on every operating day, plus a fuller progress report at the agreed interval, which in CBEST is usually weekly.

  • Progress against objectives, and current access.
  • Planned next steps, and any new risks.
  • Detections or blue team activity observed.

Done when: each day's update is logged in the operation record.

items.title: Keep evidence and a timeline
items.body:
Each operator keeps a timestamped log of every action, which supports deconfliction during the operation, the report and the replay.

  • Time, source, target, action and outcome, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques.
  • Infrastructure used, and accounts and files created.
  • Evidence for each flag, stored encrypted.

Done when: the timeline is complete for the whole operation.

items.title: Close the active phase safely
items.body:
At the end of the active phase, the red team stops all activity, removes what it placed and confirms this with the white team.

  • Remove access mechanisms, accounts, files and scheduled tasks created during the operation.
  • Take down the operation's infrastructure.
  • List anything that could not be removed, for the client to deal with.

Done when: the white team has confirmed the clean-up in writing.

items.title: Reveal and replay with the blue team
items.body:
The white team tells the blue team about the operation, then the red and blue teams walk through the timeline together so defenders can learn from it.

  • Step through each action, comparing it with what the blue team saw and did.
  • Identify missed detections and slow responses.
  • Run joint sessions to test improved detections.

Done when: the replay has been held and its findings are recorded.

items.title: Report and agree remediation
items.body:
The red team lead delivers a report the white team can act on, and the client agrees a remediation plan. In CBEST, the Control Group drafts the plan and the regulator reviews it.

  • Attack paths, objectives reached and the full timeline.
  • The weaknesses behind each step, and the detection opportunities.
  • Owners and dates for each remediation action, plus lessons on how the operation ran.

Done when: the report is delivered and the remediation plan is agreed.
